# Kuvo Link

The GPUI desktop reaches its local box over loopback HTTP and other boxes over
paired relay or SSH. Boxes also exchange end-to-end encrypted peer mail. The
relay forwards ciphertext and keeps setup leases. See [How Kuvo works](../docs/architecture/how-kuvo-works.md).

The box host is TypeScript in `box/src`. `scripts/build-box.sh` writes the
link to `swift/KuvoLink/Sources/KuvoLink/Resources/kuvo-link.js`. The generated
asset's path has historical naming. The desktop client is in `gpui/kuvo_box`.
Shared wire fixtures are under `vectors/`.

The Swift desktop and iPhone apps are retired. Installed-client compatibility
keeps their wire fields, signed device records, legacy Mac callbacks and APNs
support. The names `phone`, `phones` and `host` below also occur on that wire.

## Keys and addresses

Each device (a phone, a Mac, a machine) has:

- a **static key**, an X25519 key pair, which identifies it to the devices it's paired with;
- a **relay secret**, 32 random bytes, which it shows only to the relay.

Its **address** is the first 16 bytes of `SHA-256("kuvo-link address v1" || secret)`. The
relay checks a connection's secret against the address it claims, so address verification needs no account database. Only the device itself can receive what's sent to its address.

In text (links, JSON) keys, secrets, addresses and tokens are base64url without padding.

## Format versions during an update

A computer's Kuvo folder carries one layout version in `folder-version.json`. An absent
file denotes layout 0. The startup gate refuses a future version or a migration in progress
to a future version before opening the folder for writes. The ordered steps checkpoint
their in-progress and completed versions in the same atomic file. Layout 1 adopts the
deployed layout in place. During a legacy Mac move, that step imports the earlier app's
data into staging, and rehome publishes the checkpoint with the imported files.

Existing family markers validate their own contents. An absent JSON format marker denotes the pre-marker layout (version 0). The link state
(`run/link.json`) and Work Queue number ledger (`run/work-queue/numbers.json`) now write
`formatVersion: 1` beside their existing fields. Readers upgrade old files in memory and persist
the version with a normal atomic write. The ledger commits it under the writer lock. Work Queue
owner files, labels, handoff and forwarded action receipts use additive version 1. Setup cards,
welcome files, move journals and manifests, and server and bridge rendezvous records also add
version 1 beside their existing fields. Conversation queue entries and waiting payloads use
additive version 1. The artifact index and vault activity log mark each JSON line, including
compacted lines. The managed accounts and rehome folder arrays have a header entry that the
legacy readers filter out. The signed vault pause envelope uses its existing v2 marker.
Insights adopts its existing database as SQLite `user_version = 1` in the same transaction as its
schema step. These readers report unsupported versions before writing any replacement.

For authenticated box-to-box mail, the v1 Noise prologue stays the same. The JSON inside now
includes `formatVersion: 1`. An absent field is the original body, which has the same payload
shape. A box ignores an unsupported explicit version before dispatch, without acknowledging the
mail, and logs the refusal. The signed document's `v` still applies to its signed bytes.

The desktop writes `x-kuvo-route-version: 1` on routed HTTP, relay and SSH requests. If the header is absent,
the original route body shapes apply. Routed replies advertise version 1 in the response
headers (`routeVersion: "1"` in a `box route` reply over SSH). An unsupported explicit request
gets HTTP 400 and `code: "unsupportedFormatVersion"` before dispatch. An unsupported stored
format found before the reply starts gets HTTP 409 with the same code and the format name.
The desktop accepts legacy replies with no marker and declines an explicit unknown version. Route features still
govern whether a route exists. Socket handshakes and upstream protocols retain their own rules.

A layout change adds a tested, replayable folder step from n to n+1. Layout 1 preserves
the existing files so pre-marker builds can still use them during rollback. A future
incompatible layout requires stopping older writers and a compatible rollback plan.
Computers in an updating fleet continue to exchange messages using their wire versions. See the format inventory in
`.claude/notes/848-U-versions-inventory.md`.

## The relay

One WebSocket per device, binary messages, first byte the kind. Opcodes `0x04`–`0x06` are retained APNs compatibility.

| Kind | From | Bytes | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `0x01` hello | device | `secret(32)` | Must come first. A second connection with the same address replaces the first (closed with 4002). |
| `0x01` welcome | relay | `address(16)` | The secret was fine; this is your address. |
| `0x02` send | device | `to(16) payload` | Pass `payload` to the device at `to`. |
| `0x02` deliver | relay | `from(16) payload` | Something sent to you. |
| `0x03` unreachable | relay | `to(16)` | Nothing is connected at `to`; what you sent is dropped. |
| `0x04` register | phone | JSON | `{"token", "environment": "sandbox"\|"production", "topic", "senders": [address]}`: send pushes to this APNs token, only from these addresses. Kept for 90 days; the phone sends it again whenever it connects. |
| `0x05` push | host | `to(16) payload` | Push `payload` (a mail frame, below) to `to`'s phone. |
| `0x06` pushed | relay | `to(16) status(1)` | 0 sent, 1 no phone registered, 2 not one of its senders, 3 Apple refused. |
| `0x07` gone | relay | `address(16) reason(1)` | The device at `address`, which you sent something to on its current connection, has a new connection (0, replaced) or none (1, left; any other reason reads as left). Whatever sessions you had with it are over. |

Known kinds keep their lengths, and a device skips a kind it doesn't know once it's welcomed, so a
new kind goes only after welcome. A device never sends `0x07`. The relay handles a connection's
sends in the order they come, and what it sends back for them comes in that same order, as one
stream: each `unreachable`, and each `deliver` of a send to the connection's own address. Boxes
rely on it to tell a start the relay dropped from one that got there ("Starts", Sender side), so a
relay that answers sends to your own address ahead of `unreachable`s for sends before them could
have a start that got there said not to have started.

**Gone.** The relay keeps, for each connection, the devices that sent it something on that connection
(at most 1,024) and the connections it sent to (at most 256); past either, nothing more is recorded.
A connection's own sends to its address (a bridge checking its connection) and sends that come back
unreachable record nothing. When a connection stops being the one at its address (a hello with the
same address replaces it, or it closes), each device it recorded hears `gone` once, and both lists
are cleared: a device is recorded again only by sending again. `gone` isn't queued or repeated: a
device that wasn't connected misses it, and needs no repeat, because losing its own relay connection
ends all its sessions anyway. What a replaced connection still sends as it closes is dropped, so no
frame from the old connection follows a `gone`. The relay sends every `gone` for a hello before it
reads anything from the new connection, so a device hears `gone` before anything the new connection
sends. A device ends its sessions with that address: a phone's streams fail (replaced is "closed",
left is "offline"), and a handshake still on its way starts over under a new session number, since it
may have reached the new connection. A host drops that phone's sessions, as on `unreachable`. A
connection that dies without closing stays listed until the relay's pings notice, up to about a
minute, which is why a phone still checks on a request that goes unanswered (below).

**A host never forgets a session while its relay connection stays up.** It ends one only with the
phone told (a close), or by the phone's own doing (a close, a new handshake from the same phone, the
phone unreachable or gone). A host's sessions end with its relay connection, which the relay tells
the phones about. Phones count on this, and don't check a quiet session before sending on it: a frame
that comes on a session the host doesn't have is answered with a close all the same.

**Historical deployment.** The relay that sends `gone` preceded phone builds that understood it. Behind a relay from before it, such a phone still works but isn't told: a stream that
only listens doesn't end when its host starts again, and the first request after a host restart fails
once with "closed" (the host closes the session it doesn't know), the next one opening a new session.
Older phones keep checking quiet sessions, and skip `gone`.

`payload` is at most 65,600 bytes. The relay closes a connection that sends anything else
(4000), a wrong secret (4001), far too much too fast (4003), or one too many from the same
IP address (4005). A device a little too fast, or sending faster than the one it sends to
takes in, is held back: the relay stops reading from it for a moment.

The phone pings the relay over its WebSocket every 25 s, and counts the connection as gone (closes
it, and connects again) when the pong doesn't come back in 10 s and a second more for each 64 KB it
has handed its WebSocket since the last ping that was answered, a minute more at most: the ping goes
out behind those, and a picture on a slow connection holds its pong up as long as it takes to send
(#144), while a path gone dead behind a big body is still noticed within about 70 s.

A client also keeps its own pong to the relay's ping from waiting behind a body: a relay from before
the change below ends a connection whose pong is about a minute late (kuvolink.porigam.com.tr did on
2026-11-16), and a picture on a slow connection takes longer than that to go. The desktop app hands its socket one relay message at a time, reading what came in
between, with its system send buffer set to 256 KB (a Mac's grows to 4 MB), so its pong goes within
seconds whatever it's sending.

The relay counts a device as there while it answers its pings or sends anything: a phone sending a
picture on a slow connection has its pong behind it, later than the relay's next ping (#144).
**Historical deployment:** that relay went out with or before the phone build that sends messages again.
Behind a relay from before it, a big picture on a slow connection is still cut off there, and goes
again from the start each time, until its two minutes are up.

An APNs push carries `{"aps": {"alert": {"title": "Kuvo Code", "body": "New activity"},
"mutable-content": 1}, "f": "<sender's address>", "k": "<payload, base64>"}`. The phone's
notification extension decrypts `k` with the key of the host at `f`, and replaces the text,
the category (for its buttons) and the thread.

## Link frames

What one device sends another, inside the relay's `payload`:

```
kind(1) session(4) body
```

`session` is a random number the client picks for each session, so frames from an older one
can't be confused with a newer one.

| Kind | Body |
| --- | --- |
| `0x01` | Handshake message 1, client to host |
| `0x02` | Handshake message 2, host to client |
| `0x03` | A transport message: one encrypted message (below) |
| `0x04` | Close: no body. Either side stops the session. |
| `0x05` | Mail: one message, encrypted for a device that may not be connected (`session` is 0) |

## Sessions

Sessions use **Noise_IK_25519_AESGCM_SHA256** ([the Noise protocol](https://noiseprotocol.org/noise.html)),
with the prologue `kuvo-link v1`. The paired client starts with the box's static key. The box checks the client's key in the first message.

The first message's payload is JSON:

```json
{"v": 1, "name": "My Desktop", "app": "<version>", "client": "desktop"}
```

`pair` is there only while pairing. `client` (`clients.kind`) says what the client is: `desktop`
for Kuvo Code's desktop app, which reaches each of your computers' boxes as a paired device of its
own ("Paired phones", `kuvo/devices/pair`); left out, or anything else, it's a phone. A desktop
client is a remote client like a phone for everything it may do (never the app on the box's own
computer); the one difference is that what it sends a conversation isn't marked as a phone's (no
`<from-phone>` block, "A message's parts"), so a phone that says `desktop` only loses that note.
Paired by token, what it said is kept with its pairing. The host answers if the client's key is one
it has paired, or if `pair` is the token it's showing; otherwise it sends a close. Its answer's
payload:

```json
{"v": 1, "kind": "mac", "name": "My MacBook", "app": "0.4.0", "engine": "2.0.30"}
```

`kind` is `mac` or `machine`. Each side checks `v` and closes the session on a version it
doesn't know.

For legacy setups, if pairing by token is waiting for a standby-backed save, the authenticated second message includes
`waiting` and `save`. The box opens no session. The client retries with `save` in the first
message, using the same static key and addressing the setup's current primary. The signed proof
binds the operation to the device key and the pairing it created. A committed save opens a
session only while that exact pairing is still valid. The second message carries the updated
receipt; a pending, interrupted or no-longer-valid pairing carries `waiting` and opens no session.

Transport messages then go both ways, in order (the relay keeps the order of one
connection). Any message that doesn't decrypt ends the session.

**Historical reach behavior** (#443, `Reach` in the retired KuvoClient). With the line (below,
"The line"), its silence alone says a computer isn't connected: 30 s without a line or a beat.
What follows is for a computer with nothing followed on it. A computer under
a heavy load answers late and drops its link now and then, and is still there. Its event feed
down, a client says nothing for 10 s (at most that what's on screen is being read again); then it
checks (`kuvo/info`, or the engine's `api/info` through a tunnel) and only a check with no answer
within 30 s (or one that finds no engine there) makes it "isn't connected". A check that answers
keeps it in reach, checked again 10 s later while the feed stays down. A request isn't given up on
while the computer is there (the phone's waits up to 10 minutes with nothing back; the link's own
checks fail what's on a session that's gone), and a read that fails because the link went is read
again, not shown as a failure.

### The line

Feature `line`. A client opens one stream to each box, and everything it follows there comes on it (docs/architecture/message-delivery.md, rule 2).

- `GET kuvo/line?watch=<topics>[&line=<id>&after=<n>][&once=1]` opens it. `watch` is base64url JSON, `{name: route}`. Each route is one the box already follows: a list's `…/events` (one JSON state a line) or a conversation's events (`api/event`, `kuvo/agents/api/event`). The box runs each topic through its own routes, as the asker of the line, so a topic is allowed exactly what its route is.
- `POST kuvo/line/watch` `{line, watch}` changes the topics of an open line. It answers `{line}` at once. A `404 {fresh: true}` means the box doesn't know the line, so open it again with every topic.
- **What comes on it**, one JSON object a line:
  - first `{hello: {line, fresh, beat}}`;
  - then `{t, n, d}`: what topic `t` said. `d` is a state, or one event;
  - `{t, n, refused: {status, message, said?}}`: the box turned the topic down. After a 4xx the topic ends. After a 5xx the box tries it again by itself;
  - `{t, n, gap: true}`: an event topic's source dropped, went quiet for a minute, or wasn't ready. Read what it's of again;
  - `{beat}` every `beat` ms while it's quiet. A beat has no `n`.
- **Resuming.** `n` counts each line on the line. Reopen with the same `line` and the last `n` you got as `after`. If the box still keeps them (4 MB, for 2 minutes after the stream drops, with its topics still running), it sends every line after `after`, then the live ones, with `fresh: false`. Otherwise it answers `fresh: true` with a new id, and each topic starts over from its state now. A client takes that as a snapshot, and reads again what an event topic is of.
- **Once.** A box reached in a way that can't keep a stream (a one-shot `box route`) is asked with `once=1`. It answers the hello and each topic's state now, then ends. Ask again every few seconds.
- **Offline.** A client counts a computer as away only once its line has been silent for 30 s. With nothing heard for 15 s, it reopens the line. A slow or failed request never makes a computer away, and a dropped stream is never shown: each view keeps the last state it received.


#### Setup-wide list topics

Feature `line.setup-lists`. Follow these routes on the nearest box's `kuvo/line`. Each topic
sends a whole replacement snapshot. An older box can still be read on its original per-computer
routes.

| Topic route | State |
| --- | --- |
| `kuvo/setup/sessions/events` | `{sessions, projects}`. Sessions have `id` and the usual session-list `facts`. Projects have `directory` and the usual listed project `facts`. Project paths and pages belong to the project's computer. |
| `kuvo/setup/waiting/events` | `{waiting}`. Each row gives `session`, `since` (ms), optional `title` and `asks: {kind, summary}` for the conversation's oldest ask. Its complete cards and replies use the owning box's `kuvo/sessions/<id>/asks` routes. |
| `kuvo/setup/queues/events` | `{queues}`. Each row gives `session` and its `queue`, the same held or paused queue overview as `kuvo/sessions/queues/events`. |
| `kuvo/setup/runs-on/events` | `{computers}`. Each choice gives `computer`, `offered` (models and provider names in the form of `kuvo/models/offered`), and `agents` (available coding agents as `{id, name}`). Away computers are omitted. For folder-specific models, ask `kuvo/models/offered?folder=…` on the chosen computer. `offered.known` says which catalogs were readable. |

Each session, project, waiting and queue row has `computer: {id, name}` and `away`. Use the
public box key in `computer.id` to address its routes. The local box uses `here` while it has
no peer identity. Key rows by computer and row ID. An away row includes `lastSeen`, the time
in milliseconds when the receiving box last received its snapshot.

Session, waiting and queue rows carry `actions` with available controls. Away rows have empty
actions. On sessions, `open` opens the conversation and `manage` opens its owner-provided
`…/actions` menu. On waiting rows, `review` opens the owner's asks. Queue rows offer `open`
to open the conversation, `pause` or `resume` for the box's `…/queue/hold` or `…/queue/resume`,
and `messages` for the per-session queue. The owning box validates each action when asked.

For **Runs on**, address `POST kuvo/sessions` to the chosen box by the usual local, paired
relay or addressed SSH route. Pass its public ID as `computer` alongside the ordinary start
fields. A successful response echoes the destination as `computer: {id, name}`. The wrong
box returns `409` before creating anything. A local start can omit `computer` or use `here`.


#### Opening a conversation through another box

Feature `line.peer-conversation`. A bot's existing `session` is the ID of its conversation.
On the nearest box, use `kuvo/peer-session/<computer>/<session>/<resource>` as a GET or a line
topic, where the computer is the owning box's ID. Use the bot's home computer or the session
row's `computer.id`.

- `session` and `messages` return the owner's session and message page. The page takes the
  usual message query.
- `events` streams that conversation's live events. The owner chooses the runtime and filters
  the feed by session. The line's usual gap rule applies after a source drops.
- `queue` and `asks` give their current state. Follow `queue/events` and `asks/events` on the
  same line. Queue and ask actions use the owning box's existing addressed routes.

Send ordinary messages through the nearest box with
`POST kuvo/data/messages?session=<session>&computer=<computer>` and the usual stable message ID.
The nearest box keeps its receipt and the owner delivers it. The setup list can identify the
owner even when its agents announcement omitted the session.

## Mail

Pushes and other messages for a device that may not be connected use
**Noise_K_25519_AESGCM_SHA256** (both static keys known), with the prologue
`kuvo-link mail v1`: one handshake message carrying the payload. A host's push carries a
notification, below.

A host mails another host the same way, with a relay `send` of a mail frame (`kind` 5, session
0): what your computers share goes as signed documents ("Documents"), and peers mail each other
their agents and letters ("Peers").

### Documents

The signed document exchange includes four original document kinds: which computers a primary enrolled (`peers`), the phones
each box pairs and removes (`phones`), each box's view of your personalities
(`personalities`), and changes to setup authority (`leadership`). Each origin signs its own; any box passes a copy on; no clock decides anything.

- **Keys**: each box and Mac has a signing key (Ed25519) beside its static key: a Mac in its
  Keychain (`sign`), a machine in `run/link.json` (`sign`, the 32-byte seed), made with its other
  keys. A document's origin is that key's public half. Trust comes from SSH: setup gives the
  member the primary's (`macSign`) and its answer gives the primary the member's (`sign`). The
  primary's peers document names each box with both its keys, so members learn each other's from a
  document they already verify. A box made anew (its folder gone) is a new origin. The next SSH setup
  names it.
- **Format**: `{"d": <bytes>, "s": <signature>}`, base64url without padding. The bytes are JSON,
  `{"v": 1, "kind", "origin", "n", "body"}`, as the origin wrote them, and the signature is over
  `"kuvo-link doc v1\0"` and the bytes. A box checks the signature before it reads them, and keeps
  and passes on the bytes as they are, so no one needs a canonical JSON. `n` is the version, a
  whole number from 1 to 2^53−1, one more with each change. A document is at most 512 KB of
  bytes. Held to `vectors/docs.json` (KuvoLink's `Documents`, the bridge's `readDoc`).
- **Taken**: a box takes a document that verifies, from an origin it takes that kind from, newer
  than the one it has; at the same version, the one whose bytes' hash sorts first, so every box
  keeps the same one. One of its own further on than it knew (it lost count), by a document or a
  digest, moves its count past it, up to 2^52 (one claiming more isn't taken). It takes `peers`
  from its setup's main computer and from its own Macs (those in `macSigns`, given in setup: each
  is yours, #783), never at a lower epoch of the setup it keeps
  ("Your setup"); `phones` and
  `personalities` from those Macs, from its peers and from itself. Documents from an origin it no
  longer takes them from go.
- **`peers`**, one per primary (and per legacy Mac enroller): `{boxes: [{key, sign, address, name,
  kind: "mac"|"machine", id?}], moved: [{session, key}], left: [key], setup?: {id, epoch, primary}}`:
  the primary itself and its signed members, the same document for all of them, and the setup it
  leads ("Your setup"). Each box leaves itself out when it builds its list of peers. `left` names
  the computers the primary removed. A box that finds itself there and no longer among `boxes`
  drops that enroller, as `leave` does. The primary mails the document to the member it removes.
- **Legacy Mac front** keeps the app-owned Mac’s side (bridge 0.9.62): it signs the Mac's documents with the
  Mac's signing key (from the app, in memory only), takes its machines' and passes them on, and
  mails them on its relay connection, as a machine's bridge does; its peers are the machines its
  app set up (`kuvo/link/peers`, "This Mac's box: the relay"). It takes `peers` only of its own (a
  copy it lost count of), and `phones` and `personalities` from its machines and itself.
- **`phones`** carries `{setup?, phones: [{key, name, address?, pairing, kind?}], removed: [{key, pairing}]}`.
  When the issuer has a setup, the signed `setup` field names its ID. A reader that knows an
  issuer has led another setup requires this field to distinguish old lists from current ones.
  A removal targets one pairing generation.
  Managed setups publish the primary's device grants for compatibility. A checkpointed box uses
  accepted membership and access as its authority. `kind: "desktop"` identifies the desktop app
  in client lists. The inbound switch leaves signed grants and removals available to peers.
  Older setups still read signed phone lists from their enrollers.
- **`personalities`**, each box's view: the library (`{personalities, removed}`, "Personalities").
  A box meets a view it takes with its own, and signs its own again if it changed; views aren't
  passed on (each box's own already has what it took). Its own goes past 512 KB never: a change
  that would take it there is refused.
- **Exchange**, inside mail, as `"docs"`: `{give: [{d, s}]}`; `{part: {whole, i, of, d, s}}` for a
  document too big for one mail (40,000 characters of `d` each, `whole` the SHA-256 of all of
  `d`); `{have: [[origin, kind, n, h]], reply?}`, a digest of what the sender has (`h`, the first 8
  bytes of the bytes' SHA-256, base64url). A box sends its digest to each peer as it connects to the
  relay, and with its agents every ten minutes (so one that missed what it was given gets it then).
  To a digest, a box gives what the sender lacks or has older (of what that box would take), and,
  unless it's a `reply`, answers with its own digest, marked `reply`, when the sender has something
  newer. A document it took goes on to its other peers that would take it (not back where it came
  from, nor to its origin); one of its own that changed, to all of them. A box that would take it
  is one its setup's document, or one of its Macs', names (with its origin, for `phones` and
  `personalities`). Over SSH, setup carries the primary's documents (`docs`) and its answer carries
  the member's. A box gives documents to peers whose signing keys it knows.
- **Device authorization after reconnect.** Members request a fresh confirmation with
  `phoneSync: {id, origin}` (`id` is 16 random bytes, base64url). The primary sends the signed
  peers and phones documents and, in a checkpointed setup, the accepted shared values. It
  follows with `phoneSync: {id, list, peers, ack: true}`, with document fingerprints as `n:h`.
  Managed members wait for the primary and require checkpointed grants to match accepted
  membership. Legacy members can confirm an inherited desktop grant from a peer or use their
  cached list when every peer is unreachable. They close revoked sessions as removals arrive.
  A waiting handshake returns the pairing reason and `waiting` without opening a session.
- **Later**: each box's agents (`{"agents"}`, "Peers") are a list of its own too, still sent as
  they change and every ten minutes.

### Your setup

Your **setup** has one **main computer**, whose box signs who's in it. Every other computer is a
**member**. The setup chooses its first main computer automatically. You can choose another member
once both computers are connected. On the wire, `primary` means the main computer and `epoch` means its term.

- **The setup** has an id (`set_` and 16 random bytes, base64url) and an epoch (a whole number, one
  more with each change of authority, never lower on any box). Its main computer's peers
  document names it: `setup: {id, epoch, primary}`, `primary` the main computer's static key, which
  the document names among its `boxes` with the document's signing key ("Documents"). Both
  `mac` and `machine` can identify the primary's box.
- **Kept** in `run/link.json` as `setup: {id, epoch, primary, sign, role: "primary"|"member",
  aside?, conflict?}` (`sign`, the main computer's signing key). `aside`: kept only so a lower
  epoch of it is never taken, and followed for nothing else (its main computer stopped naming it).
  `managed: true` means the setup follows signed leadership changes, independent of legacy numbering.
- **Who leads one**: the first box you set up independently creates its setup at epoch 1. A
  standalone machine's keeper creates its local identity and setup before there is any device or
  member to reach. A new member follows the computer that enrolls it over SSH. A machine's primary
  role holds when it adds members. Legacy Mac leadership still follows "Numbers": a box its Mac
  let go waits for that Mac, and a Mac numbering through another Mac sets its setup aside until
  it leads again. A primary whose keys were made anew creates a new setup. On a later SSH setup it
  supplies its previous static keys (`replaces`) so the member lets those keys go.
- **What a box takes it from**: a member follows the setup named by the computer that enrolled it
  over SSH. When older links name several enrollers, the member keeps the setup it follows,
  or takes the setup it numbers from ("Numbers"). A setup set aside makes way for one another
  enroller leads. The primary's signing key (received over SSH) is the setup's trust root.
  The member refuses a lower epoch of the setup it keeps. If another trusted enroller offers
  the same setup at the same epoch, the member keeps its primary and records
  `conflict: {primary, epoch}`. An empty standalone machine can give up its one-computer setup
  when it joins the enroller's setup. A member drops its setup when it receives a signed removal. The primary of an active setup does
  not expire as an enroller. The SSH and stored fields named `mac`,
  `macs` and `macSigns` still carry these trust records, including for a Linux enroller.
  The discovery card is a hint and grants no trust.
- **Existing links**: boxes keep direct connections established over SSH, including links from
  older releases. Each box follows one setup. Extra computers named in old agents mail, and
  old directory and numbering flags, carry no membership. The SSH setup command refuses an
  additional setup on an account already enrolled, while reconnection and key rotation still work.

- **`POST kuvo/setup/handover {primary, epoch?}`** (`setup.handover`). An authenticated client
  can ask any member. The box forwards the request to the current primary with the setup id and
  epoch. The primary asks the chosen member to confirm the same setup and epoch by authenticated
  peer mail. Every enrolled box must already have advertised support. An offline member can catch
  up later. A target that cannot confirm leaves the old primary in charge.
  The primary returns `202 {primary, epoch}` after committing the change. Delivery may still be in
  progress. A request for the primary already in effect returns `200` with that key and epoch.
  A conflicting epoch returns `409 {message}`. Clients follow `kuvo/setup/events`.
- **Lease authority.** New setups start with a signed epoch-1 certificate and checkpoint.
  The main renews a 60-second relay lease every 10 seconds. Upon expiry, an enrolled
  always-on computer can claim immediately (other computers wait one more minute,
  and the relay observes its restart grace). The new holder signs the next epoch's
  certificate and starts with the accepted setup snapshot. The former main must
  have a fresh lease for setup-wide writes. A sole computer can save while offline.
- **Relay contract.** `POST /setup-lease` accepts `{data, signature}`, base64url.
  The Ed25519 signature covers `"kuvo-link setup lease v1\0"` and the JSON bytes.
  The request includes `{action, setup, computer, sign, at}`. The write actions
  `claim`, `renew` and `transfer` carry `term` and the number high-water mark
  `high`. Bootstrap and holder writes carry a roster of computer keys to
  signing keys. A transfer names `target`. The relay checks the signature and
  enrolled key, and returns `{lease, remaining, startsIn, takeoverIn, relayHost}`
  when it has a record. The lease names `holder`, `sign`, `term`, `expires`
  and `high`. A transfer starts at the previous lease's expiry to fence the
  old holder's cached grant. See `relay/src/leases.ts` and
  `box/src/link/setup/{relay-lease,lease,takeover}.ts`.
- **Unlinking the main.** With other members, the removal path arranges a handover
  to an eligible replacement before it unlinks. If no replacement can accept,
  the box reports the refusal. See “Computers” and `setup/removal*.ts`.
- **Release choice after handover.** Members take newer fleet releases from the certified
  primary. Same-version repair can still use copies held by peers. File permissions and OS
  approvals are enforced where the files and processes live.

- **`GET kuvo/setup`** (and `kuvo/setup/events`, a line now and one at each change), on every box,
  for every client: `{setup, epoch, standby?, primary: {key, name, kind}, you: {key, role}, computers: [{key,
  name, kind, role, app}], conflict?, startsFromOthers: {value, default}, heldBy: [key], welcomed}`. Facts only, the same on
  every box of one setup (but `welcomed`, this box's own): `kind` is `mac` for a Mac with the app (`app`), `machine` otherwise; in no
  setup, `setup`, `epoch`, `primary` and `you.role` are null and `computers` is empty.
  `startsFromOthers` is the #181 switch (not built yet): `value` as you set it (`link.json`'s
  `startsFromOthers`, `on` or `off`), or null, and `default`, what it is then: off on the main
  computer (and on a Mac in no setup), on everywhere else, so it follows the role. `heldBy` is an empty list.
  `welcomed` (`setup.welcomed`, #733): whether you've had Kuvo Code's first run with this box (each
  box its own: the desktop uses its own welcome flag first and can read this for compatibility), kept on it
  (`run/welcomed.json`), so every client of it agrees and one installed again doesn't
  welcome you again. **`POST kuvo/setup/welcomed {"welcomed": true | false}`** sets it (`false`:
  the first run is to be had again), from any client of the box, and answers `{"welcomed"}`
  (`kuvo/setup/events` says it too); `400` without a yes or no, `405` for anything but `POST`.
  A Mac moved from an earlier Kuvo Code counts as welcomed: its move writes the file ("Moving this
  Mac's box", What the move carries), so you land in your sessions, not in the first run.
  **`GET kuvo/setup/ready`** (`setup.ready`): whether a first run has anything to ask about your
  accounts on this box → `{"ready", "runs", "needsYou": [<account id>], "pending": ["engine" |
  "agents"]}`. The box decides it, so no client keeps the rule: `runs`, a model that needs an
  account runs here now, as a picker offers it (one of the engine's that isn't `free`, or any of a
  coding agent's; never one being retired, one its agent keeps out of its picker, or a Custom Auto
  list; "The models offered"); `needsYou`, the plans Accounts lists (`listed` and `plan`, and not
  `added`) whose `state` is `ended` or `problem`, the coding agents' first; `pending`, the sides
  that can't say yet (not running, not answering in time, or, the coding agents', an account
  signed in whose models are still being listed): what's said of them may change in a moment;
  `ready`, `runs` with none needing you and both sides having said their lists. Where it's `ready`,
  a client's first run passes over its accounts step and goes on to where to work; otherwise it
  shows it, and while anything is `pending` it may wait a moment and ask again. Always `200` to a
  `GET` (or `HEAD`), whatever can't be said; `405` otherwise. Read as it's asked (the accounts anew
  each time; the models as the box keeps them, read again once its engine or bridge says
  something changed), so a client asks again after a sign-in.
- **Only the primary adds computers and pairs devices** (`setup.mainOnly`). A member forwards
  the desktop app's pairing request to the primary (`kuvo/devices/pair`). A member gives pairing
  links and legacy add requests a `primary` key with a message naming that computer:
  - `POST kuvo/phones/pair`: `409 {"message": "Pair new phones from <main>.", primary}`, and
    `kuvo-link.js pair` prints those words and stops (exit 3), with no pairing made. A
    pairing link made before the box became a member pairs no one;
  - adding computers, SSH uninstall, and writing `kuvo/link/peers` go through the primary.
    `DELETE kuvo/computers/<key>` and `PATCH kuvo/computers/<key>` can be sent to any member.
    Checkpointed members also forward legacy machine deletions that carry a roster key;
  - `GET kuvo/hosts`, as a Mac answers it: the machines the document of the setup it follows names
    (itself too), each `{kind: "machine", name, address, key, relay, machine, anotherMac: false,
    removed: false}` (`machine`, the id the main computer's app knows it by), by name. Only what
    that document says: a machine it leaves out isn't listed, and `anotherMac` and `removed` are
    always false. The primary is left out because the device pairs with it. Set aside (its main
    computer leads no setup now), it lists what each of its Macs' own peers documents names, all
    yours. `503 {"message"}` before it holds that document, or while it has no relay.

  **Adding from any client** (`computers.add.from-any-client`). The existing
  `kuvo/computers/add` routes connect to the current primary, including when a client asks a
  member. SSH runs on the primary and uses its SSH configuration and keys. The primary keeps
  the attempts and answers. A phone's pairing must still be valid when the primary acts.
  Once an attempt is saved, the accepted membership and its receipt decide the result.

  **`POST kuvo/computers/add/code`** returns `201 {code, expires}` from the primary.
  The code contains the relay and the primary's public relay identity plus an opaque 192-bit
  token. Treat it as private and give it only to the installer (`sh kuvo-install join`,
  with `--app <bundle>` on macOS and the code on standard input). The primary stores the token hash in layout 19. An unused code
  expires after 15 minutes and is scoped to the issuing setup and epoch. The installer
  exchanges Noise-encrypted mail with that primary. An authenticated availability reply precedes the local enrollment
  reservation. The confirmed claim pins the new computer's
  keys and address, and a lost answer can be retried with the same code and identity for
  up to 24 hours. The primary sends its signed roster only after the membership is accepted.
  A computer already in another setup must be unlinked before joining. An unclaimed
  standalone box without members or pairings can join. Code enrollment leaves SSH
  configuration on each computer as it was.

  A rotation-capable Mac helper reserves a fresh Keychain identity for each new
  enrollment attempt. The Box retries the same rotation if its reply is lost.
  If independent work prevents the applicant from adopting the accepted roster,
  it cancels with the same code and provisional identity. The primary commits a
  revocation for the exact provisional roster entry, leaving the applicant’s
  work and credentials alone. The same cancellation can be retried after a lost
  reply. An activation acknowledgment closes cancellation after local adoption.

  **Choose sign-ins and keys** (`computers.add.credentials`, folder layout 20).
  `GET kuvo/computers/add/credentials` asks the current primary for
  `{items: [{id, kind: "key" | "sign-in", label, integration?, checked: true}], renewing, unavailable}`.
  The checklist carries names and IDs. Its default ticks are suggestions. The client sends the
  IDs the user chose as `credentials` on that add. Both `POST kuvo/computers/add` and
  `POST kuvo/computers/add/code` accept this array. An omitted or empty array copies no
  sign-ins or keys. Existing destination sign-ins and keys stay. Renewing sign-ins and
  sign-ins for integration servers stay on the source.
  A member refuses to forward an add to an older primary until the primary supports this choice.
  SSH records the selection's digest and original eligibility before writing to a fresh account.
  Before copying starts, a retry can change the selection. Once copying starts, the retry must
  use the same selection or clear the interrupted installation first. An installer code binds the
  selected values when the code is issued. The main computer keeps that copy encrypted and sends
  it after accepting the membership. Retries use that copy, even if a source value has since
  rotated. The joining computer acknowledges after saving the copy. The main computer erases
  the transfer and keeps a receipt so a lost acknowledgment can be answered again.
  A configured catalog integration is carried as its trusted configuration
  when all its keys were selected. Unlink waits for that copy to stop before clearing the
  credentials. Wipe removes the installation.

- **How a client connects.** A box's computer list can include `ssh`, possible destinations
  for the client's own SSH access. Each client keeps Auto, SSH or Relay per computer key and
  can also keep its own SSH alias for that key. Auto checks SSH and otherwise uses the relay.
  An explicit route stays on that route. A local box is reached directly. Primary and member
  roles have no bearing on this choice. A lost SSH reply to a write returns to the caller. Retryable operations reuse their original identity.

  A client over SSH runs `~/.kuvo-code/bin/kuvo-start route-to` (or `route`), its request on
  standard input. The keeper selects its own engine. GPUI retains an engine-picking
  fallback for older installs without the keeper launcher. A resident release passes
  both verbs over an owner-only socket to its shared dispatcher (`server/resident.ts`,
  `server/ssh-pipe.ts`). The selection survives a restart so a missing socket cannot
  fall back to one-shot dispatch. `route` keeps OS-account authority and its allowlist.
  `route-to` proves the addressed box and paired device in the resident process.
  Addressed SSH streams response bytes. It has no terminal socket upgrade.

  On layout 22 and later, `kuvo-link.js box route-to` accepts `{computer, hello}` on standard
  input. `computer` is the expected box public key and `hello` is the first Noise IK message
  (base64url, prologue `kuvo-ssh v1`, payload `{v: 1, client?, app?, setupProtocol?}`). The box answers with
  `{hello}`, the second Noise message with payload `{allowed}`. Both endpoints prove their
  keys and the device must be paired on the destination. The same client-version check runs
  before dispatch over either transport. An SSH update refusal puts `reason`, `title`, `message`
  and `target` in the authenticated response. After verifying a successful answer, the
  client sends `{request}`, a sealed, base64url JSON object with `method`, `path`, `headers`,
  optional `body`, `bodyText` or `bodyBase64`, and `stream`. Each envelope occupies one line.
  The paired device, request headers including idempotency keys, and route version have the
  same meaning over SSH and the relay. A client probes with `GET kuvo/info` before using a
  destination. The response includes `computer`. With `stream: true`, the response starts
  with `{status, routeVersion, computer, type}` and the body follows as it arrives. Standard
  input stays open for that stream.

- **Merging two setups** (layout 23, `setup.merge`). Choose the primary that stays. The joining
  setup's primary gives up its role and every one of its computers joins as a member. Their
  identities and data stay on their own disks. A single computer joining on its own must first
  unlink from its old setup. The SSH setup command refreshes an existing membership under that
  setup's signing key. Both setups use the same relay so their paired devices can still reach
  the computers they know.

  `POST kuvo/computers/add/merge-code {source, computer}` asks the retained setup's primary for
  a private code bound to the joining setup ID and primary key. The answer is `201 {code,
  expires}`. `GET kuvo/setup/merge` on the joining primary returns `{can, why?, pending?,
  completed?}`. A pending result gives the target setup and primary keys and the operation ID.
  `POST kuvo/setup/merge {code}` on that computer uses the encrypted installer exchange and
  returns `200 {operation, setup, primary}` once the computer has accepted its new membership.
  Retry with the same code, or send the pending operation as `resume` when requesting a new code
  from the same retained setup.

  Before sending the signed export, the joining primary fences its setup and records its departure. Legacy layouts can carry a pending predecessor receipt. The export names its roster, device grants and
  revocations, portable preferences and the Work Queue high-water mark. The destination saves
  membership, the companion values and the number reservation in one accepted operation.
  The signed acceptance travels to the joining members when they are online. It gives them the
  retained setup's trust root. They stop accepting mail from former enrollers outside that
  setup.

  The retained setup keeps its Work Queue numbers. The joining items take a newly reserved
  block from its primary and keep IDs and setup-labelled number aliases. The box rewrites
  item links and Work Queue references in item text and notes. A lookup can name an old number
  as `set_<origin>:#<number>`. `kuvo/work-queue/refs` includes the indexed historical matches
  under `aliases` even when the active number names another item. Each joining computer keeps
  its original ledger with the merge receipt. Device
  revocations defeat stale grants. Unrelated preference fields come across, conflicting
  values use the existing offline edit choices, and deletions stay deleted.

  A local migration of an older installation can use the same code exchange through
  `joinSetupMerge(code)` in the joining primary's box. Bring its setup ID, computer and signing
  identity, relay, roster, device grants and original number ledger forward before invoking
  it. Keep the owned files on their original owner or use the existing ownership transfer
  rules. The accepted merge receipt gives the migration the retained setup and primary keys.

  The main computer (a box you run alone is its own setup's) and a box in no setup (one whose Mac
  is older) pair and add as before; with the main computer's app closed, adding says to open it (`kuvo/machines`, above).
  Existing pairings stay. Pairing removes no one.
- **The card**: `run/setup-card.json`, beside link.json, nothing secret in it, for what looks at a
  computer from outside its box (the app as it opens, a Mac adding it over SSH): `{setup, epoch,
  role, primary: {key, name, heard}, self: {key, name, kind}, app, computers, items, heldBy, macs}`
  (`macs`, the Macs that set this box up, `[{key, name}]`; none on a Mac). `heard`: when
  the main computer was last heard from, as this box counts it (ms, its own time off left out, as
  for its Macs' 30 days; null on the main computer itself); `computers`, how
  many the setup has; `items`, the Work Queue items here. Written as the box looks at its setup, as
  documents change it, and by `setup` and `leave` (`kuvo/setup/events` follows those too).
- **Older boxes** read only `boxes`, `moved` and `left`, and keep taking `peers` from their Macs:
  nothing changes for them. A box that knows setups names `setup` in `features`.
- **Already in a setup?** What's on a computer is judged by a box, as one verdict, which clients
  only draw. Each box found there says what it is by its card, or, an older box with none, by a few
  fields of its link.json (its Macs, when each was last heard from, their names, whether it has
  phones; never its keys). What's found is a hint, never trusted: a lie changes a warning at most.
  Per box: `self` (the judging box itself), `ours` (in its setup, or one it or its computers set
  up, one more than one Mac set up too, unless it's in another setup now; or in a setup the judging box led
  before it made its setup anew, its card naming it main), `elsewhere` (a member of another
  setup, however long its main computer has been unheard of, or a machine only other Macs set up),
  `main` (another setup's main computer, or a Mac whose app runs it in no setup), `older` (no card,
  and a Mac set it up, it has phones, or it's Kuvo Code's own box on a Mac; or a card from before
  cards named Macs, with no link.json fields beside it: it needs an update before it can say),
  `free` (nothing, or no Mac set it up and it leads nothing). For the computer: `self` if any is;
  `free` if none is anyone's; the one box's verdict; `ours` if all are; else `two` (boxes of more
  than one setup on one computer).
  - **`POST kuvo/setup/judge {probe}`**: what a Mac adding a computer over SSH found there, as its
    probe printed it (`RemoteEngineInstaller.foundProbe`, only `sed`): for `~/.kuvo-code` and each
    `~/Library/Application Support/run.kuvo.code*/box` a box ran in (only when adding to the real
    `~/.kuvo-code`; a `~/.kuvo-code` box its Mac removed, with no `bin/kuvo-start` or with
    `run/off`, left out), `box machine|app <folder from home>`, then `card <json>`, and for link.json
    `link mac|macs <key>`, `link seen <key> <ms>`, `link name <key> <json string>`, `link phones
    none|some`; then `app <folder from home>` for each Kuvo Code app's folder there
    (`run.kuvo.code*`), whether or not a box of its own ran in it (other lines are left alone;
    `mac`, the last Mac to set it up, is named first whatever its line's place). Answers `{verdict,
    joins, boxes: [{folder, app, verdict, key, name, kind, setup, role, primary: {key, name,
    heard}, macs, computers, items}]}` (`primary` of an older box: the last Mac that set it up;
    `computers` and `items` null where its card doesn't say), judged against this box (itself, its
    setup, its peers and Macs); 400 with no `probe`, or one over 200,000 characters. `joins`:
    adding it joins its setup with nothing to ask, as another setup's main computer with no Kuvo
    Code app there (no box's card says `app`, no `app` line: a Mac's app would open as a window from
    then on, which you choose) whose setup is empty (its card says no other computer and no work
    items). For any other setup already on the SSH account, Add Computer stops and asks you to
    connect to your own OS account.

  - **`POST kuvo/setup/attached`**: Kuvo Code on this computer attached to this box in place (the
    app, once the box runs, by the box's own `bin/kuvo-link.js box route` with its own engine, as a
    Mac reaches a machine's box over SSH), from then on said on its card (`app: true`,
    `run/app-attached.json`), so Add Computer can recognize an existing desktop setup. Any `box route`
    caller may say it (the app here, a Mac over SSH, this box's own agents), and the app beside its
    own box; 403 from a phone or the relay. The attachment stays recorded.
    Answers `{}`.
  - **`kuvo-link.js here <root>`**: Kuvo Code on a Mac (the app, and its keeper), before it starts
    a box, with `KUVO_HOME` its own box's folder (in its app folder) and `root` the machines'
    folder (`.kuvo-code`, or a test's); without either (or with them the same) it stops, exit 2.
    Prints `{verdict, use: "own"|"attach", opens: "main"|"window", runs, box, own}`, `box` and
    `own` as `boxes` above. While a move of this Mac's box into `~/<root>` is unfinished (its
    journal there, "Moving this Mac's box"), `{verdict: "moving", use: "wait", opens: "main", runs:
    null, box: null, own: null}`, before anything else: no box starts until `rehome --resume`
    finishes it. `runs`, for the box in `~/<root>`: `gone` where its Mac removed it
    (`kuvo-start off` leaves `run/off`, which only a Mac's start there takes away, and then its way
    to start, `bin/kuvo-start`, goes with its keys, leaving its link.json and card: no
    `bin/kuvo-start`, or `run/off`, whatever still runs), else `running` (its keeper,
    `run/box.pid`, runs `kuvo-start` now) or `stopped`; null with none there. A Mac's own box made
    there before it first ran (`box/kind` says `mac`, no card or link.json yet) is a box there too,
    with its verdict `free` and no name: never taken for none. A `gone` box is no
    box: as with none (`box` null), and the probe leaves it out too. `opens`: `window` where the box it uses is a member
    of a setup another computer is main of (a Mac mini another Mac set up, one that can't say yet,
    the old main computer after a handover, a Mac that joined: never main by itself, only by Make
    This Mac the Main One), else `main`. An app whose own box ran (its folder has `run/`
    `setup-card.json`, `link.json`, `serve.json` or `keeper.json`, or its own engine kept your
    sessions: an `opencode*.db` in `KUVO_ENGINE_DATA`, the engine's data folder the app gives its
    box, as a version from before its box had a folder, or one that quit cleanly, leaves no record
    there; never the folder alone, which the app writes in with no box) keeps using it (`ours`,
    `free`, or `two` beside another setup's `~/.kuvo-code`); one with none uses the `~/.kuvo-code`
    box that's there, in place (`attach`: never a second box on one computer), with that box's
    verdict; with neither, its own. It writes nothing, and makes no folder. The app attached to a
    box that's `stopped` starts it again in place (by launchd, through its Mac's launch agent
    `run.kuvo.code.machine` where it's there, else its own `kuvo-start`), and says one that won't
    start so, to try again, rather than waiting on it.

### Saving setup-wide changes

The lease-holding main commits setup membership, device grants, settings,
personalities and labels. It signs and publishes a snapshot of the accepted
values. Members verify that snapshot and retain it for the next main. A member
forwards setup-wide changes to the main. An unavailable or stale authority
can keep an operation waiting or refuse it without applying an unverified
change. The sole-computer exception is described under “Your setup”.
See `box/src/link/setup/shared.ts` and `box/src/shared/data-declarations.ts`.

A deferred request keeps its operation ID and original authority. Retrying a
receipt reads or settles that operation and always checks current access.
Revocation fences further action by the old pairing. See “Authority carried
with deferred work” and “Paired phones”.

#### Legacy setup authority and receipts

The following contracts describe unconverted layouts and retained proof
readers. Current setups use the relay lease, main-only saves and the relay's
number floor.

- **Leadership record.** The outgoing primary signs a `leadership` document with `n` equal to
  the next setup epoch. The body names `setup: {id, epoch, primary}` and `previous`, and carries
  `boxes`, `moved`, `left`, `devices` (grants and removals), and `numbers`
  (the allocation counter and grant receipts). It saves the certificate and its demotion in a
  single durable `run/link.json` replacement before sending anything. The destination installs
  its primary role from that certificate and signs subsequent membership and device lists with
  its own key. After the transfer, only the primary publishes setup device grants and removals.
  A receiver takes only the next epoch of its setup. The preceding primary signs when the
  epoch has no standby. With a standby, planned transitions normally use its signing key.
  Ranked takeovers and replacing an unreachable standby use the rules below. For a planned transition the primary durably fences itself and saves its signed
  proposal in `leadershipPending` before sending. The standby signs the same body with the
  primary's detached signature in `approval`. It commits once before it replies. An interrupted
  primary resends the proposal and installs the same certificate when it hears it. The
  certificate names the next standby with `standby` (a static key in `boxes`) when one is
  appointed. The new primary's peers document repeats that key and `numberCeiling` for new
  SSH enrollments. A member that already follows the setup changes authority only through
  the certificate chain.
  At that epoch, only the certified primary's membership document counts. Members keep the
  verified certificates by epoch and trade them in the regular document exchange, oldest first,
  so a member can cross multiple epochs even with the old primary offline. Folder layout 2
  reserves this state while adopting existing link state in place.
- **Standby selection** (`setup.takeover`). Once every enrolled member has advertised support,
  the primary chooses one reachable member. A member advertises its preference based on whether
  it runs Linux, which is treated as more likely to be always on. Set `alwaysOn` to true or false
  in the box's `setup-takeover.json` to override the platform default. Equal preferences sort by
  static key during bootstrap. A client can `POST kuvo/setup/standby {standby, epoch?}` on any box.
  In a ranked setup this pins the chosen computer first in signed membership, until the user
  changes the choice or removes the computer. On a first assignment, the choice is stored
  with the signed assignment and the pin is saved after the standby accepts and grants a
  lease. Automatic replacement and retirement preserve any pin for a remaining computer.
  The primary checks the target answers at this
  epoch. A reachable standby normally approves replacement, even
  when membership removal initiated the change. A setup with no reachable eligible member
  waits to appoint a standby. A missing standby can still hold its delegation and cannot be
  replaced by the primary alone.
- **Successor rank.** Layout 14 records `successorOrder` in signed, accepted setup
  membership. The list contains each enrolled computer's static key once. Linux and
  configured always-on computers are preferred at bootstrap, followed by other computers
  enrolled as machines. A longer recent stretch of observed availability moves a computer
  up among unpinned computers. Tied observations keep the accepted order. Rank refreshes
  are ordinary standby-acknowledged membership revisions and keep the epoch. The first
  available computer in the accepted order becomes standby through a signed handover. A
  fallback standby leaves the pin in place. A signed epoch enables the successor
  chain once all current computers advertise `setup.successor-chain`. Older setups
  keep their existing standby delegation until they can make that transition.
- **Primary lease and saves.** The current standby sends an authenticated challenge every
  ten seconds. The primary answers with a fresh nonce and the standby returns a lease
  response for that exchange. The primary measures sixty seconds from its answer, using
  wall time and uptime. The lease in `run/setup-lease.json` is bound to the setup, epoch,
  standby and, in a ranked chain, the active certificate. An expired lease, or an outstanding leadership proposal, fences shared setup
  changes. Everyday local work continues using the grants it already holds. A shared save
  is acknowledged by the current standby. If it stays unreachable, the primary can
  propose the first available successor as replacement. That successor durably accepts
  the checkpoint and new epoch before the primary can renew its lease and save through it.
  When the approver of a pending leadership proposal remains unreachable, the primary can
  supersede that proposal with a standby assignment in the same proposed epoch, including
  when the ranked chain has yet to be accepted. A returning candidate adopts a newer
  first assignment signed by the same primary for the same epoch and predecessor.
  The primary stays
  fenced until the replacement accepts and grants a lease. A promoted primary in a
  delegated setup waits for a standby lease before handing leadership to another computer.
- **Takeover.** A ranked successor probes the primary and every higher-ranked successor
  in the signed order, including any that outrank the assigned standby. After missing
  the primary for about three minutes
  (the sixty-second lease plus a two-minute margin), the highest-ranked reachable
  successor signs the next epoch using its accepted checkpoint. Lower ranks give earlier
  ranks time to answer before taking over. Restarting or losing the relay resets the
  observation period. Concurrent probes share one response window, independent of rank depth.
  Retained `delayMinutes` settings are ignored. There is no approval prompt.
- **Reconnecting after a split.** A partition can leave two writable primaries temporarily.
  On reconnect the higher verified epoch wins. At equal epochs, the rank in the last common
  epoch checkpoint decides between different primaries, with stable computer keys settling any
  remaining ties. For the same primary at the same epoch, only a newer signed first-standby
  assignment can replace the accepted certificate.
  The loser installs the winning checkpoint and steps down. Shared setup edits that only
  existed on the losing branch are discarded. Computer and device removals and credential
  revocations from either verified branch are carried forward as a union. Local work and
  its files stay with their owners. A successor may also be missing a save that only the
  failed primary and standby ever stored.
- **Number reservations.** A delegated epoch reserves a bounded range above the certified counter.
  Only the standby can certify a new bound. With folder layout 4, the primary saves each grant
  through the standby before issuing it. Takeover retains those grants and skips the outgoing
  epoch's remaining reservation. Existing local items and leased blocks remain usable.
- **Legacy reachability during leadership changes.** A restarted or reconnected member catches up
  with certificates in order. A pending proposal can finish after the initiating request
  times out. The existing primary may not be unlinked. The removal route and link CLI answer
  “Choose another main computer first.”

A setup that delegates to a standby advertises `setup.shared-saves`. Its primary
stages edits for primary-owned data kinds from the Box data declarations. It keeps
one outstanding save per kind in its private link state. Other kinds and work
owned by individual computers can continue. A client that times out waiting for
the receipt gets HTTP 202 with `pending: true`. A subsequent read shows the
accepted value once it arrives.

The primary uses an active lease to send a signed `setup-shared` document to the
designated standby. The document identifies the setup, epoch, data kind, and
next sequence and carries the replacement value. The standby persists the
value and a signed receipt before sending it. The receipt names the same setup,
epoch, kind and sequence and covers the primary's exact proposal signature.
Retries receive the same receipt. The primary checks the current lease, epoch,
standby key and proposal before applying the edit, publishing it, or replying
that it saved. An ordinary member can take published settings only from the
primary signer of its current epoch.

Takeover carries the accepted shared values, access removals and allocation
ledger into the signed leadership certificate. A handover or standby
replacement carries the same accepted values. The former standby receipt
authority ends when it signs the next epoch. An outbox entry interrupted by
an epoch change is kept locally for inspection. A caller must resubmit it
against the new epoch if the standby had yet to accept it.

The primary saves Work Queue grants before it hands them out, including blocks
it requests for itself. Each box consumes its own blocks locally when it is
offline. An item stays awaiting a number when its box has no block left. The
new primary keeps the existing grants and advances beyond the old epoch's
number ceiling, including any part reserved under a version that predates
shared saves.

### Data owners

A desktop client can ask `GET kuvo/data/owner?kind=<declaration>&id=<record>` on its box, with
`queue=<owner>` for a Work Queue record. Setup-wide kinds use the current primary. Computer-local
kinds use `computer=<key>`, else the box being asked. A conversation, bot or group chat lives, by
one rule, on this computer if it has it (its session list, its bots, its group chats); else where
this computer's own move journal says it sent it; else on the one computer that says it has it
(`agents.owns`, "Peers"). When none does, there is no owner: the reply is 404. A Work Queue item
is its queue's, in the queue a move journal says it was handed to. The feature is `data.ownership`.

The reply carries `owner {key, name, scope, local, reachable}` and the current accepted name.
`state` describes the observation available to the reader.

| State | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| `received` | `data` contains the page, including an empty list, and `lastReceivedAt` is the local receipt time in milliseconds. |
| `absent` | The owner confirmed the record was absent. The receipt time is retained and `data` is omitted. The observation applies across conversation offsets. |
| `neverReceived` | There is no usable observation for this page. The time is null and `data` is omitted. |

`refresh` describes this request. `live` means the owner answered with data or confirmed absence.
`unavailable` means the owner could not be reached. `failed` means the read failed, including a
failure of a runner on a reachable owner. `withheld` means a refusal or a read held by the Box.
`metadataOnly` identifies declarations with an ownership lookup alongside their own read routes.
A page or confirmed absence reused after an unsuccessful refresh is marked `stale`, with its
original receipt time. A remote access or ownership refusal fences previously saved pages until a
fresh read succeeds. Session absence requires a settled miss from both possible runtimes.
Concurrent page reads can require a retry when a newer observation reaches the cache first.

Supply repeated `message=<id>` and `file=<name>` to check references. Message availability is
relative to the returned page. Local live reads can verify inline attachments and managed files
referenced by the page. Saved and remote reads flag the attachment references as unavailable
through the owner-read service. A file label alone is not a file grant. Conversation reads return
the engine cursor. Pass it as `offset` to read the next page.

A normal paired-client `POST kuvo/sessions/<id>/send` to a known remote owner returns a pending
operation. When the client already knows the owner of an unlisted conversation, it can use
`POST kuvo/data/messages?session=<id>&computer=<key>` with the same message body. For a group, use `group=<id>` in place of `session=<id>` and supply
`text`. Send a stable message ID. The serving box saves the unsent message before answering 202. A committed receipt has
an `acceptedAt` time from the owning box. Poll `GET kuvo/data/messages/<operation>` on the box
that saved it. Pending messages and receipts survive a restart. If acceptance cannot be safely
determined after an owner interruption, the client should show the interrupted status and open
the owner's conversation before offering to resend. Send Now and commands require the owner's
normal client connection. The peer outbox takes inline attachments up to 128 KiB of message JSON.

### Offline field edits

A paired phone or desktop client uses `data.offline-edits` after the Box enables folder layout 7.
`GET kuvo/data/edits?kind=<kind>` returns `{owner, stale, revision, fields, choices, deleted}`.
For `queueItems`, add `queue=<conversation>` and `id=<wqi_id>`. For `botSettings`, supply
the bot ID. Supply `computer=<key>` as an address hint when the owner has not been
discovered. A serving box with a previously received owner view can return it as stale.

Submit `POST kuvo/data/edits` with a new client operation ID, `ref` (the same address),
`baseRevision` (the revision read before editing), and only the `fields` being changed.
For a new Work Queue item, generate its permanent `wqi_` ID and send `create: true` with
`baseRevision: null`. Use `delete: true` to delete an existing item at a known revision.
Queue fields include title, body, status, priority, labels, assignee, due, and order
(`{before: id}`, `{after: id}`, or `{top: true}`). Add `notes: [{id, text}]` and
`attachments: [{id, file: {name, uri}}]` with stable IDs. Attachments carry inline data.
The edit envelope can be up to 512 KiB. Edit the text of an existing note under the
`note:<id>` field returned by its owner.

A Box with `data.session-notes` exposes ordinary text notes for an existing session.
`GET kuvo/sessions/<session>/notes` returns the owner's view with the active note IDs
in `fields.ids`. `GET kuvo/sessions/<session>/notes/<note>` returns the note's
`fields.text`, revision, outstanding choices and deletion state. These views also
accept `kind=sessionNotes&id=<session>` and the optional `note=<note>` on
`GET kuvo/data/edits`. The session ID and caller-generated note ID form the record
address. Supply that address as `ref: {kind: "sessionNotes", id, note}` for generic
proposals, or use `PATCH kuvo/sessions/<session>/notes/<note>` with the edit body
without `ref`. Use `create: true` and a null base for a new note. Update only
`fields: {text}`. Use `DELETE` on the note route with the operation ID and base,
or send `delete: true` in a generic proposal. A deleted session note ID cannot be
reused. The owner's note record carries revision history, choices and edit receipts
through a move. A Box that cannot read the notes-bearing move manifest refuses it
before taking over.

Bot settings fields include name, look, personality, jobLine, jobDetails, model, and limits.
A model change that moves the conversation to the coding agents needs a live request to its owner.
The primary accepts setup time zone, computer names, existing labels and personalities,
and usage display edits on setups that use accepted saves. Names are keyed by box key,
labels and personalities by `<id>:<field>`, and usage settings by their existing unit name.
Changes that grant access use their existing permission and membership routes.

HTTP 202 means the serving box saved the proposal locally. Poll
`GET kuvo/data/edits/<operation>` there using the operation ID in the reply. A terminal
receipt names the owner revision. `choice` carries the IDs of outstanding choices created
by that proposal, alongside any independent changes that committed. Read the owner's
current view to get the original, accepted, and proposed values. Resolve a choice with a
new operation ID, the current revision, and `resolve: {id, use: "accepted"|"proposed"}`.
Ordinary session notes and Work Queue descriptions and note text merge against the
revision the author edited. Separate insertions at the same anchor are concatenated
in ascending UTF-16 wording order, with whitespace preserved. Distinct edit IDs
keep distinct insertions even when their text matches. Replayed edits keep the
original outcome. When a historic edit has no recorded identity, equal wording is
kept once. A competing rewrite keeps the owner's accepted wording and a selectable
alternative. New queue note entries continue to use their own stable IDs.
A proposal with a retired base gets `refresh` and needs an owner view before a new edit.
A deletion defeats late edits. While Recently Deleted still has the item, its receipt is
`deleted`. After the 30-day window a compact ID fence stays and the receipt asks for a
fresh copy. Poll replies include separately recoverable pending text for a deletion,
refresh, or interrupted edit. Read `GET kuvo/data/edits/outbox` for local pending drafts and
recoverable text after a restart. Recovering that text never restores the item.

### Authority carried with deferred work

The serving Box records the submitting grant from the authenticated connection. For a paired
device this is its key and exact pairing generation in the operation's setup. Kind is a client
presentation hint. Authenticated local app or local shell operations use the serving computer's
authority, and a legacy signed SSH request carries the verified computer. A request body cannot
choose its grant. Pairing again with the same key does not authorize older work.

Peers advertise `data.queued-device-authority` to each other. A Box sends device-aware edit,
message and legacy held-bot envelopes only to owners that advertise support. Older owners ignore
these envelopes even if their previous capabilities are cached. The owner verifies the sending
computer, the current owner and the submitting grant before new work, including after grant
refresh on a member's relay reconnect. A durable owner outcome can still be replayed after
revocation. An unaccepted operation cannot run under a revoked grant. Accepted setup proposals
follow the accepted setup epoch and authority. Pending predecessor receipts retain their original proof rules. Grant visibility follows the setup's
existing partition and authority rules.

Unattributed old message and edit envelopes can recover an existing outcome but cannot authorize a
new write on an updated owner. A stopped edit retains its recoverable text and attachments on the
serving Box. A managed setup exposes old untracked held-bot drafts with an explanation and holds
them for review. Tracked legacy held-bot fields combine only when their submitting grant matches.
A revoked held-bot action can retain its draft and refusal in the Box's held list.

### Peers

With `line.setup-lists`, peers mail `{setupLists: {at, sessions, projects, waiting, queues, catalog}}`
using the same authenticated envelope as their agents' lists. Each box publishes its own rows.
A large snapshot is split into `setupLists.part` envelopes using the same part framing as documents.
A receiver takes only a complete, newer snapshot from a current peer, records when it arrived, and
keeps the last copy under `run/peers/<key>/lists-v1.json`. The publisher resends periodically to
recover dropped mail. A relay unreachable notice or prolonged silence marks the peer away. The
receiving box stamps the computer, reachability, last-seen time and available actions when it
merges the rows. The copies are runtime data and are excluded from backup and restore.

A live conversation read uses authenticated peer mail `sessionFollow` with a subscription `id`.
`open` gives the allowlisted session read `resource` and its `client` (the requesting computer
or the original device pairing). The owner rechecks membership and pairing during the stream.
It answers with numbered `part` envelopes carrying a response head, body bytes (base64), a
heartbeat or an end. The subscriber renews the lease with `keep: true` and closes it with
`stop: true`. A missing part ends that opening so the line can reopen it. This channel grants
read access to that conversation's listed resources. Mutations use the existing owner routes.

Your computers talk to each other over the relay, Mac or not. A Mac connects to
the relay when the phone link is on or it has at least one machine; a Mac on its own makes no
connection.

- **Who**: each of a box's Macs' peers documents ("Documents") names its boxes: that Mac, and its
  machines whose bridge signs (`id`, the machine's name on that Mac). A box's peers are every box
  they name, itself left out, whoever passed the document on; in a setup, its main computer's
  document first ("Your setup"). Only a Mac says who a box's peers are. Its bridge runs while it has peers or phones. Setup also gives the machine's `id`.
- **Mail**: a box opens mail from its Macs and its peers, and drops the rest. Every mail has `at`
  (milliseconds). A sealed mail frame is at most 65,600 bytes, and one larger isn't sent: letters'
  words and lists are cut to fit.
- **Agents**: `{"agents": {"at", "list": [{session, name, kind: "bot"|"session", id?, project?,
  about?, machine?, look?}], "features"?}}`: a bot's `id` (`bot_…`, as group chats name their
  members) and `look` (`{color, shape, face}`, as `kuvo/bots` has it: a colour, shape or face the
  apps don't draw is kept as the plain look's, `graphite`, `round`, `calm`), and `features` as the box's
  `kuvo/info` names them (the box that takes them keeps the first 300 names), and `setup` (the id of the setup it follows, where it follows one: the
  usage panel's settings go between the boxes of one setup), and `computer` (`{version?, engine?, system?,
  working, atWork?, waiting?, asking?, oldApp?, addresses?, kuvo?, release?, agents?}`: Kuvo Code's version there, its engine's, its system as people know
  it, how many of its sessions are at work and which, how many wait on you and which (`asking`, ten
  at most, `{id, title?, asks?}`, `asks` what it asks in its box's words; since #781, for the menu
  bar of your other computers, "In the menu bar"), and, on a Mac's box, that the old app is
  attached to it, for `kuvo/computers`, "Computers"; and, on a machine, where else its Macs may
  reach it over SSH (`addresses`: its tailnet's IPv4 addresses first, its host name, its other
  networks' IPv4 addresses, never a loopback or link-local one, nor a container's or VM's bridge; eight at most, each a host name or
  IPv4 address, others dropped as the mail is taken: Keeping them up to date, below), and `kuvo`
  and `release`, the Kuvo version it runs and the signed release it holds ("Updates", Your
  computers follow each other), and `agents` (`{state, why?}`, how its coding agents stand: "The
  coding agents' state"); to each
  peer; told again at its next round, within a
  minute, as it starts or stops working at all, else with the rest). Beside `agents`, the same mail
  carries `zone: {zone, n, zoneinfo?}`, your time zone's pick, by the same rule as `computer` ("Your time zone"). A box sends its bots and its 40 latest
  sessions (its engine's and its coding agents') when they change and every ten minutes, and
  `owns`: every record it has (its bots, then its sessions without subagents', newest first, then
  its group chats; 5,000 at most), each as the first 6 characters of the base64url SHA-256 of its
  ID, one after another. This is where any computer finds an older conversation ("Data owners").
  A box from before `owns` is found by what it lists. Each box
  keeps the newest list from each peer. The relay keeps nothing, so a box that has just connected adds `"ask": "agents"` to
  what it sends first (its agents; a Mac's digest), and whoever gets it tells that box its agents
  again at once (within a minute before bridge 0.9.63), once in ten seconds at most for each.
  - A machine's bridge writes `run/agents.json` (what `list_agents` reads there) from its own
    agents and its peers', relay or not, keeping its own as last written while it can't say now
    (its engine starting).
  - This Mac's box does all of this for the Mac, as a machine's bridge does (bridge 0.9.63; the
    app did before): its own agents are its bots and its engine's and coding agents' sessions, its
    `features` as its app gives them (`kuvo/link/config`), and it writes `box/run/agents.json`
    (what its group chats name with `&`).
  - Each box leaves out what doesn't live there (`kuvo/moves`' `away`), and its mail says what it
