- **Down**: `503 {message, reason: "agentsDown", action?}`, the message one plain sentence of why:
  - `engine`: "The coding agents start once the engine is running." (the engine's own line says
    why it isn't);
  - `notInstalled`: `bin/kuvo-agents.js` isn't there;
  - `outdated`: the bridge's program is from before its keeper kept it (it asks for the engine's
    port and pid, and ends): put over the release's by an older Kuvo. A repair puts the release's
    back ("Updates", Repaired from the release it runs), so Try Again is offered; where the last
    repair found no sound release here (`run/repair.json` `damaged`, or `none` for a reason other than `busy`), it says
    the next update brings them, with no Try Again;
  - `keeper`: nothing runs that starts it again (its keeper, `run/box.pid`, isn't running);
  - `crashing`: it keeps stopping, and its keeper waits before the next start (`run/agents.retry`,
    in seconds since 1970, as `engine.retry`): "…Kuvo tries again in about N minutes.";
  - `stuck`: the bridge its keeper started (`run/agents.pid`) never said where it listens;
  - `notStarting`: none of these, and no bridge for two minutes;
  - `app`: a box in a retired Mac app's folder, with what that app said (`run/agents-stopped`).
  `action` is `{label: "Try Again", route: "kuvo/agents/start"}` for `keeper`, `crashing`, `stuck`,
  `notStarting` and a repairable `outdated`. Codes, paths and the bridge's last words go to the box's log, never to people.
- **`POST kuvo/agents/start`** (Try Again, one at a time): the keeper's `kuvo-start bridge-again`
  repairs Kuvo's files from the release, ends a bridge it started that hasn't said where it listens
  a minute on (by its noted pid, under the launch's lock), forgets its wait after failures
  (`run/agents.now`), starts the keeper if it isn't running, and starts the bridge. Answered once
  that's done (45 s at most): `200 {}` once it runs, else `503` with the state as above. `405` for
  another method; `409 {message}` where there's no keeper to ask.
- A client draws `message` as it is, once (no words of its own before it), with `action` as a
  button where it has room: Settings › Accounts in place of the coding agents' list, the line above
  a conversation's composer, and the usage rings (in the rail and the menu bar), which keep their
  last readings, marked as updating, while restarting, and say the message while down.
- A box tells its peers the state with its agents mail (`computer.agents`: `{state: "running" |
  "restarting" | "down", why?}`), so a computer whose agents are down can be told apart from
  afar.

### Updates

For a versioned release, prepare verifies the signed pack, exercises the staged engine, link and
bridge, checks the keeper's shell syntax, and asks the staged link
`box route --internal kuvo/info`. The prepared tools and plugin live at
`versions/<version>-<sha12>/bin`. The keeper stops the box's workers and changes the `bin` symlink
with one rename. The plugin directory follows `bin/opencode-plugins` and the selected keeper names
the engine. The existing `bin/kuvo-start` launch path stays in use. A matching engine version,
launcher and installed plugins let the engine keep its process and running turns. Ahead of a
restart, the box lets running engine turns and background work finish. It also waits for bridge conversations using
engine models to finish before stopping their bridge, even if the engine stays up. New engine
messages wait during the switch and its startup check. If work is still running after about five
minutes, the attempt defers and lets waiting work go before trying again. If the installed
updater predates this wait, the staged keeper checks for work before stopping anything and
allows Try Again if it finds a turn still running. After a restart, the keeper uses
`run/previous` to restore the previous target if the selected release can't start and answer within
two minutes. The keeper asks the bridge to make way (`SIGUSR2`): it lets go of every holder, at
work or between turns, and stops none. The restarted bridge adopts each: turns under way go on in
their sessions, and an agent between turns takes its session's next message. During handover,
the outgoing bridge leaves each held turn open, even after its holder connection closes.
Launch setting changes only recycle a process once its conversation's reported background work
has finished. A missing saved compaction value in a Claude Code or Codex holder means the default.
Antigravity's turn goes on from its
place in its transcript, which the bridge writes to the holder's record as it makes way. Only an
agent it can't take up is stopped, and its turn ends as interrupted: one from another Agent SDK or
an older Claude Code, or an Antigravity turn whose place couldn't be written (a subagent at work,
or a request of its own being answered). The macOS Helper is the signed supervisor for those workers. Its backing bundle lives
at `helper/Kuvo Helper.app`, with `bin/Kuvo Helper.app` continuing to resolve there.

**Repaired from the release it runs.** Every box keeps the signed release it runs, whole: as the one
it holds for your other computers (`updates/release`, "Your computers follow each other"), or, once
a newer one is held there, apart in `updates/running` (gone once it runs another).
`kuvo-link.js repair` checks Kuvo's own files here against it: the manifest (`boxes.json`) by its
signature, the pack by the manifest's SHA-256, each file by the SHA-256 the pack's `box.json`
names (only the names an update would write). A file that's missing or differs is put back from
the pack, whole, with the pack's mode, in the order an update writes them, under the update's lock
(`run/.updating`, so no update, rollback or second repair meanwhile); the keeper's own script keeps
its engine line (`V=`), which is the box's to change, and one that differs only there is sound.
`bin/.own`, what an older Kuvo kept apart, goes once a look finds the files `sound` or `repaired`,
never before. Where no sound release of the version it runs is kept here (an older updater kept
none, a newer one is held in its place, or the one kept was damaged), the box gets one: the
`repair` command fetches it from the release feed (`<feed>/v<version>/boxes.json`, and its pack
beside it), and the fleet pulls it from a computer of yours that holds it (`release` mail, as below,
whatever blocks updates here, never while one runs), each checked as an update checks a release,
kept apart in `updates/running` and never offered as an update. A box hands the one it runs, kept
apart, to a computer of yours that asks for it, as it hands the one it holds. Only from the release this box runs
(`bin/box-version`): a held release of another version is never used (`none`, `otherVersion`), so a
repair never goes up or down. A held release whose pack isn't what its manifest says is never used
and is removed (`damaged`): the box's next update brings a sound one. Tar failing on a pack that
is what its manifest says, or files it couldn't write, is `none`, `failed`, and nothing is removed.
Not while an update, its trial or a rollback runs, nor within an hour of a Mac's note that it puts
its files in place (`busy`). Each
look is noted in `run/repair.json` (`{at, result, version?, files?, why?}`). The keeper starts one
as it starts, each hour, once `run/attached` is newer than that note, after its coding agents'
bridge didn't start, and before Try Again (`kuvo-start bridge-again`). Its Mac bundles aren't
repaired: what keeps them running does.

Legacy installers used the following setup and upgrade rules. The running release is still identified by `~/.kuvo-code/bin/box-version`. It holds that
app's version, written by a Mac after it sets the box up, or by the box when it updates itself.
- **Older or unmarked box**: a Mac installs its own engine, bridge, helpers, agents bridge and
  keeper, then writes its version. (An older Mac also kept copies of the box's tools in `bin/.own`,
  which a box keeps until a repair from its release finds its files sound: "Kuvo Code 0.5 to
  0.7.2".) Its engine launches note `"box": <version>`.
- **Newer box**: a Mac leaves everything as it is.
  - Every script that would write one of its files reads what it was given and stops.
  - It connects to the engine running there, and doesn't start it over for its own settings.
  - If that engine isn't running, the box's keeper starts the one it has.
  - A script's runtime `$E` is the Mac's engine version when it's there, else the newest there,
    by version.
- **Setup**: a Mac that does this says so with `"tolerates": 1`. The bridge keeps it per Mac
  (`tolerant`), and drops it with that Mac.
- **Setup** also sends the Mac's ID (`macID`, as its engine launches name it). The bridge keeps
  `tolerantIDs[macID]`, set again at each setup, and notes in `run/launchers.json` which Mac
  started the engine (from `run/engine.json`'s `notes.mac`).
- **Setup** also sends the Mac's name (`macName`), which the bridge keeps by the Mac's key
  (`macNames`), dropped with that Mac, for `kuvo/info`'s `macs`.

A Mac with Kuvo Code 0.7 or before still connects, and puts its own files there as it always
did: the box keeps working as itself ("For released Macs").

**A box updating itself** takes only what a key pinned in `kuvo-link.js` (`UPDATE_KEYS`) signed;
`scripts/set-box-key.sh` makes that key.
- **What a release is**: `boxes.json` from `https://github.com/serhatandic/kuvo-code/releases/latest/download/`,
  `{manifest, signature, key}`. The manifest is `{kuvo: "box/1", version, released, engine,
  linux: {x86_64|aarch64: {url, integrity}}, darwin: {x86_64|aarch64: {url, integrity}},
  pack: {url, sha256, size}}`: a box takes the engine for its own system and kind. The signature is
  Ed25519 over `"kuvo-box v1\n"` and the manifest's bytes, by a pinned key
  (`scripts/sign-box.mjs`). The pack holds `box.json` (each file's SHA-256, and `engines` and
  `downgradeSafe`, the release check's, "A new engine") and the files, laid
  out as `~/.kuvo-code`: `files`, `bin/<name>`, `bin/runtime/<name>` and
  `config/opencode/plugins/<name>`; and `bundles`, Mac bundles (the box's helper, signed), each
  `{"bin/<name>.app": {<path in it>: <SHA-256>}}`. A box from before bundles passes `bundles` over,
  so a release with one still updates it. A bundle holds only folders and the files `bundles` names
  (no links, no part starting with a dot), or the release isn't taken. `scripts/box-release.sh`
  builds it from the box's own sources, with no app: the keeper's files (`kuvo-start`,
  `kuvo-launch`, `kuvo-setsid`, `kuvo-wake`, `kuvo-npx`, `runtime/node`, as `box/src/keeper` has
  them, the engine's version written in from `box/src/shared/engine-pin.json`, which is also where
  `box.json`'s engine and its builds come from), `.kuvo-boot` (the SHA-256 of the first three,
  each as its name, a newline and its bytes, joined by newlines), the engine's plugin
  (`box/src/plugins`), the link, the agents' bridge (with a last line `// kuvo-agents <16 hex
  digits of its SHA-256>`, which a Mac from before boxes updated themselves tells it by) and the
  browser as built, the catalogs (`integrations.json`, `integrations-mac.json` and
  `mcp-catalog.json`, written from the one table in `box/src/shared/integrations`), the bots'
  words (`box/src/shared/bot-words.json`) and `box-version`; then each Mac bundle it's given
  (Kuvo Helper, signed and notarized already, `scripts/build-helper.sh`). The same files pack to
  the same bytes on one system: entries in name order, one fixed time, no owners, gzip without a
  name or time.
- **From a folder here** (`box.update`, with legacy offer handling below): Kuvo Code carries its version's release
  (`Contents/Resources/box-release`: `boxes.json` and `box-<version>.tar.gz`, as
  `scripts/box-release.sh` made them), for it to offer the box on its computer
  as it opens. The local installer can also offer a release. The box uses its
  update and fleet rules to decide what to prepare. A legacy app-folder box
  is updated with its own app.
  - `POST kuvo/box/update {from: "<folder>"}`, from Kuvo Code only (this Mac's app, or a Mac's
    `box route`; a phone gets 403): `from` is a full path to a folder with `boxes.json` and the pack
    its `pack.url` ends in, beside it. The box checks it as it would a download: a pinned key's
    signature, a version newer than its own, the pack's SHA-256. Its own version is taken too when
    the pack's files (`box.json`'s SHA-256s, its bundles' on a Mac) aren't those in place (an app
    rebuilt under the same version); with the same files, it's what the box has. Then it keeps both in
    `updates/offered` (the folder may go, the app updated again; a newer one offered replaces it)
    and answers 202 with `kuvo/update`'s status.
  - Refused: 400 without a full path; 409 when it isn't set up, is blocked (as below), its version
    isn't known, it's updating already, or the release is older than the box, its own version
    with the same files ("with these same files"), or older than what's offered already; 422 when it can't be read, isn't a release, isn't signed with a pinned key, or
    its pack isn't what it says. Other methods answer 405.
  - **Legacy in-place installs** take it the old update way, in a process of its own (`kuvo-link.js update --offered`, as Update
    Now's), at the next look (every 20 seconds while one waits, and at each ten-minute round),
    whatever is at work, its age and the hour (the Kuvo Code it came with is there already); one with
    another engine than the one running waits until nothing runs. It waits, untouched, while the box
    is blocked, its engine is stopped on purpose, or an update runs or is on trial. Taken, or no longer newer than the box, the offer goes. One that fails goes too,
    and its version rests a day (`offerFailed` in `run/update.json`; offered again sooner, it's
    refused with 409), as it does when its judge took an update to it back (below), so a release
    that never runs well isn't tried at every offer. One that failed
    before anything changed (its engine's download, offline) stays, and is tried again an hour on,
    then a day after each next failure (`offerFailed.tries`); offered again meanwhile, it's there
    already (202).
  - Its engine, when the box doesn't have it yet, still comes from the manifest's URL.
- **Legacy check and timing** (in-place `bin`): as soon as a newer release reaches it, whichever way: Kuvo Code on this Mac offers the
  one it carries (above), another of your computers holds it (below), or its own release check
  finds it (`boxes.json` from GitHub, a minute after its link starts and once in every six hours
  after, at any hour, each box at its own point in them, offset by its computer's name and folder
  so they don't all ask at once: `run/update.json`'s `round`), always (there's no switch). Its own check takes a
  release once it's three days old; the other ways, whatever its age. Or now (Update Now,
  `POST kuvo/update {now: true}`), whatever its age. Either way, whatever is at work there: an update
  stops nothing. A release with another engine than the one running, whose `box.json` lists the
  running one in `engines`, takes its code at once and changes the engine later, without cutting a
  turn ("A new engine"). A release without compatibility for the running engine waits for that
  engine's work to finish. The box's Update Now route also waits in that case. It checks for a
  signed release immediately and can retry one that failed before. It returns 409 when an update
  or trial is under way or the box has been stopped.
- **Fleet versions** (`update.fleet`): the main holds the newest eligible signed
  release from the feed, an update request or a member's offer. Members can stage
  that candidate and report `staged` or `cannot` in peer facts. The main must
  have its own verified staged release. It switches once all reachable computers
  are ready or five minutes have passed since the first readiness. Away computers
  are excluded. Members switch to the main's running release when ready, checking
  its pack hash when known. A returning computer catches up. See
  `box/src/link/updates/fleet.ts`.
  - **Admission**: staging and being behind leave ordinary work available. The
    box can still refuse an unauthorized request or a protocol or operation it
    cannot safely handle. Clients display the answer. Older builds may send
    the predecessor `computer-update-required` or `client-update-required`
    reason fields, `503` or `426`, or an authenticated refusal hello with
    `waiting`, `reason`, `title` and `target`. These shapes do not mean that
    current staging fences normal work.
  - **Request API** (`update.fleet` feature): `GET kuvo/computers` and each NDJSON snapshot on
    `GET kuvo/computers/events` can include a top-level `fleetUpdate` and
    `computers[].fleetUpdate`. They are present once the setup has an accepted target. An older
    computer that has not reported its progress can still be shown behind.
    - A row has `{current, target, state, canRetry, line, lastFailureAt?, currentSha256?, targetSha256?}`. `current` can be null.
      `line` `{words, tone, short?}` is what the row shows, all the box's: `words` ("Ready for
      beta.41", "beta.40 · Can’t be reached: updates when it’s back"), `tone` (`done`, `working`, `warning`
      where it can't update for a reason you can fix, `blocked` where it can't until the next
      release, `off`), and on `warning` the few words a narrow place shows (`short`). `canRetry`
      says Try Again is offered on the row. A client draws these and decides neither.
      `requiresUpdate` is a predecessor compatibility field. States are `up-to-date`, `behind` (optional `reason`), `updating` (`stage:
      "downloading" | "waiting" | "switching"`, optional `runningTurns`, null if unknown),
      and `failed` (`reason, rolledBackTo, nextRetryAt, failedAt`). Times are Unix milliseconds.
      Today's boxes say `up-to-date`, `ready`, `getting-ready`, `updating` with `stage: "switching"`
      (`line` "Switching to beta.42…", tone `working`), `cannot` and `off` ("Can't be reached:
      updates when it's back"). A row only moves forward while a computer switches: one
      restarting into the release says `switching` (its own box says so while the release is on
      trial), a peer that goes quiet right after it was ready reads as switching for ten minutes,
      and any peer keeps the state, sessions at work and agents it last told for two minutes of
      quiet (a restart, a relay reconnecting) before it reads as `off`. A switching computer
      counts as ready in the summary, which stays shown (`stage: "switching"`) until it's done.
    - The summary is `{target, targetSha256?, done, updating, behind, failed, stage, dismissed, failures}`.
      Its stages are `behind`, `downloading`, `waiting`, `switching`, `failed` and
      `finished`. Show an active update while `!dismissed && stage !== "finished"`.
      `failures` is a list of opaque failure identifiers clients can retain with a dismissal
      when their stream switches computer.
    - `POST kuvo/update/retry {target, targetSha256?, key?}` returns `202` with the row's update
      state or `409 {message}` when the target changed or `canRetry` is false. Without `key`, or
      with this computer's, it's this computer's own Try Again. With another computer's `key`, the
      box passes it on to that computer by peer mail (`{release: {retry: {version, sha256}}}`), which
      retries as its own Try Again does: `404` for a key that isn't one of your computers, `503`
      where that computer can't be reached now. Clients ask the box that lists your computers. A computer can
      retry after failure or five minutes without progress. Its relay owner consumes the request
      and starts the same no-cut path used by automatic updates. In a setup with an accepted
      release, `POST kuvo/update {now: true}` uses the same eligibility rule.
    - The summary's `shown`, `title`, `detail` and `warning` are the words to draw: shown while
      computers get ready ("Updating to beta.41 · 2 of 3 ready", off computers left out; `detail`
      "Everything works on beta.40 while your computers get ready.") or where one can't update for
      a reason you can fix (`warning`: "spare-linux can't update to beta.41", `detail` its name and
      reason, Try Again on its row). Hidden otherwise.
    - Check for Updates (`POST kuvo/update {now: true}`) on a member answers `202` with `message`
      (its main checks now, or once it's back) and keeps the request in `run/fleet-check.json`; its
      relay owner sends the main peer mail `release` `{check: true}` once the main is reached, and
      the main looks at its feed. A main that predates it ignores the mail.
    - `POST kuvo/update/dismiss {target, targetSha256?}` to the stream source returns `200` with the summary
      or `409 {message}` if the target changed. The source remembers the request for the paired
      device, or the local installation (local callers can distinguish themselves with a stable
      `x-kuvo-client-id`, 32 lowercase hex digits). A new target or a new failure reopens it.
  - **Held**: a box keeps the newest signed release it has (`updates/release`: `boxes.json` and
    `pack.tgz`) from the moment it's checked there: Kuvo Code here offers it (`kuvo/box/update`,
    and the 409 "with these same files" too), the box fetches it (once the pack's SHA-256 is
    checked), or a peer hands it over. It hands it over at once, before or while it takes it itself,
    and whatever came of that: computers can stage in parallel. Each judges activation by its own health rule and can roll back its code. A newer held release is never replaced by an
    older one. A machine set up over SSH holds none until it gets a signed one. Only a release whose
    manifest says `spreads: true` is held to hand over (`scripts/sign-box.mjs` with
    `KUVO_BOX_SPREADS=1`: the release workflow and the private feed): a build signed for trying an
    update is taken where it's offered and never handed on. The pack is kept by the name its
    address ends in, and checked against the signed SHA-256 before it's served.
  - **Told**: its agents mail's `computer` says `kuvo` (the Kuvo version it runs; a Mac's `version`
    is its app's) and `release` (the version it holds), "Peers".
  - **Told at once**: the box's link watches `updates` and, as a newer release is held (whichever
    process kept it), tells its peers in agents mail right away.
  - **Moved**: peer mail `release`, one pull at a time. `{want: <version>}` → `{version, boxes,
    size}` (`boxes`, the signed `boxes.json` as it is) or `{version, none: true}`; then `{version,
    part: <i>}` → `{version, i, d}` (`d`: the pack's 30,000 bytes from `i × 30,000`, base64), up to
    sixteen asked at once. Nothing more is asked until `boxes` verifies (a pinned key, the version
    asked, newer than the box, a size from 1 byte to 100 MB). An answer from another peer, or for
    another version, is dropped. A pull that hears nothing in a minute asks again for what it waits
    for; one that makes no progress in five minutes leaves that peer. Whole, the pack is checked
    against the signed SHA-256, moved into a folder of its own (`updates/incoming/release`) and
    offered to the box itself from there (as above, checked again), and taken; an offer refused for
    an update under way here is offered again at the next look, any other refusal rests that peer
    an hour; the engine comes from the manifest's URL, as for any update. Only the
    box with the relay connection pulls (resident, or legacy `run`); a box that starts again begins anew.
  - **Never** older, its own version, unsigned or signed by a key it doesn't pin, with an engine
    older than the one running (refused before any part is asked), or from outside its peer list.
    A refusal because an update started here is looked at again a minute later.
- **This Mac's app follows** its Kuvo: the desktop app registers its version with `kuvo/box/app`
  (`{desktop, version}`), and while Kuvo on this Mac runs a newer version, this Mac's row in
  `kuvo/computers` says it (`appCheck: <version>`): the app looks for its own update then, in the
  background, once for each version (Sparkle's `checkForUpdatesInBackground`, which installs as you
  set it). The app is never needed for the box to be current, and nothing opens it for this.
- **Never**:
  - in another folder than `~/.kuvo-code`;
  - while its engine is stopped on purpose (`run/stopped`), or its version (`bin/box-version`)
    isn't known;
  - to an older version; to its own version only from a folder here, when its files aren't those in
    place (GitHub's release of the version it has is "current");
  - to an engine older than the one running (`run/engine.json`'s `version`): it may have written
    what the older one can't read (409 for an offered one);
  - over an update still on trial (`run/update-trial`), whichever way it's asked for (the release
    check's, Update Now, an offered release, `update --from`, the installer's, `box update-now`): "Its last
    update is still being checked: try again in a few minutes." What it kept to go back to stays as
    it was; how the last update went (`last`) stays, and the release check looks again in that round
    (as when something is at work);
  - with another engine than the one running that its `engines` don't list, while a conversation
    works there or a browser ask waits, but on your word (Update Now);
  - while a Mac that started the engine in the last 30 days isn't in `tolerantIDs` as `true`;
  - while a Mac with Kuvo Code 0.7 or before connected in the last 30 days, since the box was last
    marked ("For released Macs").
  - When the newest release has no `boxes.json`, it's "current", not a failure.
- **How**:
  1. It checks the pack's SHA-256, each file's, and the engine's npm `integrity`.
  2. It tries the new engine (`--version`), the new bridge with it (`selftest`), and the new
     keeper (`sh -n`).
  3. With another engine version, it first checks there's room to keep the engine's data. It keeps
     each file it replaces in `updates/rollback`, and writes `restore.sh` and `run/update-trial`.
     Nothing is stopped, but with another engine version its `engines` don't list (one they list
     changes later, "A new engine"): then only the engine, its keeper's
     `engine-stop` (a keeper from before that has none: `stop`, which ends its bridge too), run (as
     its `start` and `restore.sh` are)
     with HOME spelled as the running engine's command line has it, so a keeper of any age knows
     that engine as its own (any run of slashes taken as one); an engine its record names that's
     still running then, its command line this box's engine's, the update ends it itself (TERM,
     then KILL after ten seconds). It goes on only once the engine
     has stopped; if it can't stop it, nothing has changed, and it starts the engine again. With another engine version, it keeps
     a copy of the engine's data (`opencode.db` with its `-wal` and `-shm`) whole or not at all in
     `updates/backups/<date>-<engine>-to-<engine>` (the latest only, the one before taken away
     first, so its room counts; kept 30 days, then taken away at the next confirm or ten-minute
     round): nothing ever puts it back, it's there to restore by hand as a last resort.
     - `restore.sh` checks each step and keeps what was kept until it's all back.
     - It puts back code only, never the data: what the engine wrote since is kept. With a newer
       engine, once that was put in place and started (`updates/rollback/engine-started`, noted
       just before the keeper's start), the keeper it puts back starts the new engine (its `V`), as
       the older engine may not read what the newer one wrote; before that, the old engine goes
       back with the rest. So it does when the update itself takes it back because the new engine
       never answered and the data is as it was copied (each file's size and time).
     - Putting back stops nothing either, as an update doesn't: but a newer engine that never
       started goes (`engine-stop`), and the old one starts; and a keeper put back from before the
       keeper kept the coding agents' bridge (one without `bridge)`) gets the whole box stopped and
       started again, as its bridge only ever starts with its engine.
     - Never two engines on one box's data: each engine start (`kuvo-launch`) notes its engine's
       pid in `run/engines/<pid>`; a start that finds no noted engine running (`run/engine.json`)
       first stops each noted one still running as that box's engine (`…/engine/…/opencode serve
       --port`), by that pid, never by name; the keeper's stop drops the note of the engine it
       stopped. Engines started before this note existed aren't known, and are left alone.
     - A rollback an update from before kept with the engine's data in it (`updates/rollback/data`,
       which its `restore.sh` would put back): `kuvo-start rollback` moves that data to
       `updates/backups` first, and runs `restore.sh` only once it has; the keeper that puts back starts the engine
       that ran meanwhile (`run/engine.json`'s `version`) where that's newer than its own `V`.
  4. It swaps file by file: `bin/box-version` first, `bin/.kuvo-boot` last. A bundle goes whole, in
     among them: the new one staged beside it (`<name>.app.new`), the old one put aside
     (`<name>.app.old`), the new renamed in, the old removed. The box doesn't restart a program
     running from the old one: what keeps it running does. `restore.sh` puts a kept bundle back the
     same way, and takes one away that wasn't there before. On Linux a release's bundles are left
     out. Then, with another engine, it starts that (`kuvo-start start`); otherwise it only makes
     sure the keeper runs (`kuvo-start box`).
     One update runs at a time, by its process (`run/.updating/pid`, the link's), always one of its
     own (`kuvo-link.js update …`), never the server or bridge that asked, so stopping that one
     meanwhile doesn't stop the update. While it runs, `setup` doesn't restart the bridge, and
     nothing runs `restore.sh` or judges it.
  5. Each piece takes the new code by itself, nothing cut short:
     - Kuvo's server for clients (`serve`, a Mac's, which Kuvo Helper keeps running; `serve --kept`,
       a machine's, which its keeper keeps), and its link (`run`) hold no turn: each looks every 30
       seconds at the code in place (`bin/box-version`, the SHA-256 of `bin/kuvo-link.js`) against
       what it loaded, and once they differ, no update being under way, it leaves, and what keeps it
       running starts it again on the new code. Clients reconnect. (Only one started from the box's
       own `bin/kuvo-link.js`; an app's own box is started by its app.)
     - The coding agents' bridge makes way for the new build ("A new version while it works"),
       never cutting a turn, and the keeper starts the new one.
     - The keeper (`kuvo-start keep`) starts itself again on its new script (`bin/.kuvo-boot`).
     - Kuvo Helper looks at its bundle every ten seconds (its program, `Info.plist` and
       `_CodeSignature/CodeResources`, hashed): a new build in its place, no update under way, it
       stops what it started (the engine and bridge run on, detached) and exits 75, which its launch
       agent's `KeepAlive` (`SuccessfulExit` false) has launchd start again, on the new build. It
       exits cleanly (0) only when it's stopped on purpose: the box turned off (`run/off`), Stop Kuvo
       on this Mac (`run/paused`), launchd or you quitting it, another copy running, or a refusal
       only you can clear. A crash is restarted too.
     - A Kuvo Helper from before that doesn't leave by itself: its `serve`, started again on the new
       code, hands it over once ("This Mac's box: its helper", A helper from before beta.31).
     - A `serve`, `serve --kept` or `run` from before this (an update into it, taken by the box's
       updater from before, or by the installer an app carries) doesn't leave by itself: while an
       update is on trial, the keeper ends the one `run/serve.json` or `run/link.pid` names, only
       while that number runs the box's `kuvo-link.js` and started before `bin/kuvo-link.js` was
       written, for what keeps it running (its helper, the keeper) to start the new one.
     - A bridge the keeper keeps also makes way for the engine its keeper starts now, where that's
       another than the one it runs on (`waits` as for a newer build, checked on that engine); until
       it has, confirming an update keeps the engine folder it runs from.
  6. **One health rule** judges it, the same on every box. The judge is the updater's own process,
     which stays once it has swapped (the installer's, which an app waits on, starts one of its own:
     `kuvo-link.js update --settle`), holding `run/update-judge.pid`. When an update is on trial and
     no judge runs (its updater went: the machine went down, or the update was taken by a box from
     before this), the keeper starts `update --settle`, which takes the judging up where it was
     (`trial.judged` in `run/update.json`); three of those that never got to look
     (`run/update-settle.tries`) and the keeper puts the code back itself (`kuvo-start rollback`).
     Every ten seconds it looks at:
     - `kuvo/info` from the new files (`box route`, run on the keeper's engine): it answers, and
       its `features` hold every feature the box said before (`trial.features`);
     - Kuvo's server, where one is wanted (a Mac's own box; `run/serve.needed`): it runs, and one
       started since the swap answers `kuvo/info` (one from before is waiting, not unwell);
     - its link, where it's wanted (`run/link.needed`): it runs;
     - the engine: it answers `api/session?limit=1`, or is starting (its log grows), or it's
       stopped on purpose (`run/stopped`, `paused`, `off`);
     - the coding agents' bridge, while the engine runs where the keeper keeps it: it answers
       (whichever build: one making way is waiting);
     - none of these started again more than three times while it's judged.
     Well, once all of them hold through five minutes of the judge's own running time (a computer
     asleep doesn't count it down: two looks' time at most counts between looks): `trial.healthy`,
     then confirmed: what was kept and other engines go, `last` says it updated, and what waited
     for that goes on (integrations' keys no longer needed). Unwell, once a piece fails three looks
     in a row over a minute at least, or starts again more than three times: `kuvo-start rollback`
     puts the code back (never the data), `last` says it failed and went back, in words, and the
     version rests a day (`offerFailed`). Nothing else says an update is well: not the relay's
     welcome, not a server, not a timer. A rollback that didn't get it all back is carried on by
     the next judge, not judged again; after three tries `kuvo-start rollback` gives up, ends the
     trial and starts the box as it is (never left stopped). Only one rollback runs at a time
     (`run/.rolling-back`), and one judge (`run/update-judge.pid`, made only where there's none).
     An updater cut off after it stopped the engine for a new one (`trial.engineStopped`) has its
     judge start it first. While Kuvo is stopped until it next starts (`paused`) or off, nothing is
     judged; the next start's keeper starts a judge again. A bridge that won't take the new build
     (`renewal.waits: "restart"`) counts as failing.
  7. It notes what it installed (`updates/installed.json`, its `files`, never its bundles). At each
     ten-minute round it checks the files against that note. A Mac notes `run/mac-installing` while it puts its files in place, and marking the
     box clears it. Drift seen on two checks, and not while a Mac is installing, means a Mac with an
     older Kuvo Code put its own files back. The box then keeps its version mark, so no other such
     Mac takes it further back, says why, and doesn't update itself for 30 days.
  - What the new engine did during a trial that's rolled back is kept: data is never put back.
  - The coding agents' own data (`agents`) isn't kept for a rollback.
- **State**: `run/update.json` holds `{latest, checked, last: {at, result, message?, from?, to?}, engine?: {at, result, from, to, message?},
  running?, trial?, round?, offerFailed?: {version, at, takenBack, tries?, message?}}` (`tries`:
  how many times in a row that version failed here, put back or not; kept while a take of it is on
  trial, and forgotten once that's judged well). `trial` is
  `{from, to, at, swapped?, features?, dataKept?, judged?, healthy?}` (the judging so far, as above).
- `kuvo/update`:
  - `GET` answers `{setUp, version, engine, latest, last, updating, blocked}`, and while a newer
    engine waits to take the running one's place or does, `engineChange` `{stage, from, to, line}`
    (`stage` `waiting`, `holding`, `swapping` or `back`; `line`, the words a client shows), and how the
    last change of engine went, `engineLast` `{at, result: changed|back|failed, from, to, message?}`.
    `updating` is the step under way (`checking`, `downloading`, `downloading the engine`,
    `checking it`, `installing`, `starting`) or null. `blocked` is why it can't update, or null.
    `offered` is the version of a release offered from a folder here that waits to be taken, and
    only there while one does. `offerFailed` `{version, at, takenBack, message?}` is how taking such
    a release last failed (taken back once it was in place, or before anything changed, when it
    stays offered and is tried again), apart from the release check's update (`last`); gone once one's
    taken. With `box.update.no-cut`, `waiting` is present when the target computer knows of a
    newer release or a part of an installed release is still taking over. It carries
    `{version, reason, detail, sessionsAtWork}`. The reason names the state, the detail gives the
    box's words, and the count includes turns awaiting approval. A null count means a running
    process could not be reached. Query the route on each computer whose progress is shown.
  - `POST {now: true}` starts one, in a process of its own (`kuvo-link.js update --now`, or
    `--offered --now` for an offered release): 202 with the status (`updating` `checking`), or 409
    `{message}` when it's not set up, is blocked, is updating already, or its last update is still
    on trial. The release check's goes the same way (`update --round <round>`, which notes the
    round once it went, unless something was at work). Other methods answer 405: there's nothing to turn off.
  - Over SSH, `kuvo-link.js box update-status` and `kuvo-link.js box update-now` use the same
    status and no-cut update path.
- `kuvo-link.js update [--now] [--from <folder>] [--round <round>]` updates from a shell, `--from`
  from a release in a folder there (a full path), taken at once, whatever its age. `update --offered
  [--now]` takes the release offered with `kuvo/box/update` when it's due (with `--now`, on your
  word), and does nothing otherwise. Only in a test's folder,
  it also takes `--url <boxes.json> --key <public key>`, or `--key` with `--from` or `--offered`.

#### A new version while it works

The in-place updater and its worker handover contracts are retained for older installs.
Current versioned installs switch the checked `bin` link as described above.

A Mac that connects puts its own files on a machine (above) while the box works: its sessions may
run day and night, so a piece waiting for "nothing runs" might never take them. Each piece takes a
new version without cutting a turn:

- **The coding agents' bridge** (`bin/kuvo-agents.js`) reads which build it runs as it starts: the
  last `// Built from Packages/Box/src/agents <hash>` line in its bundle (`scripts/build-agents.sh`
  writes it; a Mac's own `// kuvo-agents <hash>` line may follow it). It looks at the bundle in its
  place when the file changes, when a turn ends, and every 10 seconds. It makes way for another
  build there only:
  - while the box isn't updating itself (`run/.updating`, held by a link process that still runs);
  - while it runs on the engine its keeper starts (the version folder of its runtime,
    `engine/<version>/opencode`, is `bin/kuvo-start`'s `V` while that one is there, else the
    newest there): a bundle a Mac brought with a newer engine it didn't start, as sessions were at
    work, waits for that engine, which starts it (`waits: "engine"`);
  - once the bundle has answered a check on this engine (`<engine> kuvo-agents.js selftest`, which
    prints `ok <build>` and exits): one that doesn't waits for a restart (`waits: "restart"`);
  - once it has run eleven minutes, and while what keeps it running will start the new one: the
    engine's launch (`RemoteServer.agentsScript`) starts it again five seconds after it ends, and
    gives up after five runs in a row; a launch since October 2026 starts that count again after a
    run of ten minutes (its loop says `-ge 600`), one from before never does, so there it goes
    only while it has started fewer than three times (one `"url"` line each in `run/agents.log`; a
    start that ended before it said where it listens has none, so two are spare; a log it can't
    read counts as full). Its parent is that loop (`kuvo-agents`, `-lt 5` in its command line,
    read once a minute at most); started by anything else it doesn't go; where the command line
    can't be read, it counts as one from before. One its keeper keeps (`KUVO_AGENTS_KEPT=1`, below)
    always may: the keeper starts it again whenever it ends, on the engine the keeper starts, so it
    doesn't wait for that engine either, and checks the bundle on it. Otherwise it waits for a restart
    (`waits: "restart"`), holding nothing. Each renewal is one of those runs. A check that couldn't
    run (it couldn't start, a signal ended it, a minute went by) is tried again at the next look.

  A keeper-managed bridge starts a compatible replacement as a standby with its own port. If
  all active turns can transfer, the current bridge seals its session writes and records the
  holder generations, replay ranges, and pending approvals in `run/agents/handover.json`. The
  holders keep the replay ranges through the switch. The replacement takes control once the
  previous bridge exits, publishes its port, and replays into the existing session and reply. A
  client reconnects for events. The keeper starts the saved previous build if the replacement
  exits or fails to publish within a minute. Only the active bridge writes the store.

  Codex, Grok, Claude Code 2.1.268 or later with the same Agent SDK, Antigravity (`agy`, or ACP 1.3.0), and
  Cursor with the same worker SDK can transfer when their journal is complete. Antigravity's ACP
  server keeps its native session and answers the original prompt request after an approval.
  Cursor's worker keeps its SDK run alive and sends updates with that run's ID. Open forms,
  steered turns, shell commands, bridge-owned MCP connections, and Antigravity's separate
  subagent transcript activity fall back together to Renewal. Sandboxed Codex, Claude Code and
  Grok also use Renewal because their launchers depend on the original bridge. A standby-compatible build can
  start a bounded drain at once. On the first upgrade from a bridge that predates holders, the
  keeper checks that the replacement can start and requests one clean bridge restart. That
  bridge marks its active turns interrupted through its normal shutdown. The engine stays up
  independently. The keeper marks the transition so future upgrades use live handover or Renewal.

  Renewal goes:
  - **At the first quiet moment**: nothing has run for half a minute: no turn (a subagent's, a
    message being handed to one or on its way to a subagent, the files kept after one, a session
    being deleted), no `!` command of yours, no discussion in a group chat here (a chat talking, a
    bot's answer being read), no request coming in (counted until its answer begins: a download's
    body, or the event feed, isn't waited for), nothing an agent
    left running in the background, no side question being answered, review being read, handoff
    being written, goal being checked, or sign-in waiting for you; a turn ending, or a request that
    can start something (any but `GET` and `HEAD`) coming in, starts the half minute again. Reads
    don't: the link asks the bridge whether it answers (`GET api/info`) every half minute, and
    clients read what they show; each is waited for while it's answered. Then it holds new turns, and a
    second later, if it's still quiet, it makes way (what it has is kept): it lets go of every agent
    it holds, stopping none, and exits, and its launch starts the new bundle, which takes each up. If that second wasn't quiet, it lets go and looks again.
  - **When there isn't one**: after an hour, in the night's window (02:00 to 05:00 in your time zone),
    or after a day whatever the hour, it holds new turns: a message (or a summary, a note) that
    would start a turn stays in its session's line (`inbox`, kept with the session, marked `held`,
    and switched to `delivery: "steer"` so it goes first). Turns under way go on to their end,
    steering into them too; a group chat's seat (`metadata.kuvo.seat`) isn't held, so a discussion
    under way goes on to its end (a new one, a message of yours to a chat meanwhile, starts too, and
    is waited for, within the half hour below), and so does a turn an agent starts on its own (a command it left
    running ended). Then it goes, whatever else is under way (a side question, review, handoff
    or sign-in): each ends as it does at any restart, and says so. What its held agents left
    running in the background goes on with them. Half an hour after it began holding, still not gone (a turn waiting on you
    overnight, an update of the box that never finished), it lets go: what it held starts, and an
    hour later, that night still or the next, it holds again.
  - The new bridge, once it's up, starts what was held, each once (`held` cleared as it's woken).
  - Its own build put back in place meanwhile, it lets go of what it held and goes on.
  - A group chat held on another computer whose discussion this bridge's bot is in isn't known
    here: going between that bot's turns, and back after more than 45 seconds, that computer goes
    on without it for that discussion.
  - On every box in a home of its own (a machine's, a Mac's), whose keeper keeps its bridge. A Mac's
    box in the app's folder: the app's keeper starts the whole box again from a newer app once
    nothing runs on it.
- **Data formats**: `agents/sessions/*/session.json` and `run/link.json` are additive object
  formats with `formatVersion: 1` on writes. Readers accept unstamped legacy records. Writers
  refuse records stamped with an unsupported version. The bridge uses the shared
  `folder-version.json` upgrade runner before opening a Kuvo folder. Layout 18 reserves the
  bridge handover and program and engine drain recovery records. It leaves existing session
  files in place, and their v1 stamp is added on the next save. A rollback to the previous
  layout can still read these session files while the update is on trial. Both bridges must
  advertise the same folder layout to transfer live, so the saved bridge can reopen it if the
  standby fails. Across layouts the bridge waits for a quiet restart.
- **The browser keeper** checks for attached clients and open asks before giving way to a newer
  build. Older keepers continue serving until their normal idle shutdown.
- **The bridge apart from the engine**: the keeper keeps the bridge running (`kuvo-start bridge`,
  each round while the engine runs and no bridge does, with the engine's backoff: one that ran
  under ten minutes makes it wait longer). It starts it through `kuvo-launch` with `KUVO_BRIDGE=1`,
  in the environment the engine gets, a port and password of its own (`KUVO_AGENTS_PORT`,
  `KUVO_AGENTS_PASSWORD`), `KUVO_AGENTS_KEPT=1`, and notes it in `run/agents.pid`. The bridge
  follows the engine by `run/engine.json` (looked at every two seconds), so an engine started again
  (a crash, a hang ended, an update's new engine) never ends it or a turn on it; the engine's launch
  neither starts nor ends it, and `engine.json` no longer names it (`bridge.json` does). The
  keeper's `stop`, `restart`, `pause` and `off` still end it with the engine. A bridge a launch
  from before started beside its engine (its loop restarting it while that engine lives) runs on
  until it ends; a bridge of this build, even started so, never ends with its engine.
- **The link** (`kuvo-link.js run`) has no turns: `setup`, which a Mac runs as it connects, starts
  a newer one over the one running, as before.
- **The engine** isn't ours to hold turns in: its turns end where they began, and it changes between
  them ("A new engine"). A Mac starts a newer one only when it connects and nothing runs there
  (otherwise it keeps the one at work, and puts nothing in its place).
- `bridge.json`, on a machine, says `{pid, port, password, build, renewal}`: `build` as above,
  and `renewal` `{since, holding, waits}` while another build is in its place (`since` in ms;
  `waits` is `quiet`, `holding`, `engine` or `restart`, as above), else null.
- `kuvo/info`'s `pieces` (a machine's) says which version each runs against the one in place:
  `{link, agents, engine}`, each `{running, current, behind}`.
  - `link`: `running` is `run/link.version` while the link runs (null otherwise), `current` the
    version of the link answering, `behind` when they differ. Through the running link (a phone)
    that's its own version; a Mac asks with a process of its own (`kuvo-link.js box route`), from
    the files in place.
  - `agents`: `running` is the build its bridge says (null while none runs, or one from before
    builds were said runs), `current` the build of `bin/kuvo-agents.js`. `behind` while one runs
    that isn't that build; for one that doesn't say, while the bundle is newer than its
    `bridge.json`. `renewal` is its `bridge.json`'s `{since, holding}` while it's behind, else
    null. `waits`, while it's behind (else null), is what it waits for: its `bridge.json`'s, or
    `restart` for one that doesn't say its build (from before bridges made way by themselves),
    which takes the new one when the engine next starts.
  - `engine`: `running` is the running engine's version (null when none runs), `current` the one
    its keeper starts (`bin/kuvo-start`'s `V`, while that one is there, else the newest there).
    `behind` while that one is newer.
  - A client shows a line while one is `behind` (`MachinePieces`, in KuvoClient, its words for
    the coding agents by `waits`), and says nothing otherwise. A Mac's own `kuvo/info` has no `pieces`.

#### A new engine

This is the legacy engine-swap path for installs that still use in-place updates.

The engine is unmodified, and its turns live in its process: a turn can't move to another engine,
and two engines never run on one box's data. So a newer engine takes the old one's place between
turns, what's sent meanwhile held on the box, never cut:

- **The release check** (`scripts/engine-check.mjs`, run as a release is built): the link and the
  coding agents' bridge as built answer `selftest` on the pinned engine and on the one the release
  before ran (`engine-pin.json`'s `previous`), and that one opens what the new one wrote (a data
  folder it made, opened by the new one, which migrates it and writes to it, opened by it again:
  both conversations listed and read, and written to; where the code doesn't answer on the one
  before, `engines` names the pinned one alone). `box.json` says what it found: `engines` (the pinned one,
  then the one before; the pinned one alone without a check) and `downgradeSafe` (true only where
  it was found so). A box running one of `engines` takes the release's code at once, its link tried
  with both engines (`selftest`); its engine waits in `engine/<version>`, the new keeper's `V`.
  `updates/installed.json` keeps `engine`, `engines` and `downgradeSafe`; a confirm keeps the engine
  running, the keeper's, the one the bridge runs from and those `engines` names (the one before is
  kept to go back to).
- **The swapper**: the keeper starts `kuvo-link.js engine-swap` (on the keeper's engine) each round
  while an older engine than its `V` runs, no update runs or is on trial, and none runs already
  (`run/engine-swap.json` names its process). It says where it stands in that file, `{from, to,
  since, stage, holding?, letGo?, pid}`:
  - `waiting`: nothing held. It looks every ten seconds; nothing at work on the engine for half a
    minute, it holds: no conversation at work (`api/session/active`), and, in each folder it has
    open (`api/debug/location`), no question or permission waiting, no terminal and no command
    running (as closing a folder counts them), nor a browser ask waiting. The time that comes (below)
    begins no hold while an open terminal or a question waiting on you is there (holding wouldn't
    outlast it): `blocked` (`terminal`, `ask`) says so, and its line asks you to close or answer it. Failing such a moment,
    it holds an hour on in the night's window (02:00 to 05:00 in your time zone), or a day on whatever
    the hour; at once after Update Now (`run/engine-swap.now`, which `update --now` writes).
  - `holding`: what's sent to a conversation on the engine waits on the box (below), and the turns
    under way end as they would. Once nothing is at work (looked at twice, a second apart), it swaps.
    Half an hour after it began holding, still not, it lets go (`letGo`): what it held goes to the
    engine at work, and it holds again only in a night's window at least an hour on (or on Update
    Now's word); a quiet moment still swaps.
  - `swapping`: what each conversation's inbox in the engine holds (the latest hundred updated in
    the last week) moves onto the box, waiting there in the order it would have gone, held as it was;
    then the keeper's `engine-halt` stops the engine alone (never marked stopped: while
    `run/.engine-swapping` names a swapper that runs, the keeper starts no engine; one that went
    leaves the keeper to start it), a copy of its data is kept in `updates/backups` as an update
    keeps one (no room: it rests a day), and `kuvo-start engine` starts the new one. Once that
    answers `api/session?limit=1` (one whose log grows is still starting, for half an hour at most),
    what was held goes to it, and the change is noted (`run/update.json`'s `engine`, `changed`).
  - `back`: a new engine that fails three looks in a row over a minute goes back where the one
    before opens what it wrote (`downgradeSafe`, or its data unchanged since the copy):
    `run/engine-back` (`<new> <before> <when, s>`) has the keeper start the one before for a day,
    after which the new one is tried again; what was held goes to it (`back`). Where it can't go
    back, the keeper keeps starting the new one, and what was held waits on the box until an engine
    answers (`failed`).
- **The keeper never starts a newer engine by itself**: it notes the engine it last started
  (`run/engine-ran`; each round, the one running), and while one older than its `V` ran, an engine
  started again (a crash, a restart, the machine's) is that one, until the swapper (whose start it
  lets through while `run/.engine-swapping` is held, noting it as the one to run before it starts,
  so a new one that fails is the one started again, never the one before on what it wrote) changes
  it. Its bridge starts on its own `V`'s runtime meanwhile (as written, whatever rests). An update
  that leaves its engine at work notes that one; one that starts its engine with its code takes the
  note away first. A swapper started
  where one went while it held lets go of what that one held first.
- **What's held**: while the swapper holds, swaps or goes back, and only while its process runs and
  for an hour at most from when it began holding, a message to a conversation on the engine (never
  the coding agents' bridge, whose turns the change never touches) waits on the box as one does in
  a paused queue ("The queue"): `kuvo/sessions/<id>/send`, `…/queue/add`, a wake-up, another agent's
  letter, a goal's word, a session `start_session` made, a wake-up `kuvo-wake` fires (handed to the
  box as one for a stopped conversation is), and one sent to the engine straight
  (`POST api/session/<id>/prompt`, answered `{waits: true}`); a command or shell (`…/command`,
  `…/shell`) is answered 503 with the line, to send again once it's back. Nothing is started from
  the box's queue meanwhile; Send Now and Steer put the item first. The coding agents' bridge waits
  before it starts anything on the engine (a conversation on the engine's models, a review, a group
  chat's seat) until the hold ends. What the engine's inboxes held is kept on the box before it's
  taken from the engine, so a swapper cut off between the two leaves it in both, never neither.
  If a transfer stops partway through, that conversation stays held while Kuvo clears the remaining
  inbox and then sends the saved messages in order. The queue's answer carries `line` while it holds.
  During an engine change, `kuvo/update`'s `engineChange.line` and the update line in `computers`
  tell the computer's state. Once the hold ends, what waits for each conversation the
  engine has that isn't paused goes, each once and in its order: the first to start a turn where
  none runs, the rest (and all, into one that runs) as each was sent.

### The update gate

GPUI draws the box-authored `compatibility: {state, missing?}` from `kuvo/info`
and Computers rows. The box uses [gate-required.txt](gate-required.txt) for the
expected capabilities. `open` has them, `behind` can be used with available
features and offers an update, and `held` shows the update in place of the
areas. A response without a compatibility projection is used as it is.
A box with no `kuvo/info` may have only an update view. Actual requests go to
the box. A staged or newer fleet target by itself does not refuse work.

The resident owns plan limits, usage history, Insights, artifacts, Library,
voice and Work Queue sign-in independently of the agents bridge. The private
`run/box-services.json` endpoint can name the resident itself. It has the
same authentication and route format across the transition.

A resident that manages the engine reports optional `engineState` in
`kuvo/info`: `idle`, `starting`, `running` or `stopped`. A session request
that requires a cold engine waits for the shared launch and proceeds with the
same request. Event subscriptions and active-session polling leave an idle
engine asleep. An engine with a running turn, terminal, command or pending
approval remains available. A due wake-up can start the engine without a
client connected. Parking releases the engine without setting `stopped`.
 It preserves the bridge-shaped
`kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits…` and `kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage…` routes.
Older bridges can still own these stores during compatibility or rollback.
See [bridge ownership](../box/docs/bridge-ownership.md).

The old client-computed gate and associated SSH installer and phone release
ordering applied to retired clients. Installed builds can still use the
legacy routes described under “For released Macs”.

### The browser on a machine

A connected MCP client can remain open while Chrome sleeps. After ten minutes
with no working tool, viewer or browser ask, the keeper saves open pages and
closes Chrome. The next tool or viewer starts it again.

The browser agents use on a machine (`kuvo-browser.js`, its keeper and tools) is Chrome for
Testing, run headless from `~/.kuvo-code/browser/current`. The box sets it up itself, with or
without a desktop. The current box uses this browser on Linux and macOS, x86-64
and ARM64. The old app-owned Mac layout could use its Swift app browser.

- **What**: the build this `kuvo-link.js` pins (`src/link/browser/linux.json` and `mac.json`,
  written by `scripts/browser-runtime.py`): Chrome for Testing's zip for the machine's system and
  processor, each with its size and SHA-256; on Linux also the Rocky Linux 8 packages that hold the
  libraries and fonts Chrome needs, which servers often lack. A newer pin comes with a Kuvo Code
  update (the signed release brings `kuvo-link.js`).
- **From**: only `https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/` (Google's Chrome for
  Testing) and `https://dl.rockylinux.org/pub/rocky/8/`, then `…/vault/rocky/8.10/` for a package
  moved there. HTTPS, no redirects, the address exactly as pinned.
- **Checked**: each download's size (it stops past it) and SHA-256 before anything of it is
  unpacked; one that doesn't match is deleted and the setup fails, saying so. Nothing downloaded is
  run while setting up. The box unpacks the zip and packages itself (no `unzip`, `xz` or `rpm`
  needed): nothing outside the build's folder, no link that leads out of it (checked again once
  the build is put together), no set-user-ID. Of
  the packages it takes only `usr/lib64/*.so*` (links only to a name beside them), fonts and
  licenses, by their own names.
- **Where**: `browser/.box-staging-<pid>-<random>` while it works (downloads and all, removed
  whatever happens, and by the next setup if one was cut off), then `browser/<build>` with
  `chromium-version` and `kuvo-version` (the box's version), and `current` moved to it in one step.
  A build a browser still runs from stays until nothing does; `browser/profile` (sign-ins) always
  stays. It needs about 1 GB free to set up.
- **When**: on the first browser tool call, when the live view connects, or on an explicit
  `POST kuvo/browser`. The live view gets setup progress and the browser tool waits for setup.
  A failed setup can be tried again after `run/browser.next`. A setup runs again when the
  browser cannot start because its build is incomplete
  (`--repair`: after one that went well, not again for six hours for the same build, unless asked
  `now`; one that failed waits as any failure does). One setup at a time
  (`run/.browser-installing`, taken over in one step when its process is gone). An older build
  keeps working while a newer one is set up.
- **Failures**: no network, a source that answers otherwise or too slowly, a checksum, no room. The
  first failure stops every download still going; then it notes why and tries again by itself
  after 1, 5, 15, then 60 minutes. What only an update fixes (a build Google or Rocky no longer
  has, a system or processor it has none for) it doesn't try again by itself. Only a client asking
  `now` (you, with Try Again) has it try at once; the tools and the live view wait as it says.
- **State**: `run/browser-install.json`, `{state, progress?, message?, at, failures?, retryAt?, id?,
  repairedAt?, repairedId?}`. A setup asked for says `checking` at once, before its process starts.
- `kuvo/browser` (a machine's; feature `browser`):
  - `GET` answers `{state, chromium, installed, progress, message, retryAt}`: `state` is `missing`
    (none, and none being set up), `checking`, `downloading` (`progress`, 0 to 1), `installing`,
    `ready` or `failed` (`message`; `retryAt` when it tries again, ms, or null). `chromium` is the
    pinned version, `installed` the one in use.
  - `POST {now?, repair?}` sets it up unless the pinned build's in use (or `repair`), or it waits
    after a failure (unless `now`): 202 with the status.
  - A Mac asks over SSH with `box route`. From a shell: `kuvo-link.js browser install [--now]
    [--repair]` (the setup itself, as the keeper runs it), `browser start [--now] [--repair]` (in
    a process of its own, as `POST`; `kuvo-browser.js` uses it) and `browser status`.
- **The live view** (`kuvo-browser.js connect`) says `Kuvo.installing {state, progress}` while it
  waits for the setup, then `Kuvo.hello`; a setup that failed is `Kuvo.error` with `kind: "missing"`
  and why (an older Mac then puts the browser there itself, as it did). A tool that waited says
  why, or to try again in a minute.
- **The keeper's version**: `kuvo-browser.js` is built from `box/src/browser`
  (`scripts/build-browser.sh`), which writes its keeper's version in: a hash of its source, so any
  change to the file's source (its tools' code too) restarts the keeper once a new process starts,
  closing its pages (sign-ins stay). Its `Kuvo.hello` says it as `build`, and its `version` is the
  box's `bin/box-version` (`dev` before a Mac or an update has written one). A process replaces a running keeper only while its own file is
  the one in place, and then only one of another `build`, or one from before (`keeper` a number
  below 51, and no `build`).
- Only in a test's folder: `KUVO_BROWSER_SOURCE` (an address serving `<host>/<path>`),
  `KUVO_BROWSER_PINS` and `KUVO_BROWSER_SYSTEM`; a test's folder without them downloads nothing.
- An older Mac (before this) still sends its own build over SSH when the machine has none or an
  older one. The box leaves a build of the same Chromium or a newer one in place, and that Mac
  leaves the box's (marked by a newer Kuvo Code) as it is.

### The browser's data

Every box keeps its browser's data itself, in its `browser` folder (`~/.kuvo-code/browser`; this
Mac's box in its app's folder, `<its folder>/box/browser`), and it never leaves the box but in these
answers (feature `browser.data`). This Mac's agents still browse in its app's panel until this
Mac's box runs a browser of its own (#693): until then its routes answer what its box keeps, which
no client shows yet.

- **History**: the sites its browser opened (agents' pages too), a site per host without `www.`
  and with a port where the address names one (two dev servers on localhost are two), 300 at most
  (the oldest go), each with how often and when it was last opened, the address that names it
  best (its front page's once seen) and that page's title. The keeper (`kuvo-browser.js host`)
  only notes each page as it loads, and its site's icon the first time since Chrome started, as
  Chrome fetched it as the page's own (from its `<link rel=icon>`, else `/favicon.ico`; never an
  SVG, nothing over 128 KB): a line each in `browser/visits.jsonl`. The box takes them in as the
  history is asked for, or as the keeper asks once they've piled up (`kuvo-link.js browser fold`),
  into `browser/history.json` and `browser/icons/<host>`.
  - `GET kuvo/browser/history` → `{"sites": [{host, url, title, visits, lastVisit, icon}]}`, most
    suggested first (visits count, and fade over two weeks), `lastVisit` in ms; `icon`, whether
    there's one.
  - `GET kuvo/browser/icons/<host>` → the icon's bytes, with its type (PNG, ICO, JPEG, GIF or
    WebP), or `404`.
  - `DELETE kuvo/browser/history/<host>` takes a site out (until it's visited again), with its icon;
    `DELETE kuvo/browser/history` clears it all, the keeper's notes not yet taken in too. Each
    answers the history then.
- **Website data**: the sites that keep data in the browser, by registrable domain (as near as
  can be told without the public suffix list: `example.co.uk`).
  - `GET kuvo/browser/sites` → `{"sites": [{site, kinds}]}`, by name; `kinds` of `cookies` and
    `storage` (what its pages stored).
  - `DELETE kuvo/browser/sites/<site>` removes a site's data, which signs the browser out of it;
    `DELETE kuvo/browser/sites`, every site's. Each answers the sites then (without the one
    removed, whose stored data Chrome may still be clearing a moment later). `<site>` is a name as
    the list has it (`400` for a part of one, as `com`); `503 {"message"}` when nothing could be
    removed now (Chrome starting, or its files busy). While Chrome runs, through it, in a page:
    each of the site's cookies deleted as Chrome has it (`Network.deleteCookies`), then what each
    of its hosts stored (`Storage.clearDataForOrigin`); every site's, all cookies and the cache.
    With Chrome stopped, from its profile's files, cookies first (the `Cookies` database; the
    site's IndexedDB; every site's, the profile's storage folders whole), holding
    `browser/.profile-editing` meanwhile (the keeper starts Chrome once it's gone, or once it's
    half a minute old); the rest of what a site stored is cleared in the first page Chrome has as
    it next starts (`browser/clear-sites.json`, kept until Chrome takes each).
  - The box's own calls to the keeper (these, and `siteSignedIn`, "Integrations") join with
    `Kuvo.key {key, quiet: true}`: they neither start the browser nor keep it running.
- **Settings**: `browser/settings.json`, and whether agents' tabs are left open, the file the
  keeper has always read (`browser/keeps-agent-tabs`).
  - `GET kuvo/browser/settings` → `{searchEngine, searchEngines: [{id, title}], tidiesAgentTabs,
    offersToSave, never}`: the search engine (`google`, `duckDuckGo`, `bing`, `brave`, `kagi` or
    `ecosia`) and those offered in order with their names; whether agents' tabs no one looked at
    close an hour after their last use; whether the browser offers to save a password you sign in
    with, and the sites you said Never to (hosts).
  - `PATCH kuvo/browser/settings` with any of `searchEngine`, `tidiesAgentTabs`, `offersToSave` and
    `never` (the whole list, for older callers) → the settings, or `400 {"message"}` for one that isn't right. The
    agents' tools search with the box's engine once it has one (before, the one its Mac names,
    `KUVO_SEARCH`); `kuvo-browser.js` is built with the engines' addresses.
  - `PUT kuvo/browser/settings/never/<host>` adds one host, and `DELETE` on the same path takes
    it out (`browser.data.never`). Use the host as a percent-encoded path segment, including its
    port if present. Both return the settings after the edit and can be sent again. The box
    keeps other hosts and settings as they stand when it applies the edit.
- **Taken in once, on this Mac's box**: as its own browser's keeper first starts (`kuvo-link.js
  browser take-in`; on a machine it only notes there's nothing to take), what its app's panel kept
  before (Kuvo Code 0.5–0.7), so nothing the app keeps meanwhile is left behind: its history (`Browser/history.json` in the app's folder,
  or the folder this box moved from), merged with the box's; its icons (`Browser/Icons`) for the
  sites taken; and, where the box has no browser settings of its own yet, the app's (its
  preferences: `browser.searchEngine`, `panel.tidiesAgentTabs`, `passwords.offersToSave`,
  `passwords.never`). Only read: the app's copy stays. `browser/app-data-read` says when, and
  what it took; nothing is taken again.
- **Pages kept across a stop**: the keeper keeps the pages open as it stops (`run/pages.json`, at
  most 8) with the conversation that worked in each last (`[{url, session}]`; a keeper before
  this kept addresses alone, which it still reads), and each opens again as that conversation's.

## Notifications

What the Mac shows as a notification goes to each paired phone too, as the relay's `push`
with a mail frame, sealed with the sender's static key for the phone's. Only to phones: a paired
device of kind `desktop` (`clients.kind`) is sent none, as Apple has nothing for its address. Its payload, JSON:

```json
{"t": "notify", "title": "Fixer", "subtitle": "kuvo-ai", "body": "Wants to run npm.",
 "category": "permission", "thread": "ses_…", "data": {"session": "ses_…", "request": "per_…"}}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | Who's telling: a bot's name, a session's title, a group chat's name. |
| `subtitle` | Optional: the project, or who in a group chat. |
| `body` | What the Mac shows: the request, the question, the last words of a reply. |
| `category` | What it's about, below. |
| `thread` | What it's grouped under: the session's id, or the group chat's. |
| `data` | Where it opens: `session` or `group`; `request` for a permission or a form, with `requestSession` when the session asking isn't the one shown (a subagent's), and `answerable: "0"` when its notification mustn't answer it from buttons (its words say less than it covers, as most permissions' do, or some of its text shows as dots), `alwaysTitle`, its Always button as it says what it saves ("Always Allow Edits", "Always Allow git push", "Always Allow ~/notes"), and `always: "0"` for a permission whose Always would save a wider rule than it shows (`git push *` for `git push origin main`), which a phone that can't name it gives Allow Once and Don't Allow only; `ask` for a browser ask; `quiet: "1"` for one that shows without lighting the screen or a sound (what a goal needs of you, its digest), and `wake: "1"` for what a goal needs of you where you asked to be woken. |

| Category | When |
| --- | --- |
| `permission` | An agent asks to do something. `request` is the permission. |
| `question` | An agent asks a question, or for a form filled in. `request` is the form. |
| `ask` | An agent browsing asks for a sign-in, a code or a step. `ask` is it. |
| `finished` | A run finished with a reply to you, or a conversation sent you something on purpose (`notify_user`). |
| `failed` | A run stopped with an error. |
| `report` | A bot's news: its reply to you, what it sent you on purpose (`notify_user`), a goal's digest (`quiet`) or its report. |
| `blocked` | A bot's goal needs you (`quiet`, or `wake` where you asked to be woken). |
| `message` | Something in a group chat. |
| `update` | A coding agent's update notice ("Codex 0.161.0 is available", "Codex updated to 0.161.0"); `data.notice` is its id in `kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/updates/notices`, `thread` `update:<program>`. |

**Handed over, and how it went.** A push counts as handed over only once the box's relay
connection takes it: one closing as it's handed over is held and tried again, as when the relay
isn't there (`kuvo/attention`, below). The relay answers each push with `pushed` (above). Each box
keeps the last answer for each of its phones in `run/notices/pushed.json`, by the phone's key:
`{"<key>": {"at", "outcome": "sent"|"noPhone"|"notAllowed"|"refused"|"unknown", "sent"?}}`, `at` and `sent`
(when one last went through) in ms since 1970. So a phone that hears nothing can be told from one
that was sent nothing: `noPhone` is no registration at its address (it registers again as it
connects), `notAllowed` a registration that doesn't name this box among its senders, `refused`
Apple's no, `unknown` an answer the box doesn't know. No route reads it yet (bridge 0.9.210).

A phone should ignore a category it doesn't know, and show the notification plainly.

What's news, each box decides alike (`notices/news.ts`), for your phones and its clients
(`kuvo/notices`):

- **A reply to you** is: a run that ends after your own message (or your answer, approval or
  pick, which the box passes on), and, in a conversation of yours (not a bot's, nor one an agent
  started), one after what it left running or started coming back (a command, a subagent, its
  sessions' news). Read from the session's latest turn, back to its start however long it is:
  any word of yours in it makes it yours. One whose start can't be reached counts as yours only in
  a conversation of yours.
- **A question, a permission or a failure** always is; a failure with its reason on one line
  ("Stopped with an error: …").
- **What an agent sends on purpose** (`notify_user`, "Agents' tools") always is.
- **Nothing else**: not a run of the session's own accord (its wake-up or watch, `[Wake-up]` or
  `metadata.kuvo.wake`; a goal's word to its bot), nor one answering another agent (a letter,
  `[Message from …]`, as a session an agent started gets its task). Those still leave the
  conversation unread, as a muted chat does.

The body is one short sentence in plain words, never a command line, a path, a flag or a code (those
are on the card in the conversation, and in logs): a reply's first (past headings, code and lists; a
line that leads into a list with its first item), its Markdown taken off, a path said as its last name
and a web address as its site, cut at a word to 100 characters with "…"; a question's own words the
same way; a group chat's last word the same way. What the box words itself is under 60 characters:
a permission says what it would do and at most a program, a file's name or a site ("Wants to run
du.", "Wants to edit notes.md.", "Wants to open example.com.", "Wants to work outside the project."),
so its buttons answer it (`answerable` not `"0"`) only where those words say all it covers (no
specifics, or each command line a program's name alone); a failure's reason follows "Stopped with an
error:" only where it's words and not a code. A notice's title and subtitle are cut at a word to 60
characters, and whatever else a source gives (a goal's report) is cut to its first sentence the same
way, in the box, so every client and phone gets the same short words.

The payload stays under 2,500 bytes, so the push fits the 4 KB Apple takes: a body that
doesn't fit is cut, ending in "…". Keys are sorted, as both sides write them.

Who sends it: each box, for what happens on it, so each notice comes once.

- **This Mac's box**, for the Mac's own sessions and group chats, as a machine's bridge words
  them, and for what agents ask as they browse in the Mac's panel, which its app hands it
  (`kuvo/attention/notice`, below); never a machine's. Like a machine, it holds each a little
  while a client is in use there ("kuvo/attention", below), and sends none while the Mac's phone
  link is off.
- **A machine's bridge**, for that machine's sessions (permissions, questions, runs finished
  or failed, bots' news), what agents ask for as they browse there (category `ask`), and its
  coding agents' sessions and the group chats that live there (a meeting held, a bot done with
  its part: category `message`, `data.group`), each as the Mac words it, whether a Mac is
  connected to it or not, and without a group chat's seats, as the Mac does. An ask goes once
  it's still asked a couple of seconds later, so one a connected Mac answers at once with a saved
  password doesn't. An engine run a coding agent's session started (Auto on an engine model)
  tells its news as that session's, once. A Mac connected to the machine shows the machine's
  news in its own notifications, and doesn't send them to your phones.

### kuvo/attention

While you're using a client, each box it's connected to holds your phones' notices a little, so
your phone doesn't buzz for what you're already looking at, were shown, or answer at once.

- **A client in use says so**, for a lease it renews: `POST kuvo/attention` with `{"for":
  <seconds>, "sessions": [<id>, …], "shown": [{"session": <id>, "ask"?: bool, "request"?: <id>},
  …]}`. `for` is how long it's in use from now (the box's clock, so the two clocks needn't agree),
  cut to 60; `0` says it isn't any more. `sessions`, optional, are the conversations on its screen:
  sessions by id, group chats by theirs. `shown`, optional, are notices it just showed you itself:
  each one's conversation, whether it asked you something (`permission`, `question`, `ask`; false
  if left out) or was news, and for what's asked, the request or ask it's about (`data.request`,
  else `data.ask`). The answer is `{"for": <seconds granted>}`; 400 `{message}` for a `for` that
