  "You stopped it.", with “<title>” stopped by you). Show what it said, never the words for the
  lead. `still working` shows nothing, old ones included. **Its sessions' news** (`messages.session-news`):
  each page of messages a box forwards reads such a note for the client (marked, or from before it
  was) and adds `metadata.kuvo.news`, one `{session, title, status, said}` a session it tells of, in
  order: `session` its address, `title` its title ("New Session" for none), `status` a word or two
  beside its name (`finished`, `asks`, `stopped`, `stopped by you`, `not summarized`), and `said`
  the card's words (its reply, or "It ended without a reply."; why it stopped; what it asks; "You
  stopped it."), none of the words for the lead. A client draws those as they are and reads no
  text: `[]` for one that only says a session's still working (nothing to show), and no `news` for
  one in words its box doesn't read (show its text whole). A goal started or resumed is a word in the next reply's footer; the
  rest show nothing. The same goes for the engine's and the bridge's notes (`synthetic`, `system`):
  they're for the model and show nothing, but what changed (the model or its effort, the mode, a
  summary, the project's folders) is said in a word beside the next reply's time (`ReplyChanges`).
  The agents bridge's own notes for the user ("Your PreToolUse hook failed…", "Codex asks for
  verification to go on…", "… Going on with Codex.") carry `metadata.kuvo.notice: true`, and show
  as a quiet line (`Message.Notice.isForYou`); those from before it marked them show nothing. A
  `Your answer` note `You approved: <what>` (what you approved after Auto's reviewer held it back)
  shows as "Allowed by you" on the first step after it that does `<what>` (`WorkAnswer.yours`), and
  nowhere if none does.
- A prompt a phone sends (`POST api/session/<id>/prompt`, and `kuvo/agents/api/…` alike) gets a
  block at the end of its text that tells the agent it's from the phone: a line `<from-phone>`,
  the words in `FromPhone.swift`, and a line `</from-phone>`. Every box adds it, in the same
  words (this Mac's box since bridge 0.9.64; the app did before); send the words without it. Show a
  message from its parts (`phone`), as sent from the phone. It tells the agent to keep replies short and to show files with
  `show_file`. Kuvo Code's desktop app over the link (a session whose first message said `client:
  "desktop"`, `clients.kind`) gets none: who it names with `&` is said, as for a phone, and nothing
  about a small screen.
- A message whose request arrived whole (`POST api/session/<id>/prompt`, and
  `kuvo/agents/api/…` alike) goes on to its conversation even if the phone that sent it ends its
  session or cancels meanwhile: its files are kept on the box by then. So one a client counted as
  failed may have arrived: sent again under the same `id` (as the share sheet does), it's taken
  once; under a new one, it's a second message. A command (`…/command`, which has no `id`) still
  stops with the session that sent it.
- An agent shows a file in the conversation with `show_file`, one of Kuvo Code's tools (on the
  Mac and machines, for the engine and the coding agents): a tool call named
  `kuvo-browser_show_file` with input `{"path": "<full path on the computer it runs on>",
  "caption"?}`, which fails when the path isn't a file. Show a completed one in the
  conversation's flow, as `generate_image`'s: a picture (by its extension) large, any other
  file as a row that opens it, its caption under it; get its bytes with `kuvo/file` from the
  computer the session runs on.
- A picture opened from a conversation (yours, or one an agent made, showed or took of a page to
  show you) opens among every picture of the conversation, in order, across its messages
  (KuvoClient's `ConversationPictures`): your messages' files that are pictures and those they
  sent as paths (the note of attached files names them), then each completed `generate_image`,
  `kuvo-browser_show_file` of a picture and `kuvo-browser_browser_screenshot` with `"show": true`,
  in the order of their messages and steps, up to an undo waiting to be kept; a group chat's, its
  bots' messages' steps alike. Not a step's own screenshots, nor pictures in a reply's words. A
  picture in the composer opens after them. Each is known by an id that stays: `<message>#<n>` for
  a message's nth file, `<message>@<path>` for one sent as a path, `<step>-<n>` for a step's nth
  output, `<step>-shown` for a file shown.
- `kuvo/wakes/<session>`: a session's (or chat's) wake-ups and watches, which its
  agent sets with `kuvo-wake`, as the bar over the Mac's composer shows them: `{"wakes": [{id,
  due, note, every}], "watches": [{letters, every, check, note}], "paused"}` (`due` in seconds
  since 1970, `every` like `1d`, left out for one that doesn't repeat; paused while it's archived: archive it as the Mac does,
  `PATCH api/session/<id>` with `{"metadata": {"kuvo.archived": true}}` (`false` brings it back),
  and its wake-ups wait, or come back, when the flag changes (it can go with every change to its
  metadata); a Mac sees to it, and a machine's bridge does with the Mac closed too; a session's
  first wake-up or watch made while it's archived, by a client or by its agent's `kuvo-wake` on any
  box, is held from the start, and any its box finds archived when they're due is held then; a pause of your own stays through both). Archived while it waits on you (a permission or a question, its subagents' too), either way or by the box's Remove Project, its box stops its run (and those subagents'), as a bot's Stop and Archive does: the asks go with it. `POST kuvo/wakes/<session>` with `{"due", "every"?,
  "note"}` adds one, as the bar over the Mac's composer does (`due` at least a minute away;
  `every` 30m, 2h, 1d, 1w or weekdays, at least 5m), with the computer's own clock and weekends;
  `400 {"message"}` for what can't be one, `409` with 50 waiting. `POST
  kuvo/wakes/<session>/pause` with `{"paused": true}` holds them (a pause of your own), `false`
  lets them go (not archiving's hold: they still wait until it's back, bridge 0.9.121); with `{"archived": true}` they're held as archiving holds them (a client that
  archived it on the engine directly says so, and its box stops it if it waits on you; with
  `"stop": false`, only held: a first wake-up made for one archived before), `false` lets go of only that hold. Both answer the
  list as it is then. `POST
  kuvo/wakes/<session>/cancel` with `{"wake": "<id>"}` or `{"watch": "<letters>"}` cancels one;
  `POST kuvo/wakes/<session>/now` with `{"wake": "<id>"}` sends it now (one that repeats still
  comes back at its time). Both answer `200 {}`, `404 {}` when there's no such one, `409
  {"message"}` while its conversation is on its way to another computer, or `503 {"message"}`
  when it couldn't go. Each box answers for its own sessions and bots, a Mac's and a machine's
  alike, with the Mac closed too: ask the box a conversation lives on (one that keeps none answers
  an empty list). A wake-up reaches the conversation as a
  message starting with `[Wake-up] `, its note whole (a watch's: its note, then what its check
  printed). When its agent gave it a summary (the tools' `summary`, `kuvo-wake … --summary`), the
  message carries it in `metadata.kuvo.wake.summary`, one line, and so does one that waits on the
  box (`queue/add` keeps that mark, and only that, from its `metadata`). A client's card shows the
  summary, at most two lines, and opens to the note; without one (one from before, or none given),
  the note's first sentence: its first line, Markdown's `*` and `` ` `` and leading `#`, `>` and
  `-` taken out, up to the first `.`, `!`, `?` or `…` with a space or the line's end after it
  (KuvoClient's `WakeMessage`). Each page of messages a box forwards marks such a message for the
  client (`messages.wake-cards`), with or without a summary given: `metadata.kuvo.wake` is
  `{summary, note}`, `summary` as above (the one given, else the note's first sentence) and `note`
  the whole note without `[Wake-up] `; a client draws it as a card of its own (an alarm clock,
  "Woke up", the summary, opening to the note), reading no text. An older box's page has no `note`:
  draw the message as it was. `GET kuvo/wakes` lists every session with a wake-up or a
  watch at once, for the marks beside them in a list: `{"sessions": [{session, next, watching,
  wakes, watches, paused}]}` (`next`, the soonest, in seconds since 1970, left out when it has
  none; `wakes`, `watches` and `paused` as `GET kuvo/wakes/<session>` says them, so a client reads
  them all in one call, and left out by an older box). Bots' come with `kuvo/bots`. Each box
  lists its own.
- `POST kuvo/wakes/<session>/watch` with `{"every", "check", "note"}` makes a watch, as its agent
  makes one with `kuvo-wake watch`: `every` 5m or more, 2h or 1d, `check` a shell command run on
  that computer, `note` what to do when its output changes. It answers the list as it is then;
  `400 {"message"}` in `kuvo-wake`'s own words for what can't be one (20 watches already, say),
  `404 {}` for a conversation that isn't there, `409 {"message"}` while it moves.
  `GET kuvo/wakes/events` follows every conversation's wake-ups, watches and pause on the box,
  its bots' and sessions' (`wakes.events` in `features`), as ndjson: a line now and again each
  time they change (added, fired, canceled, paused), `{"sessions": [{session, wakes: [{id, due,
  note, every}], watches: [{letters, every, check, note}], paused}]}` with notes and checks whole,
  and only conversations that have any or are paused.
  `GET kuvo/wakes/<session>/events` (`bots.wake-ups`) follows just that conversation in the
  same shape as its GET, including an empty schedule. Both routes give each entry a `summary`
  from the keeper, or the first sentence of the note if the keeper has none. A wake-up's
  `cancelKey`, where present, can be sent as `wake` even after that repeat advances.
  A watch's `next` is its next check in seconds since 1970. A check wakes the bot only if the
  watch finds a change.
- `kuvo/asks` (`GET` or `HEAD`): what agents ask you for while they browse (a box's own; a Mac's, its machines' too): a
  sign-in (the fields the page has, and the accounts Passwords keeps for the site, never
  their passwords), a one-time code, or a step only you can do. `kuvo/asks/events` is the same
  list as a response that doesn't end: a line of JSON now, and another each time it changes.
  `POST kuvo/asks/<id>` answers one: `{"answer": "signIn", "username", "password", "save"?,
  "agents"?}` (or `"saved": "<account>"`, which the Mac fills in from its vault itself),
  `{"answer": "code", "code"}`, `{"answer": "done"}` or `{"answer": "declined"}`. What's typed
  goes into the page, never to the agent. A sign-in is kept as the Mac's own card keeps it, over
  https only (a site that's `http://…` or a file has `offersToSave` false, and `save` and `agents`
  are left out): `save` keeps what's typed in the vault (a saved account's password typed anew is
  kept too), and `agents: true` is Let agents sign in here on their own, for the account answered
  with (bridge 0.9.143; a client asks for Face ID or Touch ID first when it's a saved account's).
  The answer comes once it's kept: `200 {}`, or `200 {"message"}` when the vault didn't take it
  (the page has the sign-in all the same). A `saved` account that's gone, or whose password can't
  be read, gets `422 {"message"}` and the ask stays, for the password to be typed instead. An ask has `"passkey": true` once its site asked for a passkey
  (then, or in the ten minutes before): the browsers can't use passkeys yet, so a client tells
  you to sign in another way.
- A machine's bridge answers the same three for what's asked in that machine's
  browser, with the Mac closed too: `saved` is empty and `offersToSave` false (saved passwords
  are the Mac's), and a `saved` answer gets `400 {"message"}`. A Mac connected to the machine
  lists the same asks, by the same `id`: the first answer counts, and the ask goes from both.
  The Mac's copy names the machine's box too, `box`: its link address, as `kuvo/hosts` gives it
  (left out while the Mac doesn't know it, and on a box's own list, whose asks are all its own).
  The machine's own list is the one that counts: a client that follows that box shows the
  machine's copy, and leaves out one the Mac lists (a Mac that went to sleep never says it's
  over) that the box, followed now, doesn't. An answer goes where the copy shown came from; when
  that computer can't take it (unreachable, or `503` with Kuvo Code closed on a Mac), it goes to
  the other one listing the same ask: the box a Mac's copy names, unless that box doesn't serve
  `kuvo/asks` (a bridge from before it, whose `404` would read as answered), or a Mac whose list
  has it. A `404` from a box that serves `kuvo/asks` means it's answered or no longer asked.
  The browser keeps them in `~/.kuvo-code/run/browser-asks.json` for the bridge, and waits the
  whole 15 minutes for an answer while the bridge runs, rather than a few for a Mac.
- `kuvo/groups`: the group chats that live on the computer asked, with their bots (face, name, session), who's
  talking, whether one is under way or paused, and the last thing said; `kuvo/groups/events`
  streams that list as it changes, and `kuvo/groups/<id>/events` one chat's latest messages,
  the same way. `POST kuvo/groups/<id>` writes to it (`{"text"}`, as written); `…/stop`, `…/keep-going`
  and `…/viewed` do what they say; `…/undo` (`{"message"}`) takes a message of yours back and
  answers with what was taken. A wrap-up can carry `tasks`, who does what: each with `id`, `bot`,
  `task`, `state` (`proposed`, `waiting`, `working`, `done` or `failed`), `title` (`groups.task-title`: the box’s display words for that state, including a working task waiting on a stopped conversation, drawn as sent), `started`/`finished`,
  and `after` (the bots whose parts come first; it waits for them);
  `…/start` (`{"message"}`, the wrap-up) hands each proposed part to its bot's own conversation.
  One chat's `stopped` lists the bots whose `working` part waits on their own conversation, its
  queue paused (stopped by you, or held after a run that failed; left out for none): show "Waiting: Ada's conversation is stopped" on the part,
  with Resume, which resumes that conversation on the bot's computer (`POST
  kuvo/sessions/<its session>/queue/resume`), and the part goes on.
  While a bot talks, one chat's events carry `activity`, what it's doing, its last step:
  `{"kind": "tool", "call"}` (a tool call as a message's `steps` hold them, without its output),
  `{"kind": "thinking", "text"}` (the line its thinking is on) or `{"kind": "writing"}`. Show
  them under who's talking, so a long turn doesn't look stuck. A line of one chat's events whose
  messages are as they were leaves `messages` out (only who's talking or what they're doing
  changed): keep the ones you have. The first line always has them.
  A bot's message with `report` (a task's id) is it reporting back on its part. Times are
  seconds since 1970.
  Each computer lists only its own, a Mac's as a machine's: ask each for its chats. The coding
  agents' bridge there runs them, and answers them itself (at `api/kuvo/link/groups…`, which
  the link passes on as it answers, a followed one line by line; this Mac's PhoneLink as a
  machine's `kuvo-link.js`), with every rule of what can be made or changed (503 while it isn't up
  or isn't answering: ask again; 404 only when none run there). One moving between computers isn't
  listed on either while it moves (held), and `POST kuvo/groups/<id>` and `…/undo` answer 409
  meanwhile. Moving one is on the Mac (Move to Computer), not the phone.
  `kuvo/groups/joinable` says who can be in a group chat made there: `{"bots": [<as a chat's
  members list them>]}`, every bot that lives there, the first made first, then the bots of your
  other computers that take a chat's turns ("Peers", group chats), each with `computer` (its
  computer's name). Offer exactly those in New Group Chat and Edit Group Chat for that computer
  (`features`: `groups.joinable`). A chat's members list a bot of another computer the same way:
  `id`, `name`, `look`, `session` (empty when that computer didn't say), `directory` (empty: its
  folder is on that computer) and `computer`. Don't open a member's conversation from a chat that
  has `computer`: it's on that computer, not the one asked.
- `kuvo/file?uri=<file:// URI>`: a file on that computer that an agent's reply or tool names
  (a picture it made, a file it shows you, a download), by its `file://` address, percent-encoded
  as a query value. Any file there its user can read, wherever it is: only your own clients reach
  it (never a peer), and they have that computer's terminals anyway. It answers `200` with its
  bytes and `content-type` (from its extension; `application/octet-stream` when unknown), `404
  {"message","reason":"fileNotFound"}` for one that isn't there or isn't a file (older boxes
  omit `reason`), `403 {"message"}` for one it can't read,
  `413 {"message"}` over 25 MB, or over `max` when it's given (`&max=<bytes>`: all a client would
  show of it), `400 {"message"}` for an address that isn't `file://`. Each box answers for its own files, a machine's with the Mac closed too.
  For a download to open locally, `&withMode=1` returns the same bytes with
  `content-type: application/vnd.kuvo.file; executable=0` or `executable=1`, from the execute
  bits on the opened source file. Older boxes ignore the query option and return the usual MIME.
  `GET kuvo/file/text?uri=<file:// URI>[&max=<bytes>]` (`file.text`, #708): the same file as a
  viewer shows it → `{"text": true, "encoding": "utf-8", "content"}`, its text, or `{"text": false}`
  for one that isn't text (a picture, a program, an encoding other than UTF-8, the only one read:
  UTF-8 with no NUL byte in it; a mark at its start, a BOM, isn't part of `content`), which a
  viewer says instead of showing. So no client looks through a file's bytes to tell. Refused as
  `kuvo/file` refuses (`400`, `403`, `404`, `413`), but `413` already over 4 MB, with or without
  `max`: its text comes as one answer. `GET` only (`405 {}` otherwise).
  Boxes with `file.text.path` also accept `?path64=<full path as unpadded base64url UTF-8>` in
  place of `uri` so the file name stays intact through the request path parser.
  `GET kuvo/file/info?uri=<file:// URI>` (`file.info`): the same access checks on the computer
  that owns the file. Opens it for reading to check access without reading its contents or applying
  the download size limit. Answers `200 {"exists":true,"name","size","kind","mime"}`, with the base
  name, size in bytes, and kind (`picture`, `pdf`, `text` or `other`) and MIME guessed from its
  extension. A missing path or a path that isn't a regular file answers `200` with `exists:false`,
  the requested base name and `size`, `kind` and `mime` all null. An invalid address is `400`,
  an inaccessible file is `403`, and other methods answer `405 {}`. Clients can opt in using
  `file.info`; boxes without it still serve `kuvo/file`.

### Custom Auto lists changed by id (`auto.lists`)

`kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/auto` GET returns `data.lists`, each with `id`, `name`,
`entries`, and an opaque `revision`. POST adds `{id, name, entries}`; PUT `<id>`
renames (`{revision, name}`) or sets contents (`{revision, entries}`). DELETE
`<id>` takes `{revision}` and keeps at least one list. PUT `order` takes
`{ids, was}`: both are arrays of ids, `was` the order read, and `ids` every id
once in the desired order. The names `order` and `limits` are reserved.
Changes return `data.lists` and `data.limits`. Stale revisions, duplicate adds,
and stale order return 409; read again and let the user retry. Different lists
can be changed independently. Whole-collection PUT is no longer supported.

### Goals

A conversation's goal ("/goal all tests in test/auth pass"): its agent works toward it on its own,
turn after turn, until a check after each turn finds it met. Each box runs its own, in its agents
bridge beside the engine, for the engine's sessions and the coding agents' alike, with no client
there (a machine's with the Mac closed too). The check reads the conversation and runs nothing: on
the engine, the session's model afresh, apart from the agent (OpenCode's free models answer only in
the session's own context, so there it's asked there); with the coding agents, their one-off
answer, another agent you're signed in to answering for one that has none (Antigravity, Cursor,
Grok). With none to answer, the goal pauses and says so. A client reaches them as `kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/goals…`
(the Mac app at `api/kuvo/goals…` on the bridge itself), on the box the conversation lives on, while
`kuvo/info` has `agents: true` (503 otherwise), where `features` has `goals`.

- `GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/goals` → `{data: [goal]}`: every goal on the box, a met one too until
  it's put away. `GET …/goals/<session>` → `{data: goal}`, or 404 when it has none.
- `PUT …/goals/<session>` with `{"condition", "long"?}` (at most 4,000 characters; `long` for a bot's
  goal with a plan, "Work › Goals": not briefed, checked or nudged here, only kept and paused at a
  model's limit) sets it, in place of one
  it had, and starts the agent on it at once: `{data: goal}`; 400 `{message}` for no condition or
  one too long, 404 for a conversation that isn't there, 409 for a subagent's (the conversation it
  works for has the goal), 503 when it can't be reached. A turn already under way counts only if
  the agent read the goal in it.
- `POST …/goals/<session>/pause` holds it: no other turn starts, and the box, told of it
  (`kuvo.goal.updated`, `pausedBy: "you"`, `note: "You paused it."`; one paused as you stopped a
  turn holds nothing more), stops the turn under way, keeping what was said, and holds the
  conversation as Stop does (its queue paused: what reaches it meanwhile waits on the box); for a
  bot's goal, its sessions at work stop too, and nothing of it goes on, not even at a limit's reset
  (bridge 0.9.143), nor a session one of its sessions starts (`start_session` answers 403; the bot's own
  conversation still starts one in a turn answering what you wrote there, not a letter or a wake-up). The box keeps the hold through a restart and, finding the bridge again, reads
  each goal it holds for: one resumed meanwhile goes on, one taken away leaves its conversation
  paused for Resume. `…/resume` lets it go: the conversation's queue on this box goes on, its last
  turn is checked (however it ended), and it carries on unless that met it; a bot is told to carry
  on from its plan (a box note, "Goal resumed"). Resume on the queue alone lets the conversation
  go but leaves the goal paused. Both `{data: goal}`, 404 when it has none,
  409 for one that's over (set it again instead).
- `DELETE …/goals/<session>` puts it away, over or not: `{}`, or 404.
- A goal: `{session, condition, state, note?, pausedBy?, resumesAt?, long?, started, ended?, turns,
  checking, last?}`. A goal at a model's limit carries on with a word to its agent ("the limit has
  reset"), not a check of the turn that failed; a check that meets one waits too. A `long` goal's
  turns are only kept: its plan says when to carry on. `state` is `working`, `paused` (`pausedBy`: `you`, `error` (a turn failed, said
  in `note`), `stalled` (three turns in a row doing nothing) or `limit` (a hundred turns since it was
  set or resumed; or a model's limit reached, with `resumesAt`: it carries on by itself then, a box
  restart in between too, and `note` says until when)), `met`, or `unmet` (it can't be met as asked: `note` says why). `turns`: the agent's
  turns toward it, each checked; `checking`: a check is under way; `last`: `{verdict: "met" |
  "not_met" | "impossible", reason, at}`, its reason what's left or what shows it's met. Times in
  ms since 1970.
- The bridge's events (`kuvo/agents/api/event`) carry `kuvo.goal.updated` `{sessionID, goal}` for
  each change, `goal` null once it's put away (or its conversation deleted, over or not, also while
  the box was stopped).
- In the conversation, the goal's messages to the agent are notes (`synthetic`) whose text starts
  with `[Goal] `: show their `description` ("Goal: …", "Not met yet: …") as the goal's. A turn
  you stop pauses it ("The turn was stopped."); so does one that fails. A turn cut short as the box
  stopped is checked once it's back, as any turn, and one is never checked twice. While its
  conversation is archived (`kuvo.archived` in its metadata, or the engine's own), the goal waits,
  still `working`: its last turn is checked once the conversation is brought back (bridge 0.9.121).
- There's no "/goal" in a composer any more: "/goal …" typed goes to the agent as words. A goal is
  set by the routes above, or by the agent (`propose_goal`).

### Plan limits

Each box reads the limits of your plans (a 5-hour window, a week, a model's own week, a month's
requests) and credits, for each account it runs that's signed in to Kuvo Code: every coding agent's
accounts (its own sign-in and those you added) and the engine's sign-ins. It reads them with the
sign-in Kuvo Code runs each with, never another login on the computer (your Claude Code in Terminal
on a Mac, whose box runs Claude with a sign-in of its own; the Cursor app's), and never renews one:
the agent or the engine that owns it does. (On a Mac, Codex's and Grok's own sign-ins are the ones
in `~/.codex` and `~/.grok`, as their sessions run with them; on a machine, Kuvo Code's own.) The coding agents' bridge reads them, a machine's with the Mac closed too, and keeps
the last reading in its folder (`limits.json`), through a restart. A client reaches them as
`kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits…` (the Mac app at `api/kuvo/limits…` on the bridge itself), while
`kuvo/info` has `agents: true` (503 otherwise), where `features` has `limits`.

- `GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits` → `{data: {accounts: [account], services, rows: [row]}}`.
  `accounts`: this box's own (one a peer's reading stood for a read of here, with that reading's
  windows, plan and credits where they're newer than its own, for clients from before `rows`);
  `rows`: every account across your computers (below, "Across your computers"), what a client
  lists. `services`: what
  this box reads the limits of (`claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `cursor`, `antigravity`, `copilot`,
  `openrouter`, `zai`, `ollama`, `opencode`), whether or not one is signed in now (Antigravity's
  always, since only boxes read it): a client shows those from here, and anything else from where
  it had them before; a client never adds to it. An account is listed exactly while it's signed
  in here (#778): a coding agent's as its agent says, the same word Settings › Accounts shows
  (`api/integration`'s `connections`; taken whenever Accounts or the models are listed, at each
  sign-in and sign-out here and each `integration.updated` the bridge tells, and asked again only
  when the sign-in its limits are read with changes, or once where there's none to look at:
  Codex's; a check that fails or doesn't answer leaves it as it was, never a sign-out), the
  engine's while the engine lists its sign-in (`services` still names each coding agent's
  service, signed in or not). One signed in is listed at once, read or not yet (no `windows` until it's read, or until a turn
  tells of it: a Mac's Claude); one signed out goes at once, and what was read of it with it, so
  a reading is never older than its account's sign-in. Until every agent has said once (the
  bridge just started), what's signed in by then is listed, and so is a coding agent's account
  whose sign-in is still in its folder, the same account as was last read here, as it was last
  read (so a client's rings don't blink out while the box restarts); one whose sign-in is gone
  from its folder is never listed from what was kept. One with no sign-in its plan limits could be read with (an API key, a Mac's Claude
  with an Anthropic Console sign-in) isn't.
  Each `account`:
  - `title` (`limits.titles`, #668): its name, the same in every client: its coding agent's
    ("Claude", "Codex", "Grok", "Cursor", "Antigravity"), else its plan's (the engine's sign-ins:
    "ChatGPT", "SuperGrok", "Copilot", "OpenRouter", "Z.ai", "Ollama", "OpenCode Go"; a service the
    box has no name for, capitalized), with what you called it ("Claude · Work"). In `rows`, told
    apart from another row of that name (below, "Names").
  - `provider` (`claude-code`, `claude-code@1f2e3d4c` for one you added, the engine's
    `github-copilot`…), `service` (its mark and color, as above), and for a coding agent's,
    `agent` (`claude`…) and `account` (`default` for its own sign-in, else the ID of one you
    added); `label`, what you called one you added ("Work"); `plan`, in its maker's words ("Max
    20x", "Pro"), when known.
  - `identity`: the account at its maker, 16 hex characters, the same from every box signed in to
    it (and from a coding agent's sign-in and the engine's to the same account), so a client
    lists it once. A hash of its maker's own ID for it, never the ID, an email or a secret:
    Claude's account and organization (on Linux as Claude Code keeps them beside its sign-in; on a
    Mac, whose token doesn't say who it's for, as Anthropic says in the signed policy record Claude
    Code fetches with that token and keeps in its settings folder, once it has run with it there),
    ChatGPT's account and workspace member, xAI's user, GitHub's login (from Copilot's
    answer), Cursor's user (from the access token Cursor exchanges its key for, known once Cursor
    has answered the exchange, whether or not its plan could be read), and an API key
    for OpenRouter, Z.ai and OpenCode Go. Absent where it isn't known, and
    from a box from before it: list that row as its box's own. Where it changes (signed in
    as another account there), the box drops what it kept of the one before, and the row says so
    (`problem`, `failed`) until the new one is read; Codex is read only through a Codex signed in
    as it is now.
  - `windows`: each `{id, used, resetsAt?, minutes?, model?, name?, amount?, read, source}`. `id` is its
    maker's name for it (`five_hour`, `seven_day`, `seven_day_sonnet`, Codex's `primary`); `used`,
    how much of it is gone, 0 to 1; `minutes`, how long it is (300, 10080) when said; `model`, the
    model it's for ("Sonnet", "Fable"), absent for the whole plan's; `name`, its maker's name for
    what it counts where that's neither ("Premium requests", "Web searches"); `amount`, `{used, limit,
    unit}` (`requests`, `usd`, `credits`) where the limit is a count or an amount; `read`, when
    this was read; `source`, `usage` (read from its maker) or `turn` (what a turn heard on the way,
    Claude Code's and Codex's rate-limit events, which keep a window current between reads). A
    window whose `resetsAt` had passed when the box answered has started over since (`limits.bar`,
    #668): it says `expired: true`, `used` 0 and neither `resetsAt` nor `amount` (in a row, `level`
    `calm`); a client shows it as not read since, not as used. The box tells clients again
    (`kuvo.limits.updated`) the moment a window listed starts over, so no client watches a clock
    for it. `title`, its name (`limits.titles`): `name`, else `model`, else by its length
    ("Session" for 300 minutes, "Weekly" for 10080, "Monthly", "3-day", "8-hour"), else "Limit".
  - `usage` (HTTP `rows`): display facts for the Usage page. `title` is the account title without
    a computer suffix. `computers` lists the named reading sources with `here` relative to the
    answering computer. With no windows it lists where the account is signed in. `status?` is
    `{words, warning}`. Each meter has `title, share, value, level, readAt, resetsAt?, resetLabels, freshForMs`.
    Each `resetLabels` entry is `{at, words}`, effective from `at`. Countdowns under a day round up.
    Before the first label, show “resets” followed by the local weekday and time of `resetsAt`.
    The timestamps are Unix milliseconds for the client to format in the viewer's time zone. These
    facts retain the historical reading after a reset. Draw it as old at once for an away or failing
    source, or when the time supplied in `freshForMs` has passed. That time ends at the earlier of
    the next reset, the source going away, or 30 minutes from the reading.
    The limits response also includes `usageUpdatedAt?`, the latest timestamp represented by the
    rows, including status-only accounts. Refresh may answer with `refreshPending: true`; follow
    `GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits/events` and GET the latest snapshot on each `{"changed":true}`
    line. The stream signals once when it opens and on `kuvo.limits.updated`, including refresh
    completion. Older boxes send `{}` signals. A `{"heartbeat":true}` line keeps the stream open.
    Retry a failed snapshot GET on the client's fallback timer.
    `refreshCompletedAt?` is the latest successful manual refresh time. `refreshFailed` reports
    whether the last refresh could not finish.
  - `balance` `{left, limit?, unit}`: credits left to spend, where the account has them.
  - `balance` with `limit`: what was bought (OpenRouter's total credits), so a client draws what's
    left of it as a meter.
  - `extras`: what the plan has beyond its windows, each `{id, name, kind, …}` (`name` its maker's
    own label), by `kind` (#631 E):
    - `spent` `{amount, unit, resetsAt?}`: an amount used so far with no limit to it (`unit` `usd`,
      `credits` or `requests`): Cursor's on-demand spend without a cap (`on_demand`), Claude's extra
      usage without a monthly cap (`extra_usage`), an OpenRouter key's spend (`today`, `week`,
      `month`: "Today", "This Week", "This Month", each `resetsAt` the end of OpenRouter's UTC day,
      week from Monday, or month), a Copilot organization's credits and spend this month for a seat
      it pays for by the credit (`org_credits` in `credits`, `org_spend` in `usd`; only where the
      sign-in may read that organization's billing, else none, never a zero);
    - `capped` `{amount, limit, unit, resetsAt?}`: an amount used of a limit: Claude's extra usage
      with its monthly cap (`extra_usage`, "Extra Usage", dollars);
    - `left` `{amount, unit}`: an amount left to spend, with no cap: Codex's credits (`credits`,
      "Extra Usage", whole credits);
    - `resets` `{count, expiries?, refills?, usable, agents?}`: the plan's rate-limit resets
      (`resets`, "Rate Limit Resets"): Claude's reset grants (read at most hourly an account, with
      Claude Code's own request, as Anthropic offers them to no other; `refills`, the windows the
      next one refills, `five_hour` and `seven_day`, where it says) and Codex's reset credits (the
      Codex agent's own sign-in, its home's `auth.json`, or the engine's ChatGPT sign-in); `count`,
      how many; `expiries`, each one's, soonest first (ms, 50 at most); `usable`, one can be used now
      with this sign-in; `agents: true`, agents may use them without asking (Always Allow, below).
      In a row, `usable` and `on` `{key, name, here?}` say which of your computers would use one:
      the first of its `boxes` (this box first, one heard from before one that's away) whose own
      `resets` say `usable`; none can, `usable: false` and no `on`. `agents` is that computer's.
    - `unreadable` `{message}`: what this sign-in can't read: a Mac's Claude token can only run
      Claude, so its extra usage and resets show only from a computer of yours signed in to Claude
      Code with the same account (as one row, its numbers are that computer's); alone, the row
      states this (`id` `resets`).
    A read of them that fails keeps what was read (a failed read never states none, nor a zero).
    A client leaves out a kind it doesn't know, and one whose `resetsAt` has passed (not known
    now, as a window); a box keeps from a peer's mail the kinds it knows, checked, and passes a
    kind it doesn't know on as told, only its plain fields, 1 KB at most. Absent when there's none.
    A row's are its newest reading's that had no problem (a reading without them says there are
    none now); with none, while none could read lately, the last read, before an `unreadable` one.
  - `checked`, when its maker last answered (with its limits or a problem; absent for an account
    only its turns tell of); `next`, when it's read again (absent for one that's never read).
  - `problem` `{kind, message, until?}` when the last read didn't work, with `windows` as last
    read (each with its `read`): `rate-limited` (its maker turned the read away; `until`, when it's
    read again), `expired` (its sign-in lapsed or was turned away: its agent renews it the next
    time it runs), `unreadable` (the sign-in can run the agent but not read its plan's limits),
    `ended` (its maker says the account has no plan now, a subscription that ended: Cursor's
    "no active subscription", xAI's billing with no period; `windows`, `balance` and `extras` are
    then none, `plan` as last read, and it's read again every half hour) or `failed`. Show
    `message` as it is.
- `POST kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits/refresh` reads now each account read over a minute ago, as
  often as its maker allows and never inside a hold (nor one a peer read within its time between
  reads), then asks a computer that reads it for each account this box doesn't read itself (one
  only on another computer, or one only its turns tell of here, a Mac's Claude) to do the same for
  it, and
  answers as `GET` with what's read within a couple of seconds; what comes later comes as
  `kuvo.limits.updated`.
- The bridge's events (`kuvo/agents/api/event`) carry `kuvo.limits.updated` `{accounts, rows}`
  each time either changes (a peer's word included).
- **Across your computers** (#210): every box is equal, none is a hub, and each works with any
  other off.
  - The bridge accepts readings after the link confirms peer membership. Cached readings are
    visible once that membership is confirmed. A request to spend a reset requires membership.
    An already recorded spend can still be reconciled with its original computer, using the
    same request, after that computer leaves. Before the link reports membership, agents ask
    before using a reset.

  - Each box's bridge tells each limits peer what it read of its own accounts, through its link:
    `{"limits": {at, accounts, ask?, refresh?}}`, `accounts` as its `GET` lists them, but its own
    numbers only (each account's hashed `identity`, its windows with when each was read, `checked`,
    `next`, its plan, credits, `extras` and problem; never a sign-in, a token or an ID), as many as fit in 28
    KB; `at`, the sender's clock. It's sent at once after a read, at most once a minute for what
    turns hear, again every ten minutes though nothing changed (the relay keeps nothing), and at once
    to a peer it hasn't told since its bridge started, or since its link started carrying its mail
    again (what went meanwhile was lost), with `ask: true` (tell me yours). A box answers `ask`,
    and a peer back after being away, with its own (no `ask`), at most once a minute for each peer,
    whatever it told that peer lately.
    A box from before this ignores it, and sends none. A sealed mail that doesn't fit isn't sent.
  - The receiver keeps the last from each peer (`limits-peers.json` in the bridge's folder, through
    a restart), its times moved onto its own clock where the sender's `at` is a minute or more off
    (`resetsAt`, its maker's, as it is), and a `service` it doesn't know (a newer box's) as its name
    (lowercase letters, digits and dashes, 40 at most). A computer you removed goes, with what it
    said.
  - **One read per account**: before asking a maker, a box looks for a reading of the same
    account (`service` and `identity`) by one of your own computers (never one that isn't yours,
    Whose: what such a box is told has no spend or extras, so it never stands in for a read; two
    people's Macs signed in to one account each read it) that its maker answered without a problem within the
    account's time between reads (15 minutes for Claude's, 10 for the rest). Then it doesn't ask,
    lists the account as its own still (with no numbers of its own, if it never read it), and looks
    again past that peer's next read and two minutes more: a peer that's off, or turned away, is
    taken over then. Computers that read at the same moment settle on one by the next round (the
    one that read last is fresh to the other). Holds and the one-a-minute spacing stay each box's
    own (Anthropic's limit is per computer): a 429 on one holds that one alone, and a reading with a
    problem never stands for a read. An account a box can't say who it is is always read there;
    one whose sign-in doesn't say who it is (GitHub Copilot's: its maker's answer does) counts as
    who it was last read as only while the lasting part of its sign-in (a refresh token or a key,
    not a renewed token) is as it was then: signed in again, what was kept of it goes (`problem`,
    `failed`, as above) and it's read soon.
  - `refresh: [row id]`: a refresh asked of the sender (above) for accounts it doesn't read
    itself; the receiver refreshes those of its own as it would its own refresh.
  - **`rows`**: one row per account across this box and its peers, this box's first, then each
    peer's by name. Rows of one `service` with one `identity` are one row, from any box; a row
    without one is its box's own. Two windows are one limit when they have the same `model`
    (ignoring case), `name` and `minutes` (by `id` where a window has none of the three): a coding
    agent and the engine name a model's own limit differently. Each is the one read last (`read`)
    among them. The newest reading is the one checked last (`checked`, else its newest window's
    `read`): the plan and the credits are its, where it has them, else the next newest's (and, where one of your own computers read it without a problem, the newest of theirs: a box that isn't yours is told no spend or extras); `checked`
    is the latest and `next` the earliest; a `problem` shows only when every box has one, the
    newest's. A row is as an account, named as the coding agent's where one is among them (else
    the engine's sign-in's), with the first `label` among them, and adds `id` (`<service>#<identity>`,
    or `<box key>/<provider>` for one that can't say who it is: the same on every box), `boxes`
    (each computer it's on, `{key, name, provider, agent?, account?, label?, checked?, here?,
    away?}`: `here`, the box that answered; `away`, a peer not heard from for 25 minutes, whose
    word stays as it was) and `away: true` when every computer it's on is away: its numbers are as
    of their `read`, never live, however recent; `ended: true` when its `problem` is `ended`
    (every computer that read it says its plan isn't active): it has no `rings`, and a client draws
    no ring or bar for it, listing it only where it lists accounts, as a plan that ended. A row a box can't say who it is (no `identity`) is
    never merged by its numbers: two accounts can read alike (a personal plan and a team's, each
    at 12%).
  - **Rings and levels** (`limits.rings`, #711): in a row (never in `accounts`, nor in what peers
    are told), each window adds `level`, how close it is to its limit in the box's word, the same
    in every client: `calm`, `near` (70% used or more) or `over` (90% or more); and the row adds
    `rings` `{short?, long?}`, the two circles a client draws for the account, each `{window, used,
    resetsAt?, level}` (`window`, that window's `id`), with `span: short|long` on those two windows.
    The box picks them: among the whole plan's windows (not a model's own; its plainly timed ones
    before those named for what they count, "Web searches"), the shortest under a day is `short` (a
    5-hour session) and the longest of a day or more `long` (the week, the month), the first listed
    where two are as long. A plan with one window has one ring (`long`, where it states no
    length); one with none, `rings: {}`. Where every window is named for what it counts
    (Antigravity's pools, Copilot's counts), the rings are of one pool (those whose `id` differs
    only in its last part, such as `gemini-5h` and `gemini-weekly`). Antigravity shows the pool
    with the highest share used in any current window. The first listed window resolves ties and
    picks the pool for other providers. Where every window is a model's, the first model's stand for the
    plan. A client colours by `level` and never by a threshold of its own.
    A ring whose window started over (`expired`) is `used` 0, `calm`, with no `resetsAt`, in its
    place. `bar` (`limits.bar`, #668): `short` or `long`, the ring a client with room for one bar
    draws: the fuller of the two (`short` where they're as full); absent with no rings. Since #718 a row
    also says `level` for the account as a whole, for a client's one mark of it (a gauge): the
    higher of its rings' levels; with no ring, what it has with a most it may come to, by the same
    shares: its `balance` (what's gone of `limit`) and each `capped` extra (`amount` of `limit`), the
    highest of them. It's left out where nothing says a limit (a balance with no cap, spend alone, no
    reading): that is "no level", which a client draws apart from `calm`, never as it.
  - **Cards and the rail** (`limits.card`, #952): in `GET` and `refresh` answers (never in what
    peers are told), each row adds `card`, what a client shows of the account when its ring is
    rested on, worded by the box; and the answer adds `rail`, the rings a client draws, in order.
    Words are a list of `{text, at?, as?, tone?, strong?}`: a client writes `text`, then `at` (ms)
    in its own time zone, as a time of day (`as: "time"`; with its weekday, or its date, where
    it isn't today) or a date (`as: "date"`, "Nov 30"); `tone` is `warning`, `danger`, `muted` or
    `faint`. A `card` is `{title, name, dot?, tone, left?, lines, note?, asOf?, inUse?, resets?}`:
    - `title`: the account's name on its card, the agent's with which account where you have more
      than one on the rail ("Claude · Max"); `name`, the account alone ("Max", "Lab 12").
    - `lines`: one per window, the plan's own shortest first (5-hour, then Weekly), then those
      named for what they count, then each model's; each `{window, title, left, tone, words}`:
      `left`, what's left (0 to 1) for its bar; `tone` `calm`, `warning` or `danger`.
    - How fast it's going: the box keeps each window's readings (from any of your computers, as the
      row has them; through a restart, in `limits.json`'s `paces`) and, where it has three or more
      over a quarter of a recent stretch (a fifth of the window, half an hour to a day; a quarter
      hour at least), takes the rate between the stretch's first and last. Used up: "Back at
      {reset}" (`danger`). On pace to be used up before it starts over: "38% left · runs out
      ~{about when, to five minutes}, resets {reset}" (`warning`). Otherwise "56% left · lasts until
      reset". With too few readings nothing is guessed: "56% left · resets {reset}".
    - `dot`: `danger` where a window is used up, else `warning` where one runs out before its
      reset: a client marks the account's ring with it, and the ring itself stays as `rings` say.
      `tone` and `left` (its rings' tightest) are the account's as a whole, for a mark among others
      (`unknown` and no `left` where nothing's known).
    - `note`: why there's nothing (or not everything) to show: its maker's own (`problem.unknown`,
      Google not counting Antigravity's use), what to do about a problem, "Fills in once a session
      runs on this account" before anything was read, or "No limits reported.".
    - A coding agent's last numbers stay, however old (a reader that can't answer now, such as
      Antigravity's where it isn't running, never blanks them; this box's own Codex reading too),
      until its sign-in changes or a window starts over. Where none of them was read in the last
      half hour, `asOf` says when ("as of {time}", `faint`), and nothing is predicted from them.
    - `inUse`: a turn told of it in the last half hour.
    - `resets`, only where one of its resets can be used now: `{words, action, confirm: {title,
      message, button, cancel}}`: "2 resets left · next expires {date}", "Use a reset", and the
      question asked before one's used, naming the reset it uses: the soonest to expire, as each
      maker's spend picks ("Use the reset that expires {date}?", "Codex's usage limits start over
      now.", "Use Reset", "Cancel"). Using it is `POST …/limits/reset` (below, "Resets").
    `rail`: the accounts signed in on the answering box (`here`) whose plan hasn't ended and that
    have numbers (one with nothing read yet has no ring, never an empty one), in the
    rows' order, each item `{key, rows, ring, selected, title, dot?, count?, summary?, strip?}`:
    an account a ring (`rows` its own `id`); an agent's (or, for the engine's, a service's) three
    or more accounts one ring, at its first's place: `ring` the row it draws (the emptiest with
    rings), `count`, `summary` ("17 of 20 fine": `tone` `calm`), and `strip`, each account
    emptiest first (unknown last), `{row, name, left?, tone, heading}`, `heading` the words over
    its card when shown in full (", in use" for the one in use). `selected`: the account its card
    shows in full at first, the one in use (newest), else the emptiest.
- Listing them (KuvoClient's `UsageListing.listing`, as the Mac and the phone do): one box's `rows`
  as they are, merging nothing (the Mac: its own box's; the phone: the first box in its list of
  your computers that states accounts, a machine's on Linux too), refreshed
  through that box alone, while they have every row each other box the client reaches says is
  signed in there (`here`), with that box among the row's `boxes` and not `away`. A row whose computers are all away shows "As of" its reading's time.
  **Names** (`limits.titles`, #668): a row's `title` is the box's: its account's ("Claude",
  "Codex", "ChatGPT", "Claude · Work"); where two rows would have one name, a row whose sign-in on
  the answering box is the engine's alone takes the service's name ("ChatGPT"); rows not on the
  answering box add the names of the computers they're on ("Claude · hetzner, lokum"); rows still
  alike, each on the answering box, add their other computers' names. A client shows it as it is.
  Otherwise (a computer the client reaches whose own
  rows the first box doesn't have from it as it hears it now, not `away`: just added, or the relay
  down; or a held box's older bridge, which answers without `rows`, as this Mac's own does just
  after an update from a release before them), the client merges each box's `accounts` itself, by
  the rules for `rows` above, and refreshes each (this merge, a client's own, is yet to move to the
  box).
- What's read: Claude Code's accounts, on Linux from Anthropic with Claude Code's own sign-in in
  Kuvo Code's folder; on a Mac only from what its turns hear (Claude Code's rate-limit events, every
  window from each response's headers), as the token Kuvo Code signs in with there can only run
  Claude, so an account shows once it has had a turn. Codex's, through its app-server: once as the
  box starts, then only while Codex runs there anyway, with its turns' events between. Grok's pool,
  with the sign-in in its home; of the engine's, ChatGPT's (`openai`, signed in: Codex's windows),
  SuperGrok's (`xai`, signed in), GitHub Copilot's (the month's premium requests), OpenRouter's (a
  key's cap and the credits left), Z.ai's coding plan and OpenCode Go's. Cursor's, with the Cursor
  agent's own sign-in in Kuvo Code's folder (`cursor/auth.json`, the key its sign-in made, or
  `CURSOR_API_KEY` for your own account), never the Cursor app's login: the key exchanged for a
  short-lived access token, kept in memory only, and Cursor's own answers as UsageKit read them
  (OpenUsage's rules): `total` ("Total usage": the plan's share used, or a team seat's dollars, or
  a request-based plan's requests), `auto` ("Cursor Models") and `api` ("Other Models"), the
  model pools, over the billing cycle; `on_demand` ("On-demand", dollars against its cap, `amount`
  in `usd`; a spend with no cap is no window but `extras`, `spent` in `usd`); `grok_bot` ("Grok Bot usage", its own week);
  `requests` (a request-based plan's, where its total isn't already them); the credits left
  (grants and prepaid balance) as `balance` in `usd`. Each window's `name` is that label. A sign-in
  file that can't be read just now (being rewritten) is a `failed` read, not a sign-out: what was
  read stays. Only a real box's bridge asks Cursor or Antigravity, never a test's.
  Antigravity uses only its Kuvo Code agent profile's sign-in, never an editor or Keychain login.
  It reads merged Gemini/non-Gemini session and weekly quotas (and Argon weekly where supplied),
  with the legacy per-model endpoints for older servers. Its own language server is discovered
  with ps/lsof on macOS and /proc on Linux; self-signed HTTPS is accepted only on loopback.
  An unavailable server or unreadable sign-in is stated on the row; failed reads retain the last
  result. Refused credentials are remembered by hash in the box-owned
  `usage/antigravity/<account>/refusals.json`, including access, refresh and CSRF refusals, so a restart or
  temporary refresh failure cannot resend them. A good quota answer from either Google host
  wins over a refusal from the other; only the main host refusing the token's own call, with no
  host answering, refuses the sign-in, and once any host answered a read, no later call does. A
  host or call that asks to wait (429) waits alone until its `Retry-After` (an hour without one):
  windows already read are kept and the reading is partial. When nothing was read yet (no host
  answered the summary, or a call the quota needs waits), the whole reading waits, until the
  soonest host may be asked again. These per-host waits are kept in memory, so a restart forgets
  them. A secondary plan lookup cannot invalidate good quotas.
  Token refresh uses the own agent token's OAuth client metadata (or the defaults verified in
  ACP 1.3.0); the refusal record is pruned on sign-out. Not yet: Ollama's, which ollama.com tells only the Ollama app's own signing key.
- How often: Claude's each 15 minutes, the rest each 10. Anthropic limits these reads for the whole
  computer, not a sign-in, and holds a reader off longer each time it asks too soon: Claude's
  accounts are read one a minute (counted before the request goes, through a restart too), and a
  429 holds every one of them on the box for as long as its `Retry-After` says (an hour with no
  word, doubling with each 429 of any of them, up to six), through a restart. An API key a maker
  turns away is tried again later, with longer waits; a sign-in that lapsed isn't asked again
  until it changes. A read is kept
  as asked before it's answered, so a restart meanwhile never asks again; a sign-in that lapsed or
  can't read its limits isn't asked again until it changes.
- Agents read them with the tool `plan_limits` (read only): each account's windows, how much is
  used, when each resets and as of when, what the plan has beyond them (an account with resets
  with its row's `id`, for `use_limit_reset`), and why one couldn't be read just now.
- **Resets** (#631 E, feature `limits.resets`): using one of an account's rate-limit resets, from
  any client or an agent, through any box of yours.
  - `POST kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits/reset {row}` → `{data: {confirm, row, service, count,
    refills?, on, always, expires}}`: what one more ask spends (one of `count`), the computer whose
    sign-in spends it (`on`), whether agents may without asking (`always`), and a one-time
    `confirm` id that holds 10 minutes. Spends nothing. 404 `{message}` for no such row; 409 for a
    row with no resets, none left, none any computer of yours can use (a Mac's Claude token alone:
    its `unreadable` message), or one whose maker holds requests off; 503 when the computer with the
    sign-in can't be reached.
  - `POST … {row, confirm, by?, unasked?}` → `{data: {outcome, until?, message?, row?}}`: one reset spent,
    once. `outcome` `reset` (done: the windows it refills start over; the account is read again at
    once, and `row` is as it is then), `unconfirmed` (its maker took it but couldn't say it went
    through), `nothing-to-reset` (not at a limit), `no-reset` (none to spend), `not-now` (a
    cooldown, `until` where it says), `failed` (turned away, or nothing sent: nothing used) or
    `unknown` (no answer came: a timeout, its maker failing, its sign-in turned away for now, the
    computer with the sign-in not answering within 45 seconds; it may have been used); `message`
    says it in words where it isn't `reset`. The same `confirm` again answers how it went, and never spends twice; one never given,
    for another row, or older than 10 minutes is 404. `by`: who asked (an agent's name), for the
    log.
  - **Once**: a spend is written to the box's journal (`limits-resets.json` in the bridge's
    folder, 200 at most, a month) before any request goes, with the request id its maker takes as
    the same request (Anthropic's `request_id`, ChatGPT's `redeem_request_id`) and, once chosen,
    what it spends (the grant Anthropic names next; the reset credit soonest to expire), also kept
    before the request. Asked again after a crash, a lost answer or a failure, it goes as the same
    request with the same grant or credit, and its maker answers that it's done (`already_used`,
    `already_redeemed`) rather than spending another. `unknown` and `unconfirmed` leave it open (it
    may have gone); every other outcome settles it, but a refusal here before anything goes (its
    maker holding requests off, its sign-in unreadable for a moment, another account signed in)
    leaves an open spend open, and says so. Within 10 minutes of a row's open spend, a new
    confirmation for that row is that same spend (its request here, or its id on the peer it was
    passed to), and two confirmations at once share one request; later (a day at most), the open
    one is asked again first, as itself, and the new one is that one only if it was used just now
    or still can't be told, else it goes as its own. Right before a request goes, the account
    signed in there now (its sign-in's own identity, not as last read) must be the row's: if
    another is, nothing is spent (`no-reset`), and the slot's earlier account's Always Allow goes
    off (below). Claude on Linux: its token carries no claims and Claude Code's own record of the
    sign-in can lag a new one, so Anthropic's profile is asked too, right then; its account must be
    the record's (and its organization, where both say one), and the reset is spent with that very
    sign-in (one signed in meanwhile never is), else nothing is spent, and nothing of
    what's allowed changes on that (whichever of the two lags, the newly signed-in account's
    stays). `unasked: true` marks an agent's spend under Always Allow that no one confirmed:
    refused (`failed`) where the asking box's own decision for the row is off, and again by the box
    that spends it unless its decision is on. A confirmation by the user that joins an open
    `unasked` spend (or, past the 10 minutes, asks it again first) makes it the user's, here and on
    the peer it was passed to (the same request: nothing more is spent). A peer asked to spend one follows these same rules for a new ask
    (joining within 10 minutes, settling an older one first). A client sends the same
    `confirm` again after a lost answer, and after `unknown` or `unconfirmed`; a 404 then (the box no
    longer knows it) asks anew.
  - **On the computer with the sign-in**: a box whose own sign-in can't spend it passes it to
    `on`, a peer, as `{"seat": {"kind": "reset", at, ask:
    {id, row, by?}}}`, and answers when that one does (`{"seat": {"kind": "reset", at, answer: {id,
    outcome, until?, already?, open?, message?}}}`: `already`, its maker said this request was done
    before; `open`, the spend stays open there, so it stays open here too), or `unknown` after 45
    seconds (asked again, with the same `confirm` or a new one for that row, it's asked there again
    under the same id, which that box's journal answers once). An open one that can't be passed
    there now stays open (`not-now`, saying an earlier try may have gone); a new one that can't is
    never kept. A box takes a
    reset mail only from peers.
  - **Always Allow**: `PUT kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits/reset/always {provider | row, always}`:
    agents may (or may not) use an account's resets without asking. It's the account's, by who it
    is (its row `<service>#<identity>`; 409 for one that doesn't say who it is yet): each decision
    stamped with when it was made and kept in the journal (`allowed`, by row, whether or not the box
    knows the account yet) on every computer of yours with its sign-in, here (`provider`, as
    Settings › Accounts names it here, or the `row`) and on the others among its row's `boxes`,
    told to every computer of yours as `{"seat": {"kind": "reset", at, always: {row, on, at}}}` mail
    that's kept until it's there; a decision older than the one kept is ignored, and of two stamped
    the same, an off holds. One made here (by `PUT`, or a slot signed in to another account since,
    which turns its earlier account's off, so coming back asks again) is stamped after any this box
    knows of, so it's always kept here, and told. What that leaves: a decision made on a computer
    that hadn't yet heard an opposite one made elsewhere (the mail on its way, or one of the two
    off the relay) is ordered by the two computers' clocks, so within as much as their clocks
    differ, the one stamped later holds, whichever was made later. Stated as
    `agents: true` on its `resets`, and as `agentsReset: true` on the account in this box's own
    `accounts` whether or not it has resets now (so a client can turn it off). Answering a card
    Always while the computer with the sign-in is away keeps it all the same; no reset is used then.
  - **The agents' tool** `use_limit_reset {account}` (an account's row `id`, or its name as
    `plan_limits` says it): asks the user first, every time, on the permission card in the calling
    conversation (`kuvo/work/asks`, action `resetLimits`, "Work"), unless its account's `always` is
    set; Allow uses one; Always Allow sets `always` first, then uses one; Don't uses none. Its answer
    says how it went with the account's limits after. Every use is in the conversation (the tool's
    call) and the bridge's log.
- Times are ms since 1970.

### Usage history

What each account signed in to Kuvo Code used, and what that cost, by the day (#631: OpenUsage's
history, moving to the box). Each box reads its own accounts' agents' logs on its computer, a
machine's with the Mac closed too: so far Claude Code's, in the folders Kuvo Code runs it with (an
account you added: its own folder; a machine: Kuvo Code's, not your `~/.claude` there; a Mac's own
sign-in: your Claude Code settings folders, where Claude Code runs with it, as OpenUsage read them,
each of a comma-separated `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, else `~/.config/claude` and `~/.claude`: Claude
Code's conversations there count whoever ran them, your Terminal or Claude's desktop app), never
another tool's folders (Cowork's, claude-swap's, Pi's); and Codex's, each Codex account's home's
`sessions` and `archived_sessions` (an account you added: its own home, whose history on a Mac is
your Codex's, which it links to, so counted once, with your own Codex's; a Mac's own sign-in: your
`~/.codex`, or each of a comma-separated `CODEX_HOME`, where Codex runs with it, its conversations
there counted whoever ran them; a machine: Kuvo Code's; a home with neither folder is read itself,
as OpenUsage did), never Pi's or another tool's. And what your
ChatGPT sign-in in Kuvo Code (the engine's `openai`, Settings › Accounts) used through the engine's
own models, read (only read) from the engine's databases on that computer (each `opencode*.db` in
its data folder: on a Mac the app's, on a machine `~/.kuvo-code/data/opencode`), Codex's, the same
row as a Codex account signed in to the same ChatGPT account; never your own opencode's. And Grok's, each Grok account's home's `sessions` (an account you added:
its own home; a machine: Kuvo Code's; a Mac's own sign-in: your `GROK_HOME`, else `~/.grok`, where
Grok runs with it, its sessions there counted whoever ran them, your Terminal's too; a folder two
accounts name, the first's), only each session's `updates.jsonl`, never Grok's debug log
(`logs/unified.jsonl`, which it cuts short). It prices them as OpenUsage does (its supplement,
LiteLLM's catalog, models.dev's; snapshots ship with the bridge, and each feed is fetched again
hourly, kept in the bridge's `usage/pricing`, only by a real box's bridge, in a Mac app's folder or
a machine's `~/.kuvo-code`, never a test's): estimates, not your bill, but where the maker said
what it cost (Claude Code's `costUSD`, Grok's own costs). And what the engine's own hosted models
cost (OpenCode Go, `opencode-go`, and OpenCode Zen, `opencode`), as OpenCode billed it, read (only
read) from the engine's databases on that computer (each `opencode*.db` in its data folder: on a
Mac the app's, on a machine `~/.kuvo-code/data/opencode`), never your own opencode's: a box that
doesn't know its engine's folder doesn't state it (`services` without `opencode`). And Cursor's,
from Cursor's own record of each Cursor account signed in to Kuvo Code (its dashboard's usage
events, asked with the sign-in its plan limits are read with: "Plan limits"), which is the whole
account's, wherever it ran: so a row of it is its newest box's, never a sum (below), and one of
your own computers asks Cursor for it at a time, however its plan limits' read went: of those
that read it whole lately (each tells when it last did, `fresh`, below; a read where part failed,
or that a hold stopped, isn't one), the one whose link key comes first; one that hasn't for 25
minutes, or is away, is taken over. Nothing is asked of
Cursor while its plan's sign-in was turned away as it is now, or while Cursor holds reads off. A client reaches them as
`kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage…` (the Mac app at `api/kuvo/usage…` on the bridge itself), where
`features` has `usage.history`.

- `GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage?zone=<IANA time zone>` → `{data: {zone, services, serviceTitles, scanned?, rows:
  [row], totals: {<service>: [day]}, partial?: {<service>: {away?, cut?}}}}`. The box works out the days in `zone` (the client's, so a
  Mac in Istanbul reading a machine in UTC gets its own days); one it doesn't know is its own,
  `zone` says which. `services`: what this box states the usage of (`claude`, `codex`,
  `grok`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `antigravity`): a client shows those from here, and reads the rest as it did. `serviceTitles` (`names.titles`) maps each service id in `services` or `totals` to the box's
  spend card title ("OpenCode", "Codex"); clients draw it unchanged. Unknown ids are capitalized
  word by word. `scanned`: when this box last read its logs.
  `pricing: {codex: {fallback, chosen, choices}}`: Codex's fallback model, a usage setting
  (below), `null` for none; `chosen`, whether it was ever chosen (none counts);
  `choices`, the models it may be, in order.
  - A `row` is one account across your computers, with the same `id` as its plan limits row
    (`<service>#<identity>`, or `<box key>/<provider>` for one that can't say who it is), so a
    client puts an account's limits and its usage side by side: `{id, service, provider, agent?,
    account?, label?, identity?, scanned?, boxes, away?, cut?, estimated?, accountWide?,
    days}`: `estimated: false` where its dollars are what its maker billed (OpenCode's hosted
    models'), not an estimate; `accountWide: true` where its use is its maker's account of the whole
    account (Cursor's): its days are its newest box's (`scanned`), never a sum; `boxes` as limits'
    rows have them (`{key, name, provider, agent?, account?, label?, scanned?, here?, away?,
    same?}`), where `same` marks a box
    that reads a folder another of them already does (two boxes on one computer), not added again.
    Its `days` are the **sum** of every box's own (each box reads only its own logs), each folder
    once; an `accountWide` row's, its newest box's alone. OpenCode's: a row for Go (the same row as its plan limits') and one for Zen, each only
    while it has use in the window. A conversation moved to another
    computer (`kuvo/moves`) is copied there, and the one it left keeps its copy for a while: its
    past use counts on both meanwhile.
  - `totals`: each service's days, from the same accounts as the rows. Each folder is counted
    once, and an `accountWide` row contributes its newest box's reading. `partial`: a service whose
    totals are short, `away` (one of your computers isn't answering: its share is as of then) or
    `cut` (one told less than all: its oldest days).
  - A `day`: `{date, tokens, cost, models: [{model, tokens, cost, family?}], unknown?, fallback?}`, newest first, for
    today and the 30 days before it in `zone`; `date` is `yyyy-MM-dd`, `cost` US dollars,
    `models` by name; `unknown`, models used that day that couldn't be priced, which count
    nowhere (a day with only those has no tokens and no models), unless a fallback model estimated
    them: `fallback`, the models whose rates did (their dollars and tokens are then in `models`
    under the model's own name, and it's still in `unknown`). A model with no name but a cost of
    its own is `Unattributed`. `family`, Cursor's only: the row a model shows under where that isn't
    its own name (its catalog key with `-fast` dropped: `gpt-6-high-fast` under `gpt-6`), as
    UsageKit grouped Cursor's effort and speed variants.
  - What counts (OpenUsage's rules, from ccusage): a log line with `"usage":{` that parses, with a
    valid time and version and no `null` where Claude Code never writes one; once per
    `(message.id, requestId)`, a subagent's line replaying its parent's message under another
    request counting as the parent's; an advisor's work as its own model's; a line's `costUSD`
    where it has one, else its tokens at its model's rates (1-hour cache writes at twice the input
    rate, a request whose prompt passes the model's long-context threshold at those rates
    throughout, a fast request at its model's fast multiplier).
  - Codex's (OpenUsage's rules, from ccusage): an `event_msg` `token_count` line (written as Codex
    writes JSON, without spaces) is a turn: its `last_token_usage`, else what its running
    `total_token_usage` grew by since the line before; a running total the same as the last is a
    snapshot said again, not a turn; a turn with nothing in it isn't one. `turn_context` (or a
    model on the line itself) names the model from then on, `gpt-5` for a session that never
    named one; `thread_settings_applied` the service tier (`fast` or `priority`, `ultrafast`). A
    child session's log (a subagent's, a fork's: `forked_from_id`, `parent_thread_id`,
    `thread_source: "subagent"`, `source.subagent`) replays its parent's turns first: none of those
    counts, until a `task_started` at or after the session's own start (its first `session_meta`'s
    time, else that line's own). A turn the same as another (time, model, tokens), in its log or
    another, counts once; a log in both `sessions` and `archived_sessions` (by where it is in each)
    is the first's. Priced with Codex's rules over the catalogs: cached input apart from the rest
    (at the full input rate where a model has no cache discount or the catalog didn't say one),
    the newer GPT models' higher rates for a whole request past 272k prompt tokens, the priority
    tier's multiplier (and GPT-6 Astra's Ultrafast 6x), a `-fast` alias off its base once;
    `codex-auto-review` at the model it ran on by its date, free from 2026-10-06 (UTC);
    `gpt-reserve` at `gpt-5.6-luna`'s rates.
  - The engine's ChatGPT slice (OpenUsage's `OpenCodeCodexUsageScanner`): a database counts only
    while its own `openai` sign-in is a ChatGPT one (OAuth; before opencode 2 took its sign-ins in,
    the `auth.json` beside it says), only its assistant messages from `openai` priced at nothing
    (Codex's sign-in prices every model at $0; a key's cost more), from `message` (opencode 1) and
    `session_message` (opencode 2, a compaction too, from when the sign-in was made on), a message
    copied between two databases once (by its ID). Priced as Codex's. Whether the sign-in is OAuth
    is asked of SQLite: its tokens never leave the database. A database that can't be read now
    leaves what was read before as it was (its box's `scanned` as of when it last was), and such a
    read is never kept as whole, until that database has failed three reads in a row (one that's
    always broken doesn't hold up the rest); one in WAL mode whose `-wal` and `-shm` are gone (its
    engine stopped) is read as it is.
  - Grok's (OpenUsage's rules): a transcript line holding `turn_completed` that parses, a
    `turn_completed` session update (under `params.update`, else `update`) with `usage.modelUsage`
    and a time (`_meta.agentTimestampMs`, under `params`, else the line's own; else the line's
    `timestamp`, seconds or ISO 8601). Each model in it with input tokens is its own entry: cached
    reads and cache writes come out of the input (never more than it), reasoning is in the output
    already, counts past 10^12 held there. Its cost is Grok's own where it says one
    (`costUsdTicks`, 10^-10 dollars, the model's, or the turn's when it ran one model), else its
    tokens at its model's rates. An event (`_meta.eventId`) copied into another session's
    transcript counts once per model.
  - OpenCode's hosted models (OpenUsage's `OpenCodeUsageScanner`): each assistant message, and each
    completed compaction, of `opencode-go` or `opencode` with a numeric cost, from `message`
    (opencode 1) and `session_message` (opencode 2), on the day it was made; its tokens the total it
    says, else its buckets added up; its cost as written, never priced again (a negative one left
    out); a message in both tables, or in two channels' databases, once (by its ID, the first by
    path). A database without either table says nothing. One that can't be read now gives the rows
    it gave last, in this bridge's run; one with none of its rows known (as the bridge starts), or
    every one failing, leaves what this box had as it was (not known now), until it has failed three
    reads in a row (one that's always broken doesn't hold up the rest). While one fails, they're
    read every round. One in WAL mode whose `-wal` and `-shm` are gone is read as it is. A model you reach with a key
    of your own is its provider's, never counted here.
  - Cursor's (OpenUsage's `CursorSpendHistoryFetcher` and `CursorUsageEvents`): Cursor's usage
    events (`/api/dashboard/get-filtered-usage-events` with the access token's session), a UTC day
    at a time, today and the 31 days before, a thousand to a page, four days at once, for 20 seconds
    a round at most (no page is asked after that; the days that came are kept, the rest asked next
    round). A whole read stands for a minute: a refresh or a peer's within it asks Cursor nothing. A day is whole when
    every page came with one total, as many events as it says, each inside the day; otherwise it's
    as it was known before. Today and yesterday are asked every round, an older day until Cursor
    answered it after it ended. An event with no `tokenUsage` used none; one whose time, model or
    token counts (whole numbers, not negative) aren't readable counts nowhere. Priced without
    long-context rates (an event isn't a request's whole prompt). A key Cursor turned away isn't
    sent again until the sign-in changes; a 429 (the exchange's or the events') stops the read and
    holds every read of the account for as long as its `Retry-After` says (15 minutes without
    one, while its plan's own wait doubles as other makers' do); a token turned away midway is exchanged again once. One exchange at a time per key. What came is kept per Cursor user
    (`usage/cursor-history/<a hash of the user>.json`, never the user's ID); a read with a day still
    not known leaves what this box had as it was, never a day of nothing, as does a sign-in file
    that can't be read just now (being rewritten); signed out, the account's use from this box goes.
- `PUT kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/pricing[?zone=]` `{"codex": {"fallback": <model> | null}}`: Codex's
  fallback model, whose rates estimate what a Codex model with no known price used (in this box's
  own Codex logs, not the engine's ChatGPT slice: each box prices its own with it); one of `choices` (the supplement's
  `fallback_models.codex` priced exactly by a catalog), or `null` for none (`400 {message}` for
  anything else, its `message` a client shows as it is). One of the usage settings, the same on
  your own computers ("Usage settings": `codexFallback`), kept in the bridge's `usage/settings.json`
  through a restart; read again with it at once, here and on each computer it reaches, answered as
  `GET`. `chosen`: whether it was set on any of them (none counts).
- `POST kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/refresh[?zone=]` reads the logs now, asks your other computers
  to read theirs and tell (below), and answers as `GET` once it's read here (or after five
  seconds, the rest coming as the event).
- The bridge's events carry `kuvo.usage.updated` `{services}` when the rows change (a read here, a
  peer's word): ask again, in your zone.
- Showing it (KuvoClient's `UsageSpend` and `UsageLayout`, views both apps draw by): a client takes
  a service's `totals` from one box, the one whose plan limits `rows` it lists ("Listing them"),
  else the first it reaches that states that service, and never adds two boxes' up (each counts
  your other computers already). Under the service's first account it shows Today, Yesterday and
  Last 30 Days, each in dollars (an estimate unless every row of that service says `estimated:
  false`) and tokens, in the answer's `zone` as of now (a day more than 30 before today left out),
  and Usage Trend, the tokens of each of those 31 days. A period with no use has no line, never
  $0, and a box that couldn't be read gives none. A service with use and no plan limits row
  (OpenCode's Zen alone) is a row of its own. The cards go in the order of the usage settings'
  `layout.providerOrder` (a card `claude@…` is Claude's place), the rest in the panel's own
  (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot, Grok, Ollama, OpenCode, OpenRouter, Z.ai, Devin
  last). The spend goes after the account's own lines (its limits, credits, extras and resets),
  in its service's first card's `layout.metricOrder` (the trend, Today, Yesterday and Last 30 Days
