  where that names none), a line where `layout.placed` holds its meter on that first card
  (`<card>.today`, `.yesterday`, `.last30`, `.trend`; a card `claude@…` before `claude` is
  Claude's first), and all of them while `layout` was never set. A box that lists a service without its `totals`
  doesn't speak for it. Not yet followed: cards turned off (`providers`) and the limits' own
  meters in `placed`, which the Mac judges by what it finds there (#631 H1 moves that to the box).
  The phone reads every box it reaches this way, a
  machine's on Linux too, with no Mac app open; a box from before `usage.history` answers 404 and
  shows no spend (the update gate brings it up to date).
- How often: every five minutes, and when asked; one round at a time. The event, and the mail
  below, only when what was used changed. A log is read on from where
  it was last read as it grows, and again whole when it shrank or was rewritten; what each log held
  is kept in the bridge's folder (`usage/claude-files`, `usage/codex-files` and `usage/grok-files`,
  a file a log, with a Codex log's running total and model so far, rebuilt from the logs when it's
  lost; the engine's databases are read again whole, when one or its write-ahead log changed, or
  one failed last time), and each account's use by the quarter hour, UTC (`usage/usage.json`), so a restart
  answers at once, and every zone's days come out whole (India's midnight is on the half hour).
  Kept 35 days.
- **Across your computers**, as plan limits are ("Plan limits", "Across your computers": the same
  boxes, no hub, each working with the others off): each box tells each of them its own accounts'
  use, `{"seat": {"kind": "usage", at, digest, accounts?, from?, ask?, refresh?, fresh?}}` through its link
  (in parts when it's big, as a group chat's mail is): all of it (`accounts`) with `ask` to one it hasn't told
  since its bridge or link started, and to one that asks; after a read that changed what they used
  (not only when they were read), only the last two days' slots, `from` the first slot they're
  from, the receiver keeping its older ones as told before; every ten minutes otherwise, `digest`
  alone, saying what it told is as it was; all of it again, without `ask`, when another Codex
  fallback model is chosen (which model estimated what isn't in `digest`). `digest` is a hash of all of it (each account's
  `provider`, `service`, `agent`, `account`, `label`, `identity`, `cut` and slots as kept); a
  receiver whose own, put together, isn't that asks for all of it (`ask`, at most once a minute),
  and is answered at once. `fresh`, in every mail: when the sender last read each of its
  `accountWide` accounts, by provider (its clock), so your computers know which reads it though
  what it read didn't change (a box from before ignores it). Each account is `{provider, service, agent?, account?, label?,
  identity?, scanned?, cut?, whole, places?, slots: {models, used: [[slot, model, tokens,
  dollars]], unknown?: [[slot, model]], fallback?: [[slot, model]]}, estimated?: false,
  accountWide?: true}` (`fallback`, a model whose rates estimated that slot's use of one with no
  price; `estimated` and `accountWide`, as a row's; none of them in `digest`, which a box from
  before works out without them; a box from before adds an `accountWide` account up as any other): `places`, the folders its logs are
  in (for the engine's hosted models, its data folder with the provider), each 16 hex
  characters of a hash of its computer (on Linux its machine ID, `/etc/machine-id` or D-Bus's, with
  its name; on a Mac its hardware UUID; else its name) and the folder's real path (never either); `slot`, quarter hours since 1970 (UTC), `model`, an index into
  `models`, `tokens` a whole number; `whole`, the first slot the sender has all of (a UTC midnight
  35 days back, or past what it cut): the receiver keeps none older. Told as the receiver keeps it
  (`label` 100 characters, `provider` and model names 200), so the digests agree. As many as fit in
  400 KB, the oldest left out first, an account so cut marked `cut` (and its rows elsewhere `cut:
  true`: their oldest days are short). Never a log, a message, a path or a sign-in. `refresh: true`: read yours now and tell (each box asks at most once a minute, and
  reads for each at most once a minute). The receiver keeps the last from each
  (`usage/peers.json`), through a restart. It shows cached readings only after the link reports
  membership. A peer not heard from for 25 minutes is away, and its last reading stays visible.
  A computer removed from the setup leaves the usage view.

### Usage notices

Feature `usage.notices` (required by apps): the box that read a limit decides quota notices.
`GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/limits` and refresh answers add `data.notices`, also carried by
`kuvo.limits.updated`. Each fact is `{id, row, service, window, milestone, at, remaining,
resetsAt?, forwarder?, accountName?, windowName?}`: lasting occurrence ID, limits row ID, maker's window, trigger, decision time in
milliseconds, remaining share, optional reset time. Milestones are `underTenPercent` (strictly
below 10%), `healthyToClose`, and `closeToRunningOut`. Defaults are off; the shared usage
notification, provider and visible-meter settings apply. The first trustworthy reading primes
without alerting; recovery re-arms a later worsening, meaningful reset advances clear dedup,
and reset jitter of at most one second does not. Failed or refused reads never decide notices.

Account readings carry `noticeState` per window and recent `notices` in limits peer mail so a
new reader inherits the baseline/dedup. These fields cross only between direct own computers
within one known setup, the same boundary as usage settings: the sender includes `noticeSetup`,
and the receiver takes the fields only when it follows that setup. A box following
no setup never sends or takes the fields, and a cached peer's notices/state stop applying when
the setup changes. Peers preserve the original ID and decision; they do not decide it again. The current
account holder with the smallest link key among online same-setup direct peers forwards decided
facts to phones, including facts received from another holder. Once the link has named this box,
each fact pins that selection in `forwarder`; before then, push waits. A later ownership change
never replays old pushes. If the same occurrence arrives with conflicting pins from readers
that had not exchanged yet, the lexicographically smallest forwarder wins, persisted into local
and peer copies so a peer disappearing cannot undo the agreement. An unavailable selected holder
catches up only while the fact is current:
at most ten minutes from the decision and never past its reset. Disconnected computers without
a shared current peer view cannot guarantee exactly-once background push delivery under an
arbitrary network partition. Decisions and dedup survive box restarts. Answers and peer mail
expose at most 100 current facts per account. With no layout part yet, the default visible meters
apply, including optional meters remaining off. Ordinary turn samples retain the thirty-second
disk-save limit; new notice decisions are persisted before delivery. Account-specific Claude cards
(`claude@<hash8>`) use their exact enabled/placed meters when the box can derive that card from
its sign-in and find it in settings. Sticky first-card IDs, salted record IDs, and Codex's
email-based card IDs cannot always be mapped from plan-limit identities. Without a reliable
mapping, an enabled matching meter on any card of the service family enables that warning;
this fallback can include an account whose individual card is hidden. No extra identity is
sent to recover the mapping. Ordinary directory heartbeats keep the one-minute heard-mail
throttle; a setup or notice-sharing eligibility change sends pending scoped facts at once.

Limits and usage-settings answers include `notificationAvailability: [{provider, available,
message}]` for providers whose alerts are unavailable (currently Devin, `available:false`).
The box owns both the capability and its explanation; clients filter the returned entries to
their displayed/enabled cards and draw the returned words.

The host owns the OS notification delegate and opens the usage panel for a usage tap. A usage
notification actually shown on the Mac is acknowledged through attention using its stable
`data.notice` ID (in `shown.request`), so only that occurrence is suppressed in pending phone
pushes, even when another own box is the forwarder. Silently consumed or banner-disabled
notifications do not acknowledge presentation. Native shown-ID receipts and phone receipts
are timestamped and expire after about a day.

The native notice list remains ten minutes, while agent-authored `notify_user` records are kept
for twenty-four hours for rate limits and unread-session bookkeeping. Keeping a usage fact
with its original `at` prunes other records by the current wall time, never that fact's age.

The bridge emits `kuvo.usage.notices` `{notices, push}`: `push:true` when this box is the
selected forwarder, false otherwise. The link delivers them on the existing
`kuvo/notices[/events]` path as category `usage`, with box-worded title/subtitle/body
(the panel's account and meter names, such as “Claude Weekly”), `data.notice` the stable ID,
`data.row` the account, and `data.at`/`data.expires` the maker's decision/reset times as decimal
milliseconds. Native entries keep the maker's timestamp, expire after ten minutes or at reset,
and are kept once per stable ID. The link catches up from limits on reconnect and retries unsent
pushes each minute while the fact is current; `data.ownNotices` identifies decisions this box
may forward. Queue acceptance does not consume a push: only a successful relay send records a
per-phone mark. Partial delivery retries only phones that did not take the push. The overall
mark is recorded once all intended phones took it, or notifications were deliberately off.
Journal write failures keep marks in memory and retry persistence without crashing the hold.
Only the pinned account holder pushes, through the existing encrypted notification path.
Relay push frames carry an address and sealed payload; clients cannot set an APNs collapse header.
Each app remembers shown usage IDs across restarts. A Mac that has notifications off consumes
incoming IDs silently, so enabling later shows no backlog. Apps do no threshold or pace
evaluation and have no older-box fallback.

### Usage settings

The usage panel's settings (#631 piece F) are the same on every app, whichever box it asks: each
box keeps them, and your own computers' boxes share them. They're what the panel shows and counts,
not how it looks: density, theme, transparency, animation, the menu bar's style and how each card
is opened stay each app's own. A client reaches them as `kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/settings…`
(the Mac app at `api/kuvo/usage/settings…` on its box's bridge), where `features` has
`usage.settings`. A bridge without them (an older app's keeper's, while the update gate holds this
Mac's box) answers 404: the Mac keeps a change and sends it once its bridge has the route.

- They're in parts, each changed and shared whole:
  - `layout`: `{placed, providerOrder, metricOrder, pinned, expanded, expandOnEnable, seeded}`.
    `placed` holds the meters shown, by id (`<provider>.<metric>`, as the Mac's panel names them),
    in order. `providerOrder` is the cards' order, and `metricOrder` each card's meters' order
    (`{<provider>: [id]}`), shown or not. `pinned` holds the meters pinned to the menu bar.
    `expanded` holds the meters shown only when their card is opened, and `expandOnEnable` the ones
    that go there when they're turned on. `seeded` holds the default meters already offered, so one
    you turned off isn't turned on again.
  - `providers`: `{enabled, known}`. `enabled` holds the cards turned on, and `known` every card
    offered, so a new one is offered once.
  - `totalSpend`: `{show, period?, metric?}`, the total spend card: whether it shows, its period
    and what it counts, as the panel names them.
  - `codexFallback`: Codex's fallback model ("Usage history"), `null` for none.
  - `notifications`: `{underTenPercent, healthyToClose, closeToRunningOut}`, which of the
    panel's notifications are on. They're delivered by each app, where it reads them.
  A part never set is absent: the panel's own default. Lists hold at most 1,000 ids of up to 200
  characters each, `metricOrder` at most 200 cards, and `period` and `metric` up to 40 characters.
- `GET kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/settings` → `{data: {settings: {<part>: value}, versions:
  {<part>: version}, imported}}`. `versions`: each part's version as a client names it (below).
  `imported` says whether what a client kept before has come in on this box (below).
- `PUT kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/settings` with the parts changed (`{layout?, …}`, each whole)
  answers as `GET`. With `knows: {cards, meters}`, the card and meter ids the client's app knows
  (all of them), `layout` and `providers` are whole for those alone: the ids the part held of the
  others (a newer app's) are kept, each after the nearest one before it that's still there (first
  when none is), so they keep their places. Without it, a part's ids are taken as sent. Fields of a
  part the box doesn't know (a newer box's) are kept whatever a client sends. With `based:
  {<part>: version | null}`, the version each part was changed from (`null`: the client had none),
  a part that has changed since (another computer's change came meanwhile) isn't changed: the
  answer names it in `stale`, and the client shows the box's. The Mac app sends both. The answer is `400 {message}` for a part that isn't one or isn't what it should
  be, and for a `codexFallback` that isn't one of `choices` ("Usage history"); nothing changes then.
  A part sent as it already is isn't a change.
- `POST kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/usage/settings/import` with what a client kept before (its own
  settings from before the box kept them, `codexFallback` among them) answers as `GET` with `took`,
  the parts that came in. It happens once per box: each part no box has set yet comes in, here or
  from another of your computers, and the rest stay as they are. A `codexFallback` the box can't
  price with now is left out. After the first time, it takes nothing. The Mac app does this the
  first time its box says `imported: false`, with only the parts you changed on it (a Mac still on
  its first-run settings brings none, so it never puts them over the ones you made on another,
  whichever comes first), never `providers` (each Mac turned on the cards for the tools it found:
  they're shared from the first time you turn one on or off).
- The bridge's events carry `kuvo.usage.settings` `{units}` when parts change (through these
  routes, from another of your computers, or as the box starts over in another setup): ask again.
- Each part carries the version of its last change, `{v, by, imported?}`. `v` counts on from every
  version the box has seen: milliseconds since 1970, or one past the highest seen when its clock is
  behind. `by` is the box that made it (its link key). `imported` marks what came in by import, at
  `v` its time by the importing box's own clock (an import isn't counted on from what was seen, as
  a change is). So between two imports on two computers whose clocks are off, the one whose clock
  said earlier wins, which may not be the one made first; once either is changed anywhere, the
  change wins. A client names a version as `<v>/<by>`, with `/i` after an import's
  (`versions`, `based`). The newest wins: a change over an import, the higher `v` between two changes, the
  lower `v` between two imports (so a Mac set up later never puts its first-run settings over the
  ones you made on another), and at the same `v` the `by` that sorts last.
- **Across your own computers** only: between the boxes of one setup ("Your setup"), whose
  boxes are all yours. The link tells the bridge the setup it follows now (`setup` in `PUT
  /api/kuvo/peers`, its id; `null` once it's settled that it follows none: a machine more than one
  Mac set up, or a setup set aside; not said while it can't say one: none made yet, as a box from
  before setups updates, or one it can't follow yet, its keys not read as its link starts or made
  anew. A link from before this, met for a moment as a box updates, doesn't say it either. The
  bridge takes not said as neither: it records nothing and shares nothing until the link says), and a box sends and takes
  them only while it follows one, only with its peers (the setup's boxes), and only mail naming the
  same setup.
  The settings belong to the setup they were shared in (`setup` in `settings.json`; `null` while
  the box followed none; a box from before this takes the first the link names): a box the link
  names in another setup (the setup changed), or in one after following
  none, starts over, every part and `imported` gone, so none of them reaches the new setup's
  computers, and its own Mac's settings come in again.
  Nothing goes before the link has said. Each box tells the others `{"seat": {"kind": "settings",
  at, digest, setup, usage?, ask?}}` through its link, which carries this kind only between your
  peers, whole or in parts as a group chat's
  mail is. `usage` is the parts with their versions (`{<part>: {value, stamp: {v, by,
  imported?}}}`), and `digest` a hash of all of them. A box sends all of them, with `ask`, to one
  it hasn't told since its bridge or link started. It sends all of them as they change, here or
  from another computer (not back to the box whose mail it just took, when it now holds the same). Every ten minutes otherwise it sends `digest` alone. A box takes the parts
  newer than its own. One whose `digest` then isn't the sender's sends all of its own (at most once a
  minute), asking for the other's when the mail held only a `digest`. `ask` is answered with all of
  them at once. A part a box doesn't know (a newer box's) is kept as it came, and passed on, and so
  are a part's fields it doesn't know (`digest` is of their JSON with every object's keys in one
  order), so two boxes of different versions agree (while what a part holds that a box doesn't know
  is at most 16 KB: past that the older box drops it, and the two tell each other all of it every
  ten minutes, at most once a minute each). Nothing is kept per computer: what's newer is
  taken into the box's own, kept in `usage/settings.json` (`{"kuvo": 1, units, imported?, setup?}`, `setup` an id or `null`, with `codex: {fallback}` where a box from
  before reads Codex's fallback model), through a restart. A box from before kept only that
  fallback model there: what it held counts as imported.
- A Mac app shows the box's parts in its panel and sends a part it changed, whole, with `knows`
  and `based`. Its import waits until its panel has read its layout (the usage item starts with
  the app); with the usage item off, it brings the layout as kept, once its meters were.
  It reads whether its box keeps them from `features` (`usage.settings`; its own box of the same
  version does). A change made while the box doesn't answer, before its first answer since a
  restart too, goes once it's back; one made again while the last is on its way goes from the
  version the box answered with, unless the box turned that one away (another computer's came
  first: the box's shows); one turned away though the box holds this Mac's own last (the answer to
  it was lost, and the box hasn't held another value of that part since, as this Mac last read
  it) goes again from the box's version: the app keeps what the box last said, and what's still to go,
  through a restart. Its panel's
  stores keep their own copy, so they start at once and work while the box doesn't answer; a change
  made meanwhile goes once it's back, and an answer that comes while one is on its way leaves that
  part as it is here. A part the box says again as it said it before isn't put in again. A card or
  meter a Mac doesn't know (a newer app's) is left out of its panel, and kept by the box (`knows`).
  The layout comes over in the import only when it isn't a fresh panel's (after Reset, or a change
  put back, it is). The phone shows the Mac's panel until it reads
  boxes itself (#631 piece H).

### The Work Queue

Each conversation keeps its work items in a Work Queue of its own, on the box it lives on, the
same on a Mac's box and a machine's, with no client there too: a session's, a bot's (its
conversation's), or a group chat's (`grp_…`, the queue its seats write to). Together they're one
list across your computers: each item lives once, in its owner's queue on its owner's box, and
every box shows every other's ("Across your computers"). It replaces the
hand-kept backlog file: agents write items through tools, every agent kind alike; clients show
them, and you add them, change what they say and where they stand, reorder them, delete them and
bring them back (where `features` has `work-queue.edit`, which names everything here about
statuses, priorities, labels, assignees, due days, `can`, `q` and a client's `POST` and `PATCH`; a
box without it kept categories, and isn't described here). Kept in `run/work-queue/`
(`queues/<owner>.json`, files kept with items in `files/<item>/`, `labels.json`, `numbers.json`,
`model.json`); a deleted item stays 30 days. Where `features` has `work-queue`. Times are
milliseconds since 1970.

**An item**: `id` (`wqi_…`, never shown), `number` (its `#n`; missing while it waits for one,
shown as new), `wanted` (a number an import asked for, until it's granted; beside `number`, its own
number asked back), `owner` (`ses_…`,
`grp_…`, or `usr_you`: your own queue, below), `title`, `status` (one of `statuses`, below), `order`
(its place among the items of its status, of every owner on
the box), `priority` (`urgent`, `high`, `normal` or `low`; always said, `normal` for one never
set), `labels` (`[id]`, several; only ones the view's `labels` list), `assignee` (`{kind: bot|agent,
id, name, look?}`, who it's for, a bot of the box asked with its `look`; missing for no one), `due` (`YYYY-MM-DD`, a day, no time or zone;
missing for none), `overdue` (true where its due day is before today on the box asked and it's
neither closed nor deleted: a client draws it late, and works out no lateness itself), `can` (what whoever asked may do to it, below), `progress` (`{value?: 0…1,
note?}`: how far, and what's being done now),
`sessions` (`[{session, title, working}]`: the sessions working on it, and which are at work now;
none at work on a closed or deleted one),
`noteCount`, `lastNote`, `fileCount`, `linkCount`, `handedBy` (the first owner that handed it on),
`source` (an outside source's item: `{kind, ref, url?, host?, id?, name?}`, named by `ref` and
never numbered; one that had a number keeps it, never shown again: "Issues and pull requests"),
`seen` and `keptIn` (what GitHub says of it, below), `handing` (`{to, name}`: on its
way to a conversation on another computer, unchanged until it's there), `computer` (`{key, name,
kind: mac|machine, id?}`: the computer it's on, when that isn't the box asked, as that one last told
it; `id`, a machine's name on this Mac, for a client to reach it), `created` and `updated` (`{at,
by}`: `by` is `{user: true}`, `{session, name}`, or another shape kept as it came, such as an outside
tracker's `{source, name?}`: a client shows its `name`, never takes it for you), `doneAt`, `removed`
(`{at, by}`, deleted). Whole, it has `body` (Markdown), `notes` (`[{at, by, text}]`), `events`
(below), `files` (`[{name, size, type, at}]`), `links` (`[{url, title?, kind?, ref?}]`) and
`handed` (`[{from, to, at}]`, the last 20).

**What happened to it** (`events`, for its feed): `[{at, by, kind, from?, to?, top?}]`, oldest
first, the last 50, kept with the item and going with it wherever it goes (a hand-off to another
computer, a move), as its notes do. `by` is who did it, as for `created` (`{source: "kuvo", name:
"Kuvo Code"}` for what the box did itself). A box keeps an event by its `at`, its `kind` (up to 40
characters) and its `by`, each of a size an event has; what else it says is
kept as it came, for a client to read (a newer box's `top: false` or `from: null` too).

- `started`: a session's agent said it's working on it (`working: true`), unless it's at it already:
  linked, with its own last word `started` since the item was last `done`. A session linked some other way (`sessions`, a
  hand-off) says `started` the first time it says it's working; one linked before this box kept
  events, or whose `started` went past the last 50, says it once more then. (A delete keeps no
  event: a session linked again to an item brought back, that had said `started` before its
  delete, says no new `started`.)
- `stopped`: its link went while its own last word was `started`: it said it stopped (`working:
  false`), or it was unlinked (`unlink`, or its oldest link dropped as it linked a fourth item), by
  the same `by` as that `started` but where it said so itself. One that never said it started says
  no `stopped`. Done and a delete unlink everyone and say no `stopped`: they say it. A session that
  starts again within 2 minutes of its `stopped`, with nothing between (no other event, note or
  hand-off), never stopped: the `stopped` goes.
- `moved`: you or an agent gave it another status, or another place among those of its own (`from`
  and `to`, status ids, the same for a reorder; `top` when it went to the top). Its place is among
  every owner's items of that status on the box, as the All view lists them, so a move past
  another queue's item is one; a move that leaves it where it was isn't. One's reorders within one
  status within 10 minutes of each other, with nothing between (no other event, note or
  hand-off), are one `moved`. (Neither fold reaches back in time: an event from a computer whose
  clock was ahead is never folded into.) An item whose status the box doesn't know (a newer box's,
  come by a hand-off or a move, or brought back) goes to Todo, a `moved` by the box. A session
  that says it's working on one that's Todo, Backlog or Waiting makes it In progress: a `moved`
  by that session, before its `started`. An
  item added isn't moved, wherever it's put (`top`, `before`, `after`).
- `done`: its status became Done (to Canceled, and out of either, is `moved`).

A change to its title, description, priority, labels, assignee or due day keeps no event: `updated`
says who last changed it, and when.

A hand-off is in `handed`, not here. A newer box may keep other kinds: a box keeps them as they
came, a client leaves them out. An item from before this has none (`[]`), and keeps what happens
from then on. A client puts `notes` and `events` (with `created`, `handed`, `doneAt` where no `done`
was kept at it or since, and `removed`) in one feed, oldest first. At one moment: `created`; the
box's events up to its last `started` at that moment, in its order (a move and the work it
started); notes; hand-offs; its other events, in its order; `doneAt`; `removed`. A status an
event names that the view's `statuses` don't is "another status".

**Statuses**: where an item stands, one each, the same eight on every box, never changed by
anyone: `{id, name, closed}`, listed by the view in the order a client shows them. Open:
`needs-you` (Needs you: only you can move it on), `in-review` (In review), `in-progress` (In
progress), `waiting` (Waiting: on something else), `todo` (Todo, where a new item starts),
`backlog` (Backlog). Closed: `done` (Done), `canceled` (Canceled). A status is set, by you or an
agent, never worked out: `sessions[].working` says who's at work now, whatever the status. Closing
an item (Done or Canceled) sets `doneAt` and unlinks everyone; opening it again clears it. A
session is linked to 3 items at most (linking a fourth drops its oldest link); a delete unlinks
everyone too. An item of a status a box doesn't know is kept as it came, and listed after the rest.

**Priorities**: `{id, name}`: `urgent`, `high`, `normal`, `low`, the same on every box.

**Labels**: what kind of work an item is; several on one item (10 at most), one set for every
queue (60 at most), none built in: `{id, name, color}` (`lbl_…`, or `cat_…` for one that was a
custom category; `color` one of `coral`, `orange`, `amber`, `lime`, `mint`, `sky`, `indigo`,
`violet`, `pink`, `graphite`, the bots' looks' names, a client drawing one it doesn't know as
graphite; a view lists them as `colors`, in the order a picker offers them, so no client keeps its
own list), in the order they were made. You and your agents make, rename, recolour and remove
them; removing one takes it off every item on that box first (then off the list: cut off between
the two, it's a label no item has, which removing it again finishes). Each box takes the labels of the
primary it numbers from as it tells them (its list, order, names and colours; a label of the same
id made here is the primary's from then on, as it's one set for every queue; one it removed is
taken off every item here and goes too, but only by the same primary's word: where the primary is
another computer than before, or tells no labels at all, those it no longer names stay, as this
box's own), and changes none of those itself while it numbers from another: renaming, recolouring
or removing one on such a box is refused (400), saying to do it on the first computer, and those of an item handed or moved to it; a view also lists a label
only another computer has, after its own, for its items there.

**Assignee**: who an item is for: one of the box's bots (`{kind: "bot", id: "bot_…"}`) or a coding
agent (`{kind: "agent", id}`: `claude-code`, `codex-cli`, `cursor`, `grok-cli`, `antigravity`). A
view's `assignees` (`[{kind, id, name, look?}]`, the box's bots first, each with its `look`) lists
who an item kept on that box may be for. It's a fact the item states; it starts no work, and
hands nothing on, but for one case: an item in your own queue assigned to a bot of that box goes
into that bot's queue (a hand-off, in `handed`), where its agent's tools see it. One told by
another computer names its assignee as that computer does.

**Your own queue** (`usr_you`): the items you added from a client that are no conversation's. It's
in the All view, and its own (`owner=usr_you`; `owners` names it `{owner: "usr_you", kind: "you",
title: "Your own"}`); no agent's view has it, and it never moves to another computer with a conversation.

**What may be done** (`can`, on every item of a view and of an answer to a client): `{edit, set,
assign, close, delete, restore, attach, why?}`, so a client offers nothing the box would refuse, and works none of it out
itself; `why`, where something can't be done, says so in words a client shows as they are. `edit`: its title and description (never an issue's or a pull request's: GitHub's).
`set`: its status among the open ones, its priority, labels, due day and place (nothing of an
issue while GitHub has it closed: every such change is refused, not only its status). `assign`:
its assignee, from the view's `assignees` (the bots of the box asked: false for an item another
computer keeps, which is assigned there). `close`: Done or Canceled (never an issue's: GitHub closes
it). `delete`; `restore` (a deleted one, and nothing else then). `attach` (`work-queue.attachments`):
files may go with a change to it (`files`), as `edit`, but false where the computer it's on doesn't
say `work-queue.attachments`; a client offers no way to attach without it (none from a box without
the feature). All false while its conversation
moves to another computer, or while the computer it's on isn't answering or doesn't take a
client's changes from another box; only `delete` while it's on its way to another computer
(`handing`). An item as another computer told it between boxes carries none.

**From categories** (a box that kept its items under categories, as builds before #674 did; no
release shipped them, so nothing here is for a released version): before anything
reads or changes the queues, once, one way. What was kept is copied whole first to
`run/work-queue/before-statuses/` (`queues/`, `categories.json`), in one step (a copy cut off is
never taken for it), and never changed again; each queue's file is then written whole, item by item
left as it is if it has a `status` already; `categories.json` then goes (it's in the copy) and
`model.json` (`{model: 2, at}`) is written last, so a
run cut off midway is carried on by the next to the same end. Nothing an item holds changes (its
number, description, notes, files, links, sessions, progress, events, hand-offs) but where it
stands: Next is `todo`, Later `backlog`, Done `done`; Parked is `backlog` with the label Parked
(`lbl_parked`, graphite); a custom category called "Waiting on you" is `needs-you`; any other
custom category becomes a label under its own id, in the colour the apps drew it in, on a `todo`
item (`backlog` for "Correctness sweep" and "Edge cases"). Before statuses an item was in
progress while a session linked to it was at work, which the move can't see (it runs before the
engine answers): it leaves each open item a session had said it was on (linked, its last word
`started`) where its category put it and names it (`started` in `model.json`); once the box can
say who's at work, those whose linked session is are `in-progress` (a `moved` by the box), the
rest stay, and `started` goes: looked at once, and a status is only ever set from then on. `moved` events name the statuses
their categories became, with the label a custom category became beside each (`fromLabel`,
`toLabel`: label ids), so a feed can still say where it came from. Items keep their order: within a status, in the order of the categories
they came from (Next, Later, the custom ones as listed, Parked), then their place there. Every custom category
becomes a label, one nothing was in too (but "Waiting on you", a status now); Parked only where an
item was. One process moves them over (`.moving-to-statuses` while it does: another that comes
meanwhile reads on and changes nothing; one left by a process cut off goes after two minutes), and
the copy is on the disk, its folders too, before a queue is written. A run that finds
`labels.json` there already (cut off after it, or `model.json` lost) adds only the labels an item
it still has to move over names, never one removed since. Nothing is kept for another computer that hasn't moved over yet: what one
tells without `labels` isn't taken, and an item it hands on or carries in a move under a category
is read as one read here before the move (its status from its category; its custom category's
label only where this box has it). Where the
move can't be made now (a full disk), views still answer, each item said anew as it's read, and
every change is refused (400, in words) until it's made: nothing is written under statuses
without the copy.

**Who sees what**: an owner's view is its own items, those of the sessions it oversees (started by
it, or by those, put away ones too), and those it handed on, each living once in its owner's queue,
on any of your computers: those on another, as it last told them (its `rows` say which sessions
there are under the owner, "Work"). A session's view also shows the items linked to it that are
someone else's (what it's working on, a lead's item say), unless they're deleted. That's seeing
only: its agent's tools still change, show and list only what's in its view without those, as
before (a linked item is its owner's to change). A client shows them first, as "Working on"
(`item.owner` isn't the view's `owner`, and the item's `sessions` include it).

- `GET kuvo/work-queue?owner=<ses_…|grp_…|usr_you>` → `{owner, statuses, priorities, labels,
  colors, assignees, new, today, items, owners, removed, computers}`: `statuses` say which are
  `closed` (Done, Canceled): what a client folds, counts as not open and offers only where an item's
  `can.close` says, never a list of its own (the first closed one, Done, is what finishing an item
  sets: a client's one Mark button); `colors` the colours a label may be; `new` (`{status, priority}`) is what an item
  added with nothing said starts as, for a client's form to show; `today` (`YYYY-MM-DD`) the day it
  is on the box asked, which `overdue` goes by and a client counts days from ("Tomorrow", "Yesterday"),
  never its own clock; `items` in the statuses' order, then this box's first and each other computer's
  after, by its name (each computer keeps its own order), then each one's order; `owners` (`[{owner, kind:
  bot|session|group|you, title, bot?: {id, name}, startedBy?}]`) names each owner in the view;
  `removed`, what's deleted in it here, newest first; `computers` (`[{key, name, kind, id?, at,
  away?}]`), each other computer that told of its queue, as of when, and since when it hasn't
  answered (`away`, as `run/peer-reach.json` says): its items show as it told them, but none of
  their sessions at work, as nothing there can be seen at work now (an
  item's page says the same), and nothing may be done to them (`can`). `owner=all` is every queue on the box
  and on every other computer that told of its own (the panel's All). An item on another computer
  has `computer`. `kuvo/work-queue/events?owner=` is the same as NDJSON: a line now and one each
  time it changes (a change here or by another process, another computer telling of its queue, or a
  linked session starting or stopping work). With `glance=1` (a client that shows only a count or
  chips: the phone's •••, a conversation's chips on a Mac; a client follows whole only while the
  Work Queue itself shows), either reads no issue or pull request from GitHub: each is as last read.
  With `q=<words>` (200 characters at most), either lists only the items, deleted ones too, that
  every word is in, any case: in its title, its `#n` or its issue's name, its labels' names and, of
  one kept on this box, its description and notes (of one on another computer, its last note: what
  this box was told of it); the view says `q` back.
  With `computers=`, `sources=`, `owners=` or `labels=` (each a list separated by commas), either
  lists only the items that, for each kind asked, are one of those named (one kind widens, another
  narrows): a computer by its key (`""` or its own key for the box asked), a source by its `kind`
  (`none` for an item of the queue's own), an owner by its key, a label by its id (`none` for an
  item with no label); the view says them back (`filters`). A client filters nothing itself.
  With `counts=1` (`work-queue.counts`, #711), either adds `counts` `{open, statuses: {<id>: n},
  priorities: {<id>: n}, labels: {<id>: n}, sources: {<kind>: n}, computers: {<key>: n},
  removed}`, counted from that same view, as `q` and the filters narrowed it,
  for a client that draws them (the sidebar's rows, a search's): its open items; of each status,
  priority and label
  (every one of the view's, one with none `0`); from each outside source, by its kind
  (`github`; items of the queue's own aren't in it); on each computer, by its key (this box's own
  under its own key, `""` while it has none, and each other computer of `computers`); and how many
  are deleted (`removed`). `owner=all` counts every queue across your computers. A client draws
  these and never counts the items itself.
- `GET kuvo/work-queue/items/<id or number>` → `{item}`, whole (an issue's `gh:` ref names it too,
  but its "/" can't go in a path through every client: a client asks by the `id` its chip has). `…/files/<name>` → its bytes. An
  item on another computer has `computer` and `told`. Asked by a client (as "What you do" says
  who), the box reads it whole from that computer's box ("Across your computers", Done where it's
  kept): `told: false`. Otherwise, or when that computer can't be asked now (it isn't answering, or
  doesn't take that from another box), it's as that one told it, with an empty `body`, `notes`,
  `events`, `files`, `links` and `handed`: `told: true`. Its files' bytes, for a client, come from
  there the same way, 4 MB at most (413 for a bigger one, read from that computer itself: a machine
  by `computer.id`; a Mac, its own box), with 409 or 503 `{message, computer}` as for what you do.
  One no computer told this box of (an old Done one, a deleted one), asked by a client, is asked
  of each of your other computers ("Across your computers", Found where it's kept), so a client
  asks one box, whichever keeps the item, and never each computer in turn: it comes whole from the
  one that keeps it (`computer`, `told: false`); 404 only once every one said it hasn't it; 503
  `{message, computers}` while some couldn't say (`computers`: those, as `computer` names one;
  `message` says which and why, in words a client shows).
- `GET kuvo/work-queue/refs?refs=243,12`, or `POST kuvo/work-queue/refs {refs: [...],
  conversation?}` (a list, so a ref with a comma in it, an outside one later, goes whole;
  `conversation` is taken and not used yet: it's for "issue #12" in a project bound to a tracker,
  later) →
  `{refs: {"243": {id, number?, source?, seen?, title, status, owner?, removed?,
  computer?} | null}}`: what each ref names (`#243`, `243`, an id, or an issue or pull request in a
  queue: `gh:owner/repo#12` or its page, and a linked item's old `#n`), by the ref as it was asked, for a chip; one on another computer as
  it last told it, with `computer`; null for one no computer told this box of. A client reads each
  on its own (one it can't read is as null, the others still chips), and keeps what it learns by
  the ref as asked, not by a number.
- `POST kuvo/work-queue/refs {text}` → `{mentions: [{start, end, number}]}` for a client
  editing a description. Ranges use UTF-16 code units. Code and Markdown links are skipped.
- A whole item can include `bodyMentions` and `notes[].mentions`. Each uses the same ranges into
  the corresponding text and names its target as `item`, the stable item ID. Use that ID when
  showing or opening the chip. The box saves the binding with the text so an item keeps its
  references when it moves or the number changes. `itemRelations: [{id, title, number?, kind}]`
  lists `mentions` and `mentioned-in` from the saved descriptions and notes. The link goes away
  when the last mention is removed.
- `GET kuvo/work-queue/labels` → `{labels}`.
- `POST kuvo/work-queue/labels/restore` is used by `box labels restore <file>` over the local
  box's authenticated socket and by the box forwarding it to the main computer. It takes
  `{library, force?}` with saved label definitions. Existing definitions win by ID.
  `force` allows an ID recorded as removed to be restored.
  `GET kuvo/work-queue/labels/restore` with the same body previews the merge. A box on another
  computer uses an ownership GET over the current relay connection. Its request and reply stay
  in memory. The main computer advertises `work-queue.labels.restore.preview` when it can answer.
  Both routes report `{restored, alreadyPresent, conflicts, details, save?, provisional?}`, with a receipt when supplied by the save path. Legacy standby-backed saves can return 202 and their previews can be provisional.

**What you do** (a paired phone, this Mac's app, or Kuvo Code on another computer through `box
route` with its Mac's proof for that request alone, `x-kuvo-vault-proof` as the vault takes it; anything
else, a command on that computer included, gets 403). A client sends what it does to an item to
any of your boxes, whichever computer keeps it: one on another computer is done there, by that
computer's box, which this box asks ("Across your computers", Done where it's kept), and the answer
is that box's, its `item` with `computer` as this box names it. One no computer told this box of
is looked for first, as a read of it is (Found where it's kept; 503 `{message, computers}` while
some computer couldn't say, nothing done). When it can't be done there, it
answers `{message, computer}`: 503 while that computer isn't answering or this box isn't on the
relay (said at once, nothing sent), or when no answer came in 20 seconds (a file's, 60) or that
computer stopped answering meanwhile (it may have been done: a client looks again); 409 for one that doesn't take it
from another box (an older box), changed there. One on its way to another computer (`handing`) is refused (400) until it's there,
but for `DELETE`, which calls its hand-off off (a note says so) and deletes it.
A client can send `PATCH kuvo/work-queue/items/<id> {itemRelation: {item, kind}}`
for two items kept on the same computer. `item` is the other item's ID and `kind` is
`related`, `blocks`, `blocked-by`, or `duplicate-of`. A new kind replaces the pair's
previous relation. `null` removes it from either end. Both items show the relation from
their own side, including `duplicated-by` on the inverse end. The response includes
`itemRelationApplied: true`.

An attachment can appear in a description as
`![Attachment](kuvo-attachment:draft/<index>/<encoded original name>)` during a client
save. The zero-based index refers to the `files` in that request. The box substitutes
`![<stored name>](kuvo-attachment:file/<anchor>)` and includes that `anchor` on the stored
file. A file's anchor stays with it when the item moves. To remove a picture from the item
page, use `PATCH` with `removeInlineImages: [{url, name}]`, where `url` is the picture marker
and `name` is the saved file name. The box applies it to the current description under the queue
lock and answers `inlineImagesApplied: true`. The file stays attached.

`POST kuvo/work-queue/items` `{title, body?, status?, priority?, labels?, assignee?, due?, top?,
owner?, files?, operation?}` → `{item}`. Each create requires a client-generated operation ID
in `x-kuvo-operation` or `operation`. Retry the same action with the same ID and fields.
The item starts as `todo` and `normal` unless specified. The
box decides whose queue it's in: `owner`'s where a client names one (the conversation whose queue
it's looking at); else, for a bot of this box (`assignee`), that bot's; else your own (`usr_you`).
A title is one line: line breaks become spaces, one over 800 characters is refused (400), and what's
left is cut to 200; an empty one is refused.
`PATCH kuvo/work-queue/items/<item>` `{title?, body?, status?, priority?, labels?, assignee?,
due?, before?, after?, top?, files?}` → `{item}`: only what's sent changes. `status` and `priority` by id
or name; `labels` all of them, by id or name, in place of those it had (`[]` for none; one that
isn't a label is refused, never made); `assignee` `{kind, id}`, or null for no one; `due` a day, or
null for none; `before`/`after` an item of the same status, `top` the top of its status. An issue's
or a pull request's title and description are GitHub's, and so is closing it: refused (400).
With `work-queue.attachments`, both create and edit take `files`, the composer's carried
`{uri, name?}` files: a base64 `data:` URI with the bytes, or a local `file://` URL, taken only from
Kuvo Code's app on the box's own computer (over its own server, `x-kuvo-from: app` or `mac`) and
refused (400) from a phone, the relay, `box route` or another box, so nothing reads the box's files
through an item. For an item on another computer the box sends each file's bytes there (`data:`;
409 when that computer lacks `work-queue.attachments`, asked before any file is read; 413 for more
than 4 MB in all, as much as goes between boxes with one change). An issue's or pull request's
item takes none (400), as its `can.attach` says. The box copies them into the item's own
files, as an agent's (25 MB each, 50 an item, a name taken twice numbered); an edit appends and
keeps earlier files; they go when the item is deleted for good. A client offers attaching on a new
item where its box has `work-queue.attachments`, and on an item where `can.attach`.
`DELETE kuvo/work-queue/items/<item>` and `POST …/restore`; `POST kuvo/work-queue/labels`
`{add, color?}` (a colour the fewest labels have, unless said), `{change, name?, color?}` (a label
by its id or name) or `{remove}` (taken off every item on this box, deleted ones too, then gone)
→ `{labels, label?}` (on a box that
numbers from another, that one's labels come back as it says, "Across your computers");
`POST
kuvo/work-queue/import` `{owner, files: [paths]}` (Markdown files on the box: each list line
starting with `#N` is an item, with the status of the nearest heading above it that names one
(Done; Canceled; Shelved/Parked/Later/Ideas/Backlog as Backlog; any status by its name; a
heading that names a label gives that label, on a Todo item), else Todo, Done with `[x]`; a line
`NOW:`/`NEXT:` (Todo), `LATER:`/`PARKED:` (Backlog) or `DONE:` with
refs sets theirs; the first line naming a number gives its title, every line naming it its body)
→ `{added, byStatus, waiting, skipped, said}`. An item keeps its own number wherever no other item
has it, here or on another of your computers (as each told this box), and it isn't one this box
gave an item that's gone from it (`numbers.json`, `used`: moved away, or deleted); one waiting for
its number (an import's still under way) holds it as its own. An import skips a number here already under the
same title, or waiting for it; under another title, the item is imported with a new number
(`importedAs`) and a note, and `said` names each one renumbered and its number now, as it does
those the primary refuses at once (on the primary itself; elsewhere a note says so when its answer
comes). An item an import renumbered, imported again under the same number and title, isn't made
twice: it asks for its own number back (claimed as an import's are, as `restores` too, keeping
the one it has, and `wanted` meanwhile), where no other item has it (one on its way back to its own
number lets it go); granted, every such item moves at once (two can trade), with a note, and
`importedAs` goes. One whose number another item has waits (`backGranted`, never asked again) while
that one asks for its own, and moves once it has; else, or refused, it stays as it is, with a note
(`stays`: an import doesn't ask again). So importing the same backlog again repairs an import that
went wrong, and once it has, changes nothing. Each change to an item
answers `{item}`, with its `can`.

**Tools**: `GET kuvo/work-queue/tools` → `{tools, instructions}` (MCP definitions, and what the
tool servers add to what they tell agents); `POST kuvo/work-queue/tools {name, arguments, session}`
→ `{text, isError}`, run only while the session named is making that call (as the vault's). The
tool servers (this Mac's app, and its keeper while the app is closed, and a machine's
`kuvo-browser.js`) list them and pass on every `queue_…` call. Any agent can read and change items in any queue on
the user's computers. `queue_list` includes other bots' and sessions' queues by default.
`queue_list` uses the shared summaries of items kept on other computers. `queue_show` asks the
keeping box for the item and its history, with the last shared summary as a fallback.

Other tools include `queue_add`, `queue_update`, `queue_hand` (into a session's queue, linked to it: one on this box at
once; one on another computer that takes the Work Queue's mail, by address or a bot's name, by mail,
"Across your computers"), `queue_remove` (`undo` brings back an agent's delete; only you
bring back yours; one on its way to another computer has its hand-off called off), `queue_labels` (list them, or one change: `add` with `color?`, `rename` with `to`, `recolor` with `color`, `remove`), `queue_import` (items an agent read from
an old backlog, with their numbers; each `status?`, `label?`, `done?`). `queue_add` and `queue_update` take `status`, `priority`,
`labels` (all of them, by name), `assignee` (a bot's or a coding agent's name; null for no one)
and `due`; a new item is Todo and Normal unless said (In progress, added with `working: true`). `working: true` links the caller and makes a
Todo, Backlog or Waiting item In progress (unless the same call sets its status); `working:
false` unlinks it and leaves its status as it is. `queue_list` lists by status, the open ones
unless `done`, and takes `owner` (the exact queue address, such as a bot's session address),
`status`, `label` and `query` (words in titles, descriptions and notes where available). `item` is a number (`#243` or `243`), the id of one that has
none yet (the tool says it), or the issue or pull request an item is (`gh:owner/repo#12`, or its
page); `queue_add` with `issue` adds one, `queue_update` with `issue` makes an item that issue
("Issues and pull requests"). The box that keeps the item applies the change. If that box is on
another computer, the caller's box forwards the verified agent identity with the change. Both boxes
must support `work-queue.forward.agent`. A caller's own queue, used for adds and imports, is its
conversation's (a subagent uses its parent conversation's queue and a seat uses its group chat's
queue where the group lives). Ownership, oversight and session links do not restrict edits.

Edits retain the agent's conversation address and name in `updated.by` and in the item's notes
or events. Changes to fields such as title, description, progress, links and files add an `edited` event
with the names of those fields, even when the same call also moves the item or adds a note.
Hand-offs, soft deletes and restores record an event with the actor. `queue_list` leaves deleted items
out, and `queue_show` can read a kept deleted item. Agents can restore an agent's soft delete with
`queue_remove {item, undo: true}` within the 30-day retention period. The user can restore their own
deletions. To reverse an ordinary edit, submit the earlier values with `queue_update`. The history records
the actor and affected fields. It stores no general rollback snapshot of earlier field values or files.

When an agent calls `start_session`, it can name a Work Queue item with `item`. If omitted, the
box uses the first Work Queue reference in the task text, including phrases like `Work on #1 in
the API`. Code, Markdown links and GitHub references are skipped. Before delivering the task, the box links the new session to the item if it is open,
kept on the box where the session starts. This records that the session is working on the item.

Files an agent keeps with an item come only from its conversation's folder,
its project's folders or a temporary folder (links followed, nothing hidden, no other name by a
hard link, nothing of Kuvo Code's but its own folder), 25 MB each; they're read before the change
and kept with it, all or none. For an edit sent to another computer, the caller's box checks the
paths and sends the file bytes (4 MB total). The receiving box reads only those bytes.

**References in messages** (for chips, the same in every client: KuvoClient's `WorkItemRefs`):
`#243` names item 243 when the `#` is at the start or after a space or one of `([{"'/,–-`, with 1
to 6 digits and then no letter, digit or underscore; not inside a code span or block, a Markdown
link or a web address, and not after "PR", "MR", "pull request", "issue" or "step" (someone
else's numbers; outside sources get a prefix, `gh:owner/repo#12`). `gh:owner/repo#12` (`owner` a
GitHub owner, `repo` a repository name, the number 1 to 10 digits; then no letter, digit or
underscore; not in code, a link or an address either) names the item that is that issue or pull
request (a live one here, else on another computer, and a deleted one only where none is live).
Bare numbers resolve only through the conversation's queue view (its own items, those
of sessions it started, and items linked to it), never the all-items view or another conversation's
cached refs.
Numbers 1–10 stay plain when immediately preceded or followed by "ranked", "rank", "number",
"result", "results", "spot", "place", "position", "priority" or "seller", or followed by
"on" or "in" and another word, or "Google result(s)" (case-insensitive, allowing whitespace
between words). "The", "to" and "at" alone do not
block references: "to #243" and "the #1 reason" can name visible items. Code, links and the other
exclusions above still apply. With no conversation owner, bare numbers stay plain and cause no
requests; explicit `gh:` refs keep their computer-wide lookup and chips. Clients follow the
conversation's queue for numeric chips; only explicit `gh:` refs need
the computer-wide `refs` lookup. A client draws an eligible known reference as a chip (a mark for its status: a ring in progress, a check when done, `#243` and the
title on one line; for an issue or a pull request, GitHub's mark and `source.name` in place of
`#243`, the title struck through when `seen.state` is `not_planned` or `closed`), leaving one it
doesn't know as written; the message's words never change. A chip opens the item.

**Issues and pull requests** (GitHub's, on github.com): an item can be an issue or a pull request
there, read with the box's own `gh` and its sign-in (Kuvo Code keeps no key of GitHub's for it), and
never written to: nothing here changes anything on GitHub.

- In: an agent adds one (`queue_add` with `issue`: `gh:owner/repo#12` or its page), or makes an item
  of its own one (`queue_update` with `issue`): it's that issue from then on, named by it (`source`:
  `kind` `github` or `github-pr`, `ref` `gh:owner/repo#12`, `url`, `host`, `id` GitHub's own), its
  number kept and never shown again (the old `#n` still names it), its title and description
  GitHub's (what an item said before is kept as a note; a bare `#n` in an issue's description is
  that repository's, so a client chips only its `gh:` refs). Its ref is GitHub's own name for it,
  after a rename too. One item for each issue (by its name or GitHub's id): a second is refused,
  naming the first. `gh` reads it once as it's added or linked (with its description; under the same
  lock and back-off as every read); one it can't read (not there, signed out, no such issue it may
  see) is refused in words, and nothing is added. An agent reads its description fenced off as
  outside text, never instructions.
- Read only for what a client shows: a view (and its events), an item, and `refs` read the issues
  and pull requests in them where that's due (one GraphQL query for all, 200 at most, those asked
  longest ago first; one process at a time; again after a minute while it's open, half an hour once
  it's closed, five minutes when it couldn't be found; a host `gh` couldn't read isn't asked for five
  minutes). One another computer told of is read here only once what it told is five minutes old
  (`seen.checked`): that computer reads what it shows. (It tells `checked` with what it tells, but
  a newer `checked` alone isn't a change, so it doesn't go again for that: once five minutes old,
  a box showing it reads it itself.) A view's or refs' answer waits
  3 s at most for it; the events stream doesn't wait, and its next line has it; a request answered
  once (`box route`) never waits: a read that's due goes on in a process of its own (`kuvo-link.js
  box github-read`), kept for the next ask. One found missing where it was is read again by GitHub's
  id in the same read (moved, or a discussion now; one never read here, handed or told from another
  computer, by its `source.id`, and at once where that computer found it gone or its `source.url`
  is elsewhere), and only then taken as gone; that read not made (no network) holds the host off,
  and what's kept stands. One GitHub wouldn't answer for (its `errors` say anything but `NOT_FOUND`
  for it: an organization's SAML sign-on or IP allow list) stays as it was, and isn't asked again
  until it's due. Agents' tools never read GitHub: they say what was last read.
- Kept beside the queues, `run/work-queue/seen.json` (`{reads: {"<host>/<owner>/<repo>#<n>": {at,
  value, checked?, gone?}}, hosts}`), never in them: a read changes no item and no `updated`. `at`
  is since when GitHub has said what it says (a read that finds the same moves only `checked`, so
  nothing shown or told changes with it). One found missing later (gone, or no longer visible to
  that sign-in: GitHub says the same of both) keeps what was last read, `gone`, `at` since when
  it's been found so. The same reader (`link/github/graphql.ts`) reads sessions' pull requests for
  "A session at a glance"; what the glance kept before it did (`{at, pull}`, not `value`) is read
  as `value`, and written in today's shape from the next read on.
- Each summary takes it in: `title` GitHub's; `source.name`, what a client shows in place of `#n`
  (`repo#12`, `owner/repo#12` when another owner's repository read here has that name); `seen`
  (`{state, at, gone?}`: `open`, `draft`, `completed`, `not_planned` (a duplicate too), `merged` or
  `closed` (a pull request closed unmerged), and since when; a newer box may say more); and, while it's
  `completed`, `not_planned`, `merged` or `closed`, or `gone`, `status` `done`,
  the status it's kept with in `keptIn`, `doneAt` when GitHub closed it (or since when it's gone), and
  `doneAs`, what a client shows in place of its status: "Merged on GitHub", "Closed on GitHub" or
  "Gone from GitHub". Reopened, or found again, it's back at the status it's kept with; `struck` (closed
  without being done, or gone: its title drawn struck through) and `closesOn` (`github`: Done is
  GitHub's, never a place to move it to), for clients to draw by. A client draws a `gone` one's
  GitHub mark dimmed. What another
  computer tells carries the same, so a client draws it there without `gh`; its times are taken as
  no later than when it told them. Where this box read it too, the word asked of GitHub later
  (`checked`, else `at`) is shown, this box's on a tie, and one found gone only when the other is
  too.
- Done is GitHub's: moving one into Done, or out of it while it's closed or gone (you or an agent),
  is refused in words (400); its title and description aren't changed here either.
- One item for each issue wherever it goes: an item handed here that another item here is already
  (by its name or GitHub's id) is refused back with why; `queue_hand` refuses to hand one to a
  computer that told of another item that's that issue; and a deleted one isn't brought back (you
  or an agent, 400) while another item is that issue, here or on another computer. An issue's ref
  names its live item, here or on another computer, before a deleted one (`queue_add` says where the
  live one is, rather than offering the deleted one back).

**Numbers**: each item gets one `#n` unique in its setup. The main grants
blocks and durably advances the relay-backed high-water mark before issuing
numbers beyond its reservation. A taking-over main skips the reserved floor
so it cannot issue an existing block again. Members can use already-granted
numbers while away and wait for the main when out of numbers. Current requests
reuse the allocation ID and the main retains grant receipts. See
`box/src/link/work-queue/numbers.ts` and `setup/relay-lease.ts`.

**Legacy numbering and block wire format.** The older fallback below applies
to boxes outside the current setup model. The block `ask` and `give` shapes
remain in use.

A box that
follows no setup (Macs that share a machine, and the machines numbering with them, or a box beside
an older one; kept until every box knows setups and those Macs are joined in one) takes the first
computer you set up. Each box works it out the same way from what it knows: of itself, its peers and
the primaries they say they number from ("Across your computers", `told`), a Mac comes before a
machine (a machine is always set up from a Mac), then the one set up first (`since`: when that box
was set up, the earliest it can tell: its folder's making where the system keeps that, or its oldest
item; one that hasn't said is never earlier), then by key. A box keeps the primary it numbers from
(`numbers.json`, `primary`) while that one is still one of your computers and none set up earlier is
known: it moves only to an earlier one, never back, and one whose primary was removed or forgotten
finds the next. A primary no peer names any more (the one this box reaches it through stopped
saying it) is waited for: once three days go by unheard (`numbers.json`, `lost`), or at once once the
peer it was reached through (`through`) is removed, or once that peer names another primary (it
found this one gone, or one set up earlier), the box finds the next. A peer that hasn't answered for
three days and was still found away in the last hour (`run/peer-reach.json`, and
`run/peer-reach-checked.json`, when the relay last found it not there: not one that was away when
this box itself went off the relay; a Mac put away, or set up again with new keys, that its machines
still list a while) isn't one to number from; a box that reached it through that peer follows that
peer to its next. Heard from again, it's the earliest again, and boxes move back to it, which moves
past what was numbered meanwhile (`top`). A machine set up from a
Mac never numbers on its own; while it knows of no Mac that
can be reached yet, items wait. The primary numbers its own
items from its counter; another box numbers from blocks of 50 the primary gave it, and asks for the
next when 15 or fewer are left, by mail, on its rounds: `{workQueue: {ask: {id, count, claims?,
restores?, own?, top?}}}`, sent again every 30 s until answered with `{workQueue: {give: {id, from, to, granted}}}`.
`top` is the highest number the asking box used, holds or handed out: the primary moves its counter
past it (a box that numbered on its own before, or a primary that lost its file), and past any number
its peers tell it they use. A box that stops numbering on its own asks its new primary at once. A
primary that isn't one of the asking box's peers (an earlier Mac known only through a machine both
set up) is asked through the peer that named it: `{workQueue: {ask, to: <primary key>}}` to that
peer, which passes it on as `{ask, for: <asking box's key>}` if it's its own primary, and the block
back as `{give}`; one hop only, and a box takes a block only from its primary or the peer it asks
through. The primary keeps what it gave for each ask, so an
ask sent again gets the same answer, and notes the box it gave each block (`given`, `by`). `claims`
are numbers an import wants to keep (six digits at most, what a chip reads): the primary grants
those at or above its counter and within 10,000 of it, those it granted that box before, and, for
an ask that says `own` (a box that never claims a number it gave an item, `used`), those in a block
it gave that box (its own: a box drops its leases at or below its claims, and takes a block only for
the ask under way, so a block given for an ask an import replaced is never used), and moves its
counter past them. Until those an older primary kept without whom they went to are gone from
`given`, such a block counts for `restores` (numbers asked back for items an import renumbered)
only where every other computer the primary knows told it, and of no number as high as the block's
first (its `top` or its items), and the asking box told of one as high as its last: a box that
never tells the primary (one reaching it only through a peer) could hold one unseen. An imported item waits without a number until then; an answer decides only the claims
its ask carried (one claimed later waits for its own), and one refused gets the next number, with a
note. An item made with no number left waits too, and takes one, oldest first, when a block comes; one left
waiting with nothing under way (a crash midway, a move), or still asking for its own number back, is
claimed or numbered again within a minute.
A queue file that can't be read is never written over: the change is refused and the file set aside
(`queues/aside/`); fields a newer box keeps in an item are kept as they are, and so is a queue of a
kind of owner this box doesn't know (`queues/<kind>_….json`, a newer box's): never read, shown,
numbered, set aside or written over but by a move of an owner of that name, which carries it when
every item in it reads as one here (else it's left as it is, where it is).

**Moves**: a move carries its conversations' queues (a group chat's, its own) and their files
(`move.json`'s `workQueue`, the files in the bundle's `work-queue/<item>/`), put in place under the
same owners and numbers, each item checked as this box's own are, with the labels they have (`workQueue.labels`; one this
box can't keep is left off the item; a status it doesn't know is
Todo); once it's over, the box it left forgets them. While it's under way nothing changes those
queues (a tool's change, a hand-off into one, or yours: refused, with words to try again once
it's there), so nothing is left behind. A conversation carried on as another takes its queue. An
item on its way to another computer (`handing`) goes with the move and is sent from where it lands.

**Across your computers** (bridge 0.9.211, to a peer whose agents' mail `features` say
`work-queue.elsewhere`; mail as "Peers" says, under the top-level `workQueue`):

- **Told**: each box tells every such peer its Work Queue, unasked, so the others have it while it
  sleeps: `{workQueue: {told: {id, at, kind, since, top, primary?: {key, kind, since?},
  items, owners, labels}}}`. `items` are its items as a view gives them (without `can`) (not deleted ones; the
  100 latest Done; 1,500 at most), each with `handedFrom` (who handed it on) and
  `mentionTargets` (stable IDs it mentions), an issue's or pull
  request's with `seen` and `keptIn` as this box last read it (`seen.checked`, when it last asked
  GitHub); `owners` names their
  owners; `labels` its labels (`[{id, name, color}]`); `kind`, `since` and `top` how it numbers, `primary` the
  one it numbers from (itself when it's the primary). `id` (`wqt_…`) is the same while all that is.
  It's worked out again when a queue changes and each minute (who's at work changes it), and goes
  to one computer once in 15 s at most, again each minute (sooner after a change you made from a
  client, at the next round 15 s on) until that computer answers `{workQueue: {had: id}}`, nothing
  while it's the same and had, and nothing while that computer isn't answering
  (`run/peer-reach.json`; it goes once its mail comes again, and again in full to one that asks for
  agents as it connects). The receiver keeps the newest from each peer
  (`run/work-queue/peers/<key>.json`; one older than what it has by less than ten minutes, mail
  come late, is neither kept nor had; one older by more is its clock set back, and kept), cleaned as
  it takes it, and only from a box that's one of its peers; what's kept of a computer you removed
  goes. An item two computers tell of (one handed between them, the first not told again yet) shows
  once, as the one that changed it last says; one deleted here that another tells of is that
  computer's (a hand-off called off after it got there), unless it told of it on its way here. The primary's labels are those of every box
  that numbers from it (one reached through a peer: as that peer tells them): made, renamed,
  recoloured and removed as it tells them (one it removes comes off every item on that box); those only a
  box has itself stay, after them (past 60 in all, its unused ones go; never one in use).
- **Parts**: Work Queue mail too big for one goes as `{workQueue: {part: {whole, i, of, d, s}}}`,
  as a document's parts go ("Peers"): `d` pieces of 40,000 characters of the base64url of the
  whole's JSON (`{told: …}`, `{hand: …}`), `whole` the SHA-256 of all of it (base64url), `s` empty,
  at least 2 and at most 200 parts. The receiver puts them together once the last is here (four
  under way from each box at most), checks `whole`, and takes it as if it came in one.
- **Hand-offs**: `queue_hand` to a conversation on another computer leaves the item where it is,
  unchanged (`handing`: changes to it are refused meanwhile), and sends `{workQueue: {hand: {id, to,
  from, by, at, item, files, labels?}}}` (`id` `wqh_…`; `item` the item whole, as kept; `files`
  `[{name, data}]`, base64, 4 MB at most in all, one with more refused at once; `labels` those
  it has, `[{id, name, color}]`) to the box `to` lives on now, again each minute until it answers
  `{workQueue: {handed: {id, ok, why?, retry?}}}`, from that box only. Had (`ok`), the item and its
  files go from the sender; refused for good, it's back as it was with a note saying why; `retry`, it
  goes again; given back with a note at once when you removed the box it goes to, three days after
  that box stopped being one of its peers (`handing.missing`: a computer can be missing from the
  list a while) and `to` isn't on another, and after 30 days otherwise, whether this box is on the
  relay or not; deleted, it's called off (a copy that got there already is that computer's, shows as
  its, and the one deleted here isn't brought back beside it). The receiver takes each `id` once
  (remembered 30
  days, and an item it has already is had, but one deleted here, which the live one replaces), only
  from one of its peers, into the queue of `to`'s
  root conversation (a subagent's, its conversation's; a group chat's seat refused), linked to it,
  noted as handed from `from`, with the labels it can keep and its status (Todo for one it doesn't know), with its number as it was (one
  with none takes one there at once); it
  answers `retry` while `to` moves between computers or it can't look it up (its engine starting, or
  the coding agents' bridge not running), and while the item is still on its way from it to
  another computer itself (handed back before its receipt came), and refuses one for a conversation it doesn't have, or a
  queue that's full. So the item lives once, and stays in the hander's view on every computer
  (`handedBy`, `handedFrom`).
- **Done where it's kept** (to a peer whose `features` say `work-queue.forward`): what a client
  asks a box to do to an item another computer keeps ("What you do": a delete, a bringing back, a
  change, and a client's whole read) goes to that computer's box as `{workQueue: {act: {id, method,
  item, action?, name?, body?, at}}}` (`id` `wqa_…`; `method` `GET`, or with `action` `file` and
  `name` one of its files, or `DELETE`, or `POST` with `action` `restore`, or `PATCH`; `item` its id;
  `body` a `PATCH`'s, as the route takes it; `at` when it was asked), again every five
  seconds while it's waited for, and the answer comes back as `{workQueue: {acted: {id, status,
  value}}}` (in parts when it's big), what that box's own route would answer (`value` its JSON; a
  file's `{type, data}`, its bytes in base64, 4 MB at most, else 413), taken only from the box it
  went to, with a status from 200 to 599. The receiver takes it only from one of its peers; it does it as its
  own client's (`by: {user: true}`, numbered and told as any change of yours there), and answers
  each `id` once: one that comes again is answered as it was (a few seconds after its last answer at
  the soonest, a file not again while it's waited for), never done twice; a read's answer isn't
  kept, and one asked again later is read again. It remembers each until it would be too old to take (ten minutes from when it came,
  or from its `at` if that's later; 2,000 at most, the oldest going first), a change's on disk too
  (`run/work-queue/acted.json`), so a restart doesn't do it again; one under way as it stopped is
  answered 409, that it can't tell whether it was done. One whose `at` is more than ten minutes ago
  or more than a minute ahead of its clock is refused (409). One it doesn't have (it moved on
  meanwhile, or it knows it only as another computer told it) is 404, "It's no longer on <box>: it
  may have moved", never handed on again. The asking box leaves
  it in `run/work-queue/forward/<id>.json` (`{to, act}`) and waits for `<id>.answer.json` beside
  it, so its link sends it whichever process took the request (on a machine, a Mac's `box route`
  over SSH, which has no relay connection); what's past its wait is cleared at the link's next
  round. This Mac's box, whose routes run in the process that sends, sends only what its own
  routes left there: what anything else on the Mac leaves never goes out as you. A change done there
  is put at once in what the asking box keeps of that computer's queue, as its box answered (one
  deleted taken out of it), never over newer word of that item (one it told since as changed later); and one deleted there is kept a day
  (`run/work-queue/deleted-there.json`, 200 at most, until that computer or this box has it again),
  so a client's bringing it back (Undo) and reading it reach that computer after it has told without
  it. Nothing else (agents' tools, chips) sees those.
- **Found where it's kept** (`work-queue.anywhere` in `kuvo/info`): a box tells only its latest
  items, and none it deleted, so one a client names may be in nothing this box was told. For a
  client (never anything else on the computer), the box asked sends each peer that takes `act` a `GET` with `item`
  the ref as the client named it (its number, id or issue; 300 characters at most, else no one is
  asked), all at once. A peer's answer counts when it's a whole item that ref names: a live one is
  taken at once, the others not waited for; a deleted one only once every peer answered and none
  has it live (of two deleted, the one changed last). That peer keeps it, and a file or a change
  then goes there by its id, as above. One that answers 404 hasn't it. One that isn't answering or
  doesn't answer in 20 seconds, one that doesn't take `act` (an older box), and one that refuses
  or answers something else couldn't say: while any couldn't and none had it live, the box
  answers 503 `{message, computers}` and does nothing, as the item may be there; so too, naming
  every peer, while it isn't on the relay itself. `message` says which computer and why (it isn't
  answering; it needs a newer Kuvo Code; what it refused with, in its words), and to try again only
  where one isn't answering. A client shows `message`; it asks no other box for what this one
  answers for.

### Side questions, handoffs and reviews

Three more features each box answers in its agents bridge, as it does goals ("Goals"), and its
branches, for the engine's sessions and the coding agents' alike, with no client there: `kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/…` on
the box the conversation lives on (the Mac app at `api/kuvo/…` on the bridge), while `kuvo/info` has
`agents: true` (503 otherwise), where `features` names them. Each answers `400`, `404` (no such
conversation, or nothing of it), `409` and `503` with `{message}` to show. Times are ms since 1970.
A conversation deleted takes its side questions and its review with it (`kuvo.btw.removed`
`{sessionID}`, `kuvo.review.updated` with `review: null`), also one deleted while the box was stopped.

- **Side questions** (`btw`; threads `btw.threads`): a question about a
  conversation, answered from what it knows (on the engine, from inside its context; with the
  coding agents, the conversation goes with the question), and kept out of it: the conversation
  is told nothing. A question can be followed up, in a side thread: each follow-up is answered
  with its thread so far (the latest dozen answers), and a new question starts a thread of its own,
  afresh. Each conversation keeps its own list (the newest 100), which a client shows apart from
