  off (`GROK_MEMORY=0`), never in a shared leader (`--no-leader`; on a Mac its socket in `~/.grok`
  is refused), Kuvo Code's tools through the relay; of its home, on a Mac, only what's named as its
  state (`sessions`, `logs`, `memtrace`, `debug`, `crash`, its sign-in, locks and databases), and
  in those never settings (`*.toml`, `hooks-paths`, `disabled-hooks`, `*.sh`, so a project's
  always-allowed commands too); nothing else there (its settings, hooks, status line, language
  servers, the settings xAI sends, its models' list, which names where each model's requests go,
  its program, plugins, skills or memories). In a project, `.grok`'s settings, language servers,
  hooks, plugins, agents and workflows are kept as the other agents' are.
  Cursor, whose SDK runs its tools in the process that runs it (the bridge's, otherwise), runs whole
  the same way: its SDK in a process of its own for each session (the engine's runtime run as Bun:
  `KUVO_FENCE_BUN=1`, which commands don't get), which the bridge asks over its stdin and stdout,
  Cursor's own sandbox off, stopped once it's been done 15 minutes. Your sign-in stays with the
  bridge, which hands it the key it runs with, out of its reach: of Cursor's folders it reads and
  writes only its conversations and a folder of its own for its notes, sandbox policies and computer
  use's (`cursor/in-sandbox`, never what Cursor keeps run in the bridge), and it reads its SDK.
  Antigravity runs whole too, for its sessions and its sign-in alike: its home (`GEMINI_HOME`, Kuvo
  Code's own, never yours) and its temporary folder, where it unpacks itself, written whole; its
  program and the bridge's browser catcher only read; Kuvo Code's tools through the relay. It
  writes and reads files with its own tools then: the bridge offers none (`fs` false in
  `initialize`), since it would write outside the sandbox.
  Every agent also gets the computer's MCP servers, sandbox on or off: those the engine has for the
  conversation's folder (`GET /api/config` with it, read in the engine's order), but those turned off. They reach them
  through the same relay, at `/mcp/<name>` with the session's key: the agent is told only that
  address (Claude Code over its pipe, Codex in its thread's settings, Cursor in its agent's, an ACP
  agent in `mcpServers` when it takes HTTP), never a server's command, address or keys. A URL's
  server the bridge reaches with its headers, and with your sign-in to it when you signed in
  (`/api/credential`); one about to run out, or turned down, it has the engine renew (connecting
  the server again) and tries once more. A command's server it starts for each connection (found on
  the PATH), with its keys in its environment and the engine's caches, in the conversation's
  folder; while the sandbox is on, in it, as the conversation's commands are, but with its
  integration's own folder (`KUVO_INTEGRATIONS/<one>`, where it keeps a sign-in) its to write, the
  engine's program to read (Bun, for `kuvo-npx` without Node), and Bun's cache in the sandbox's npm
  cache. One no connection has used for an hour stops. What a server asks the agent (`roots/list`,
  `elicitation/create`, `sampling/createMessage`) is answered -32601 at once, not passed on; its
  stderr goes nowhere, as it can hold its keys. Another set of servers (one added or taken away)
  starts Codex's thread, Cursor's agent and an ACP agent again and is told to Claude Code; a key you
  changed reaches the relay alone, from the agent's next turn.
  While it's on, `gaps` lists what it can't keep commands from on this computer: `services`, the
  services your login runs, and git's own files in the repositories they write (a Linux machine
  whose commands can't have a namespace of their own;
  `needs`: `"user namespaces"`, or `"util-linux"` without `unshare`); `git`, git's own files in the
  repositories they write (a Linux machine where a folder can't be made read-only in a command's
  namespace, tried in the box's own folder as it's checked: commands in a repository there don't
  run, 126, rather than run with those open to them). A client says so beside it (`services`;
  the apps don't show `git` yet). With `sandbox.needsYou` (#739), `needsYou: true` says its row
  warns, why and its button with it: while it isn't on, for any reason (Kuvo Code's own switch
  too), or is on with `gaps` `services`. A client warns by that alone, keeping no rule of its own;
  without it (on and whole, or with only `git`), a quiet line. With `sandbox.report` (#668), `services` comes with the box's
  words for it too: `why`, a sentence to show as it is (what commands can still reach, and what
  waits until the machine allows user namespaces or has util-linux), and the docs' page on what a
  machine needs as its button (`action` `help`, `actionLabel`, `opens`), so no client keeps either.
  When it isn't on, also `reason`, a word for a client to map rather than reading `why`, with what
  you can do (`action`) and the box's route that does it (`route`, where there is one). With
  `sandbox.words` (#711), the words are the box's too, so no client keeps a table of them: `why`
  is there for every `reason` (a sentence to show as it is), and `actionLabel` says the button's
  words for `action`: `retry` "Try Again" ("Check Again" for `engineMissing`), `fix` "Fix It",
  `restartEngine` "Restart Engine…" ("Restart Engine" for `engineDown`, where nothing runs to
  stop), `help` "How to Check…", `softwareUpdate` "Software Update…". A client draws the button
  with those words: one with a `route` sends it; `help` opens the docs on what a machine needs
  and `softwareUpdate` the system's own. With `sandbox.opens` (#708), the box says what those two
  open, so no client keeps an address: `opens`, the address a button with no `route` opens (the
  docs' page; the Mac's Software Update pane), and `opensHere: true` where that address is the
  computer's own (the Software Update pane: it opens the pane of whichever computer opens it), so
  only a client running on that very computer opens it, and any other shows no button, `why`
  standing alone. A client opens an address that isn't `opensHere` only when it's a web page
  (`https://` or `http://`): a box never has another computer open anything else. A state with no
  `action` (Kuvo Code's own switch off) has no button.

  | `reason` | when | `action` | `route` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `kernel` | Linux without Landlock; `needs`: `"Linux 5.13"` | `help` | |
  | `namespaces` | Linux that doesn't let commands have a namespace of their own, from a box that doesn't run without one (none does now: `gaps`); `needs`: `"user namespaces"`, or `"util-linux"` without `unshare` | `help` | |
  | `macos` | this macOS has no sandbox | `softwareUpdate` | |
  | `engineMissing` | a machine without its engine yet | `retry` | `POST kuvo/sandbox/check` |
  | `checking` | not checked yet, or its check didn't finish in time (a busy computer: never taken for a failed one). Commands still run in it then, and nothing counts on it (Auto asks first, the vault stays shut) until a check passes; tried again each minute. Five in a row that don't finish count as failed (`checkFailed`, `didntRun`) | `retry` | `POST kuvo/sandbox/check` |
  | `checkFailed` | its check failed; `check`: `folder`, `tempFiles`, `readsOwn`, `writesOwn`, `services` (on Linux, a command could reach your session's services), `didntRun` or `setup`. Commands stay in it, with nothing counting on it, until every conversation's rules here, subagents' too, ask first (Auto held), the engine's and, where it runs, the coding agents' bridge's; only then is it taken away and they run outside it. (A bridge that isn't running isn't waited for, nor a record it left: while the sandbox isn't on, or one of its agents runs outside it, a conversation there whose rules were made for Auto asks before its commands. One that runs and doesn't answer keeps it held, tried again less often while it doesn't.) Auto's reviewer lets nothing out once Auto can't be had, even one it allowed meanwhile. Watches' checks, which can't ask, wait for it to be back (`run/fence/ready` stays). On Linux, a namespace in effect that a try says commands can't have is kept while the check goes through it, and dropped (`gaps`: `services`) only if that fails, the same way | `retry` | `POST kuvo/sandbox/check` |
  | `plugin` | its plugin for the engine was changed or removed | `fix` | `POST kuvo/sandbox/check` |
  | `engineDown` | the engine isn't running | `restartEngine` | `POST kuvo/engine/restart` |
  | `waiting` | the engine hasn't loaded it yet | `restartEngine` | `POST kuvo/engine/restart` |

  `failures`, with
  `checking` and `checkFailed`: checks failed in a row (the box tries again each minute). With
  `sandbox.report` (#668), from two in a row the state adds `report`, what a report of it says (how
  many, `why` and `check`): a client offers Report a Problem beside its button then, and sends
  those words with it (adding which computer it is), never before. A box
  without `sandbox.check` in its features gives none of these; without `sandbox`, it has no sandbox
  (an older Kuvo Code, to update).
- `POST kuvo/sandbox/check` → the state, after setting it up and checking it again.

#### Asks

When the sandbox stops a command a task needs, the agent asks with its tool `sandbox_ask` (`command`,
`why`, and what it printed, `error`; `timeout`, how long it may run, 300 seconds unless it says, at
most 600). In a conversation in Auto, Auto's reviewer answers it first ("Auto's reviewer"), and in
one in Full Access nobody's asked (its commands run outside the sandbox already: one that still
asks runs at once, `Ran outside the sandbox · Full Access`). Otherwise every client is asked; on
Allow Once or Always for This, **the box runs that one command itself**, outside the sandbox: with your login shell (`-lc`), in the conversation's folder (the
engine's record of it, never the command's), with the box's environment but without the passwords
and secrets of Kuvo Code's own processes, and hands back what it printed (the last 64 KB) and how it ended. The
agent's text starts `Ran outside the sandbox · Allowed once` or `· Always for this: …` (with the
folder its commands now write in); on Don't Allow,
`The user said no: …`, and nothing runs. An ask nobody answers in 15 minutes runs nothing either, and
the text starts `Nobody answered in time` (a client shows it as no answer, not as your no). The agent
never lets a command out itself, and no tool answers an ask (a bot neither): only a client, Auto's
reviewer or Full Access. A bot's
seat in a group chat runs no commands, so it has nothing to ask: its rules deny the tool, and the box
refuses one from a seat, asking nobody.

**Stopped commands** (`approval.stopped`, bridge 0.9.190). In Auto the agent needn't ask: the box's
plugin in the engine looks at what each call of the shell tool printed as it ends, and where it
failed with what the sandbox prints (`Operation not permitted`, `Permission denied` but SSH's own,
`Read-only file system`, `EPERM`, `EACCES`; on Linux also `No such file or directory`, for the
secrets hidden from commands), tells the box's long-running process over `run/vault.sock`:
`POST kuvo/sandbox/stopped` `{session, input, output}` (the call's own arguments, and the last 4 KB
it printed). Only while that conversation is making that very call, only in Auto, and only where
the sandbox stopped it (on macOS `Operation not permitted`, which a file's own permissions or a
database don't answer; on Linux, Landlock's answers, or a hidden secret named as missing), Auto's
reviewer judges the command as it judges a `sandbox_ask` (by what you said, a bot's goal), also
seeing what it printed and, on macOS, what its log says the sandbox refused it (read for a few
seconds), as running it again outside does that too (a write to where things run at login counts as setting one up; one to Kuvo Code's folders is
never allowed). It lands in Decisions either way. Allowed, the box runs it again outside the
sandbox, as an Allow Once, in the folder the agent ran it in, within what the call has left of its
16 minutes, and stops it if the call is stopped meanwhile; the agent gets `{text, exit}` instead of
what the sandbox let it print: `The sandbox stopped it · Ran again outside the sandbox · Allowed by
Auto's reviewer: <reason>` and its output. Refused, `{text}`: the refusal's words, added after what
it printed, and the call ends as it did. Anywhere else the answer is `{}`, and the call is left as
it was. Nobody is asked.

On macOS `top` runs outside the sandbox as it is (it's setuid, which the sandbox can't start, and
shows no program's environment); `ps` stays refused in it, as it would show every program's
environment: in Auto it goes to the reviewer as any stopped command.

The tool is the box's, so an agent has it on every box (`sandbox.asks`): this Mac's tool server
(the app's, and the keeper's with the app closed) and a machine's (`kuvo-browser.js mcp`, through
`box route`) list what `GET kuvo/sandbox/tools` gives (only
while the sandbox is `on`) and pass a call to `POST kuvo/sandbox/tools` `{session, name, arguments}`
→ `{text, isError}`, which, as the vault's, the box carries out only while that conversation is
making that call. The asks, the tool and the answers live in the box's long-running process, as the
vault does (`run/vault.sock`); another passes them on.

- `GET kuvo/sandbox/asks` → `{asks: [ask], restart?, reviews?, settled?}`, oldest first, with `restart: true` while
  the box asks you to restart its agents (the state's `restart`); `kuvo/sandbox/asks/events`, NDJSON,
  the same at once and on every change. `reviews` (bridge 0.9.192): what Auto's reviewer did with
  the engine's asks to work outside a conversation's folder (`permission.asked`, action
  `external_directory`), the latest 200, each `{id, session, call?, state, at}`: `id` the
  permission's, `call` the tool call that asked (its step), `state` `checking`, `allowed`, `heldBack`
  (refused, the agent told why, listed in Auto's Decisions), `refused`, or `yours` (not the
  reviewer's: not in Auto, no folder, or it couldn't judge). Its own project, and a bot's (its
  folder, a project it made, its goal's), go ahead as `allowed` with no review. A client shows no
  card, notification or "needs you" for such an ask while it's checked or once it's decided, only a
  quiet mark on its step. A box with `sandbox.reviews.whole` lists every such ask from the moment it
  hears it (`checking` at once), takes up those already waiting as it starts again, and lists one it
  can't take up as `yours`: a client shows such an ask only once it's listed `yours`, and waits for
  nothing of its own. An answered ask (or one gone with its run) leaves the list unless the reviewer
  decided it, whose entry stays for its step's mark. While a client doesn't hear the box's asks
  (its link down or starting again, the stream cut), what it last listed of an ask stands, and one
  it never listed is yours, as nothing would list it. (A box without that word is older than the
  update gate lets through: held, never taken at its word.)
  `settled` (`sandbox.reviews.settled`): each ask the reviewer was checking or had left for you
  that's over without its word, the latest 200, each `{id, session, call?, state, at}`, `state`
  `answered` (by you, on any client, or by its engine: `permission.replied`) or `gone` (its run
  ended, its session was deleted, or its engine let it go while the box wasn't listening: an
  engine started again, a run that ended unheard). The box keeps them per ask and session, from
  `checking` to `yours` to `answered` or `gone`: as it hears an engine or the bridge again it reads
  each session whose ask it still lists as checked or yours there, and one no longer asked is
  `gone`; one it was about to check and finds no longer asked is `gone` too, never `yours`. A
  client never takes an ask listed in `settled` for one that waits, heard or not, so none is left
  with an ask that's over (a session's row saying it asks). Such a client holds nothing of its own
  for an ask the box takes up but one it heard asked that the box hasn't listed yet (it lists each
  as it hears it), which is yours, and told, should the box go quiet first, as above. It tells you
  of one (a notification) once it's listed `yours`,
  reading it from its engine then (one its engine no longer asks isn't told; where its engine
  can't be read, it's told without its words), and lets go of one listed in `settled`. The
  reviewer's own answer isn't listed `answered`: the ask goes from `checking` to what it decided. The box's
  process started again lists what still waits as it takes it up again (`checking` at once) and
  none from before. An ask: `{id, at, session?, sessionName?, bot?, botName?,
  project, command, why, stopped?, error?, always?, machine?, owner?, review?}`. `session` is the conversation's root
  (a bot's sub-agent asks as its bot's conversation). `stopped`, on macOS: what the sandbox refused
  that command, from the system's log, each `{kind, path?}` (`kind`: `write`, `read`, `connect`,
  `job`, `app` or `other`; `path`, the file, folder or address). macOS logs it a while after (on a
  busy Mac, seconds), so an ask can go up without it and get it, with `always`, in a later line of
  the events (the box reads the log again for about a minute); a client shows the ask as it is now. `always`: what Always for This would
  keep besides running it, `{kind: "write", path}`, the one place the sandbox stopped it writing,
  when that's all it stopped and it's one that may be given (below); without it, the command can
  only be allowed once. A command itself is never let out for good: what it runs (its scripts, its
  project's settings, `package.json`, a `Makefile`) is what the sandbox writes, so the same command
  asks again each time. `machine`: the machine's name, on a machine. `owner`: whose its folder is,
  which Always gives the place to (Also Allowed, below; bridge 0.9.139): a client names a bot's own
  folder by the bot ("outside Scout's folder") and the chats as Chats, whose Always is every chat's. `review`: from a box
  before 0.9.185, in a conversation in Auto, why its reviewer brought it to you, `{reason, why}`;
  since then a conversation in Auto never asks ("Approval", "Auto's reviewer").
- `POST kuvo/sandbox/asks/<id>` `{answer: "once" | "always" | "no"}` → `200`, `404` for one that
  isn't open, `400` for another answer. `always` without `always` in the ask counts as once.
- Each open ask is also a notice to your phones (as the vault's are): `<who> wants to run a command
  outside the sandbox`, the command and why, `category` `ask`, `data.sandboxAsk` its id.

On macOS the launcher tags each command's refusals in the system's log
(`kuvo-sandbox <session> <first 16 hex of the command's SHA-256>`, as `sandbox-exec`'s message), and
the box reads them for `stopped` (`log show`, the last 3 minutes). Linux's Landlock logs nothing, so
there an ask has only what the agent says (`error`) and never `always`: a folder is added to Also
Allowed by hand. Reading the log doesn't hold up the box: the ask waits on it.

#### Also Allowed

What you let a project's commands do beyond the sandbox, from Always for This or added in Settings:
a folder (or file) they write in the sandbox, at most 8 a project. Kept in the box's own
`box/sandbox-allowed.json`, which no command can write, and changed only in the box's long-running
process (another passes the routes on). A rule: `{id, project, kind: "write", path, at, by?, owner?,
gone?}` (`project`, `path`: real paths; `by`: `Mac` or the phone's name).

A bot's own folder (its folder's `workspace`) and the chats' folder are projects here too: a
bot's own conversation, and every chat (they share one folder), have their own rules. Since bridge
0.9.139 each rule says whose it is, `owner`, `{kind: "project" | "bot" | "chats", id?, name}` (a
project by its folder's name, a bot by its `id` and the name it has now, the chats as `Chats`), and
`gone: true` when its project's folder isn't there any more (a project deleted or moved), so a
client still lists it to be removed. A bot's rules go once it's no longer here (deleted, or moved
to another computer): the long-running process drops them as it next answers Also Allowed. Adding
for a bot or the chats makes its folder if there isn't one yet. A client lists them all at once, grouped by whose.

The launcher reads a project's as each command starts, from `run/fence/allowed/<sum>` (one path a
line; `sum`, the first 32 hex of the SHA-256 of the project's real path, as the launcher names its
temporary folder); a folder that's become a link since isn't given. Inside one, what's kept from a
project's commands is kept there too on macOS (git's hooks and config, the engine's and the coding
agents' settings: Linux's Landlock grants a folder whole, as it does the project).

What can't be given (`400`, and only allowed once): your home folder or the whole disk; a folder of
Kuvo Code's; a secret or a folder that holds one; and what runs later outside the sandbox: anything in
your home folder's hidden folders, `Library`, `bin` or `Applications`; the system's folders (`/usr`,
`/opt`, `/etc`, `/Library`, `/Applications`, `/nix`…); a folder on the box's `PATH` or one that holds
one; a repository's own folder (`.git`) or a settings folder of the engine's or an agent's; and the
places the sandbox already keeps read-only. Your home folder is your account's own, whatever `HOME`
says.

- `GET kuvo/sandbox/allowed[?project=<folder>]` → `{allowed: [rule]}`, that project's; without
  one, every rule here and `owners`: whom else a folder can be added for, each bot here working in
  its own folder (not a project) by name, then the chats.
- `POST kuvo/sandbox/allowed[?all]` `{project, kind: "write", path}`, or `{owner: {kind: "bot", id} |
  {kind: "chats"}, kind: "write", path}` for a bot's own folder or the chats' → `{allowed}`, that
  project's, or with `?all` everything as `GET` answers it; `400` with `message` for one that can't
  be given (and for a bot that works in a project: its rules are that project's). The same rule
  again is the one there.
- `DELETE kuvo/sandbox/allowed/<id>[?all]` → `{allowed}`, that project's, or with `?all` everything;
  `404` for one that isn't there.

A box before 0.9.139 sends no `owner`, `gone` or `owners` and answers `?all` as without it: a client
lists its rules by their projects' folders, adds for projects only, and reads them all again after
an add.

### Git

A repository's own settings (its `.git/config` and what that includes) never start a program when
the box runs git there (bridge 0.9.183), since whatever could write in the folder (a download, a command the sandbox
let out) could have named one. The fence keeps a sandboxed command from writing them on macOS, and on
Linux where commands have a namespace of their own (above); this holds on every box, for a
repository written by anything.

- Every git the box runs in a repository gets `-c core.fsmonitor=false -c core.pager=cat -c
  log.showSignature=false`, and its diffs (`diff`, `log`, `show`, `stash show`) `--no-ext-diff`.
  (An empty `diff.external` would break them, so it isn't set.) On a Mac, `-c core.fsmonitor=true`
  follows when the last `core.fsmonitor` any settings give is a yes (git's own watcher, which runs
  no program they name; never when they name one), for all but the commands that only read names
  and objects: a big repository's reads stay quick. Not on Linux, whose git has no watcher of its
  own (and before 2.36 runs a program named `true`). git starts its watcher (`git
  fsmonitor--daemon`) for the repository then, and it runs on as it would for your terminal.
- What the box does by itself (Changes' reads, Undo's snapshots, branch backups and taking one
  back, reviews' scopes, voice and artifacts' reads of what a turn changed, naming a worktree's
  branch, a branch menu's list, whether anything isn't committed, a folder's files) also gets `-c safe.bareRepository=explicit -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null -c
  commit.gpgSign=false -c tag.gpgSign=false -c credential.helper=`. Unless the command only reads
  names and objects, the box first reads, with `git config --show-scope --get-regexp`, the hooks
  any settings name (`hook.<name>.command`, which git 2.54 runs) and the filters and diff
  converters the repository's own settings name (the `local` and `worktree` scopes and what they
  include; `~/.gitconfig`'s and the system's are yours), and switches them off: a hook by
  `hook.<name>.enabled=false`, a filter's `clean`, `smudge` and `process` emptied and `required`
  false, and `--no-textconv` on a diff, `blame` or `grep` when one names a converter. git-lfs's and
  git-crypt's stay on when the program they name is the one PATH finds, or Changes would show every
  file they keep as changed. A command that can't be told not to convert (`cat-file --textconv`,
  `format-patch`, `range-diff`) isn't run, nor any where a name can't be written after `-c` (an
  `=` in it), or the read fails; Changes then says the repository names a program it won't run.
  git before 2.26 can't say the scope, so every filter or converter counts as the repository's
  there.
- What you ask git for yourself (Stage, Commit, Push, Pull and the rest in Changes, switching
  branches, a worktree made, switched, removed with what wasn't committed in it, or brought back, a project cloned) gets only
  the first set: the repository's hooks, filters and sign-ins run as in your terminal, so husky,
  LFS and git-crypt work, and what's kept of a removed worktree is stored as your `git add` would.
- Neither runs (but what only reads names and objects, which starts nothing) where the repository's
  `commondir` leads git anywhere but where it should (#429), or where git finds a bare repository
  by sitting in a folder that has a `.git` of its own (what its own files make of it once that
  `.git` is broken: `HEAD`, `objects`, `refs` and settings beside it; not by
  `safe.bareRepository`, which would reach your hooks' own git too). Where it should is: none, or the repository's own folder
  (`./`, as the sandbox leaves it on Linux), or, in a linked worktree's own folder
  (`.git/worktrees/<name>`), the repository it's one of. One leading elsewhere would have git read
  another repository's settings and run its hooks; Changes then says so, as for a program it won't
  run. (git is asked where the repository is, `rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`, and the file read only
  as a small regular one.)
- The engine's own git (its `vcs` routes and the session's diff) has fsmonitor off and no external
  diff by itself, and keeps its snapshots outside the repository; a filter or converter the repository
  names still runs in its status and diffs. Submodules' own settings aren't read: the
  settings above reach their git too, but not their filters' names.

### Paired phones

The section title and `kuvo/phones` routes retain their wire names. The shared
device grants are current for paired desktops. Phone invitations and APNs
behavior are installed-client compatibility.

The main keeps the setup's device grants. Paired desktops and installed phone clients use the same grant shape.
Each grant identifies the device's public key and pairing ID. Layout 11 removes the old voucher
fields from local device records while preserving keys, pairing IDs and removals. Signed
records from earlier versions remain readable. A standalone or legacy box can still read
pairings from before accepted membership.

- `GET kuvo/phones` returns `{phones: [{key, name, added, pairing, kind, you}]}`.
  `added` is seconds since 1970. `kind` is `phone` or `desktop` for display.
- `POST kuvo/phones/pair` issues a one-use invitation from the primary. The token is valid for
  ten minutes and, for an invitation from a paired device, only while that pairing remains
  current. A member answers with the primary's key. `DELETE kuvo/phones/pair?token=<token>`
  ends that invitation.
- `POST kuvo/devices/pair` with `{key, name, kind: "desktop"}` is the authenticated local
  desktop bootstrap. Members forward it to the primary over peer mail. A repeated request
  for the same key returns its existing pairing ID. A revoked key needs a new invitation.
  Both pairing routes share the device list and its capacity.
- `POST kuvo/phones/remove` with `{phones: [{key, pairing?}]}` removes the named grants.
  An omitted ID resolves to the current pairing. An explicit older ID cannot revoke a newer
  pairing. Any paired device or authenticated local desktop can ask through any member.
  The member forwards the actor's pairing to the primary, which rechecks it before saving.
  The change uses the membership and access receipt in checkpointed setups. A committed
  revocation closes the affected sessions and travels with accepted membership to returning
  members.

A machine keeps itself running: its keeper (`bin/kuvo-start keep`, `run/box.pid`) starts its
engine again when it ends, unless it was stopped on purpose (`run/stopped`), and keeps the bridge
running while it has something to answer: a phone paired, a pairing waiting, peers, or a vault,
which only the bridge holds (`run/link.needed`, which the bridge writes). The bridge stays up while the engine is down, and
starts the keeper when it isn't running. A Mac quitting or disconnecting leaves all of it running.

**Kept for clients** (`box.serve`, #333 piece 3). While a client wants the box's own server here
(`run/serve.needed`: `POST kuvo/box/serve {needed: true}`, from Kuvo Code itself (`403` from a
phone), which starts the
keeper too if it isn't running; `{needed: false}` lets it go), the keeper keeps `kuvo-link.js serve
--kept` running, as it keeps the link, starting it again within a round (15 s) when it ends. It
answers clients' routes as `serve` does, streams included, at `127.0.0.1`, with a password of its
own, where `run/serve.json` says (`{pid, port, password, kept: true}`, `0600`); Kuvo Code on its
computer (the app attached to this box in place) says so with `x-kuvo-from: mac` (`box.serve.mac`),
and is taken as `box route` takes it: what only Kuvo Code asks, it may, and what only its own Macs'
apps do (its link) it's refused, as there; on a Mac its port
is refused to agents' commands in the sandbox, as the box's other servers are, from the sandbox's
next look (ten seconds at most). It does nothing else: what the
box does in the background stays with its link and its keeper. It goes once `run/serve.needed` is
gone (it looks every 30 s) or another took its place, after an update (the keeper starts the new
one), and with `kuvo-start off`, which takes `run/serve.needed` away too (and stops only a server
its record says it keeps, `kept`). One at a time: one
started while another runs leaves. `GET kuvo/box/serve` answers `{needed, serving}`. Not on a Mac's
own box (`409`): its server is Kuvo Code's to run.

**Uninstalling** (`box.uninstall`, #333 piece 3). Removing Kuvo Code from a computer is the box's
own command, which the app or a Terminal line runs: `kuvo-link.js uninstall`. Before stopping,
a member asks the primary to revoke the local desktop's device key. The command removes the desktop
identity file and, on the real Mac's own box, asks the Keychain to delete the released app's item.
An unconfirmed revocation or failed identity deletion is reported as incomplete.
On the primary, the live box signs and publishes the desktop removal before shutting down.
Each peer acknowledges that it installed the signed list. If any acknowledgement is missing,
uninstall reports that spreading could not be confirmed.
When another computer uninstalls over SSH, the controller revokes access after a successful
probe and before sending the destructive command. If the reply is lost, the controller keeps
the committed revocation and reports the cleanup as unconfirmed with instructions to finish
it on the target computer. Stopping the wait after revocation keeps the final cleanup outcome.
Local and SSH uninstall run the same repeatable cleanup of the desktop folder, keys and sign-ins.
For a computer also used by another Mac, SSH asks it to leave just this setup and checks that
the command confirmed the departure before reporting it complete.
Nothing of the box
starts again, and nothing of it runs:
- the launch agent that starts it at login on a Mac (`~/Library/LaunchAgents/run.kuvo.code.machine.plist`)
  is let go of (`launchctl bootout gui/<uid>/run.kuvo.code.machine`) and removed, first, so nothing
  starts it as it stops;
- its line in your crontab (by its mark, `# kuvo-code: starts its engine again after a restart`)
  is taken out, the rest kept; a crontab that can't be read is never written over;
- `run/serve.needed` and `run/link.needed` go, it's marked off (`run/off`), and its keeper stops
  everything for good (`kuvo-start off`, run only where its script names this very folder, with
  `HOME` the folder around it, so another home's box is never touched); then whatever of it still
  runs by its records (its keeper, engine, coding agents, link, server and browser, each only while
  its process's command line says it's that one), waiting up to ten seconds for them to end.

Its folder stays, with your sessions and settings: the command says where, for you to remove (or the
app to move to the Trash). The launch agent and the crontab line are touched only for the real
`~/.kuvo-code` (a test's home uses stand-ins it names, `KUVO_TEST_UNINSTALL_TOOLS`, else leaves
both alone). It prints one JSON line: `{result: "uninstalled" | "unfinished", stopped, launchAgent,
crontab, startsAgain, left, message}` (`startsAgain`, what it found but couldn't take away, the
launch agent or the crontab line; `left`, the folders it leaves), says `message` on stderr, and
exits 0 when everything's stopped and nothing would start it again, 1 otherwise (run it again) or
for a folder that isn't a box (neither `bin/kuvo-start` nor `run`, `{result: "refused"}`), 2 for an
argument it doesn't know. `uninstall --check` changes nothing and says what it would stop: `{folder, kind, running,
starts: {launchAgent, crontab, checked}, bots, wakes, phones, computers}` (what runs of it now, by
name; whether its launch agent and crontab line are there, `checked` false where it doesn't look;
how many bots, wake-ups and watches, phones paired, and your other computers it talks to). This
Mac's box in its app's folder refuses both (exit 1, `{result: "refused", message}`): the app's own
keeper runs it, and removing Kuvo Code removes that.

On a member using the legacy save path, a standby-backed device revocation adds `save` to the result. While the revocation
is pending the command exits 1 with `{result: "pending", message, save}` and keeps the local
identity and box running. The member stores the receipt and checks the same operation with the
current primary on retry. A confirmed interruption exits 1 with the interrupted receipt; the
next invocation can request a new revocation.

**A server that hangs while running** (from 0.9.201, on this Mac and on machines alike:
`src/shared/hang.ts`). The coding agents' bridge watches the engine, and the link watches the
coding agents' bridge. Every 30 seconds each asks its server something over a plain connection (any
answer counts, an error too). Only all of this, at every look for ten minutes without a break, counts
as hung: it takes the connection and says nothing within 20 seconds; connections on this computer
work (the watch answers itself); all its threads are asleep (none running, on a disk or paused), it
used under 2% of a CPU since the last look, and nothing it started is running or used over 5% of one;
its command line is that server's; and nothing's stopped, starting or updating it on purpose, nor is
macOS asking you something (`run/stopped`, `run/.launching`, `run/.updating`, `run/.system-asking`). A
look that comes late (the computer slept, was paused, or was starved) starts the count again. A hung
server is told to stop (SIGTERM), then made to ten seconds later (SIGKILL), and whoever keeps it starts
it again as after any crash; what it started goes on, as after any crash. At most three in six hours
(`run/hung-engine.json`, `run/hung-bridge.json`, when each was ended, in milliseconds; one it can't
write or read counts as too many), then it's left for a Restart.

What it can't see: a server spinning at full CPU (from outside, that's long work), or one whose event
loop runs while its work is stuck (it answers). From outside, a call that sleeps for good looks like
one that would still return: one taking over ten minutes (a network folder that stalled) counts as
hung. Nothing watches the link, nor the coding agents' bridge on a machine with nothing for its link to
answer (where it doesn't run), nor the engine while the bridge is down.

## For released Macs

A machine is set up and upgraded by whichever Mac connects, so a box with this bridge meets Macs
that run any released Kuvo Code: 0.5.x, 0.6.x and 0.7.0 to 0.7.2 (whose bridges, 0.4.1 to 0.9.4,
a Mac put on a machine only with the phone link on, which it never was for users), and
0.8.0-beta.1 (bridge 0.9.23, which it puts on every machine, for peers). What a box does for
them, and only for them, is here; the rest of this file is the protocol as it is. Nothing below is
for phones: the phone link has never been on in a release, so no phone needs an earlier shape of
anything.

**What 0.8 keeps of this.** Kuvo Code 0.8 takes the place of every one of those Macs' apps, straight
from 0.7 (or the beta), and draws the compatibility each box reports ("The update gate"),
so nothing is kept for a client meeting an older box. The other way round still happens, on a
machine:
- A machine set up by 0.5 to 0.7.2 has no bridge and can't update itself; it gets this box when the
  first Mac with 0.8 connects. Another of your Macs still on 0.7 may connect to it after that.
- A machine set up by 0.8.0-beta.1 has a bridge that updates itself from the newest release, so
  it may carry this box before its Mac has taken 0.8.

So what's kept is of these kinds, and only these (`protocol/compat-kinds.txt` names each item's;
one not named there is of the second):
- **What keeps the box's work, files and peers right while such a Mac still connects** (its files
  put over the box's, its Stop, its visits holding updates back, its list of peers). It goes on the
  user's word, once no Mac from before 0.8 connects.
- **What an earlier version left** on a machine or on this Mac, taken in or cleaned up once. On a
  machine the box does it as it starts or as a Mac connects; on this Mac it's the box's move into
  its own home that carries it ("Moving this Mac's box", The whole move, #713).
- **Three that are neither, not decided yet** (#717's next part): messages a client writes the
  blocks of itself, which no released client sends through a box but the box's own tests still do;
  plan limits' own numbers for a client from before `rows`; and a bot's job written to its
  `bot.json` too. They protect nothing a user keeps.

What only gave such a Mac its own buttons against a newer box is gone: its Update button for an
agent's program (`POST …/integration/<provider>/update` is no route now, and the button says it
couldn't), and the branch prefix it sent with a worktree (the computer's own names the branch).
A marker in the code ends with what its item's kind says, but in the files whose bytes are the
box's release (the keeper's shell, the browser's keeper), where it keeps the date it had. The
dates below ("three months after 0.8.0", "once 0.8.0 is out") hold only until the item moves or goes as above.

**Session lists.** A released Mac doesn't read `kuvo/sessions/list`: it works its lists out from
the engine's `api/session` as it did, which the box answers as before; nothing here changes for it.
A Kuvo Code from #668 on reads only the box's list, and brings an older box up to date before using
it ("Session lists").

**Kuvo Code 0.5 to 0.7.2.** It can go once 0.8.0 has been out three months and no Mac with 0.7 or
before connects (the box notes one: `run/attached`).
- **Its files**: such a Mac doesn't know box versions, and puts its own engine, bridge, helpers,
  agents bridge and keeper over the box's as it connects, touching `run/attached`. A newer
  `run/attached` starts a repair from the release the box runs ("Updates", Repaired from the
  release it runs), which puts each of its files back where it differs. Until a box has once found
  its files sound or repaired from a release, it keeps copies of its tools (`bin/.own`, which each
  update refreshes while it's there), and its keeper puts each back where it differs once
  `run/attached` is newer than `bin/box-version`, but not while a Mac installs
  (`run/mac-installing`, an hour at most) or the box updates itself. Marking a box, a Mac puts its
  `kuvo-npx` there only with its own engine version there, which it runs. It goes on the user's
  word, once no Mac from before 1.0 connects.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 files -->
- **Messages it writes itself**: such a Mac, and every Mac and phone from before `messages.send`,
  writes a message's blocks itself and sends its text (`api/session/<id>/prompt`, `queue/add` with
  `text`): the box still tells who a phone's names with "&", adds the phone's block and the files'
  note for files it carries, and keeps the parts where there's more to them than the text ("A
  message's parts").
  <!-- compat: 0.7 own-envelope -->
- **Its keeper**: such a Mac's `kuvo-start` only starts the engine after a restart, and its
  `kuvo-launch` knows neither Stop nor the box's settings. The keeper keeps a copy of both
  (`bin/.kuvo-start-keeper`, `bin/.kuvo-launch-keeper`), runs its starts from them, and puts them
  back whenever the `kuvo-start` there has no `keep)` case (checked each round), leaving
  `.kuvo-boot` as that Mac wrote it. The bridge starts the keeper from the copy then too. The
  watchdog such a Mac's start brings, which stops its engine once that Mac's mark (`run/attached`)
  is a day old, isn't killed (nothing is by a pattern, and it noted no pid): the keeper takes a mark
  23 hours old away, keeping its moment in `run/older-mac` when it came after the box was last
  marked, so the watchdog never stops the engine, and it ends by itself once its engine isn't the
  one in `run/engine.json`. On a machine without the keeper's script,
  a Mac starts the agents bridge and the engine as that Mac did.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 keeper -->
- **Its browser's keeper**: such a Mac's `kuvo-browser.js` knows its keeper's version as a number
  it compares, and replaces one whose `keeper` is lower. The box's says `keeper: 51` in its
  `Kuvo.hello` (beside its `build`), above every such number, so those never replace it.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 keeper-number -->
- **Its browser's pages kept across a stop**: a keeper from before kept the pages open as it
  stopped as addresses alone (`run/pages.json`, `["<url>"]`); the box's reads those too, opening
  each as nobody's ("The browser's data").
  <!-- compat: 0.7 pages-addresses -->
- **Its engine**: such a Mac has Stop, which leaves `run/stopped` and the engine down until
  `POST kuvo/engine/start` (`kuvo/info` says `stopped`; Settings › Machines offers Start). It
  doesn't know a stopped engine, so it starts one over `run/stopped`; running, it isn't stopped
  any longer: the keeper takes `run/stopped` away, under the start lock. An engine without
  `notes.box` is such a Mac's, with that Mac's settings (and perhaps without the agents bridge):
  a Mac that marks boxes starts it over once nothing runs, so the box's settings apply again.
  Until then a Mac reading its group chats takes a 404 from that agents bridge as none.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 engine-stop -->
- **Its visits**: a Mac marking the box after an older visit can keep its time in
  `run/older-mac`. The box can detect files put back by an older Mac and record the drift.
  Neither launcher records nor an anonymous visit can hold the fleet’s updates. The keeper
  still takes away the old watchdog’s mark before the watchdog stops the engine.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 visits -->
- **Its settings**: its start leaves its settings in the global file and `keys/settings.json`,
  with keys in `keys/`. The first Mac with boxes makes them the box's own (`kuvo-link.js box
  adopt`): those go in `box`, key paths as the box names them, what they were made from kept in
  `box/adopted-from`, and the launch's settings lines taken out, so no start writes them back.
  Until then a machine's bridge answers `kuvo/config`, `kuvo/keys`, `kuvo/mcp/catalog` and
  `kuvo/integrations` with `409 {"message"}`.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 settings -->
- **Leaving the engine running**: such a Mac stops a machine's engine as it quits unless
  something waits there (a wake-up, a group chat at work), or, from 0.7.0, a phone used the
  machine in the last week (`run/link.seen`, which the bridge touches as a phone asks).
  <!-- compat: 0.7 leave-running -->
- **Its bots' descriptions**: it reads a machine's bots from their `bot.json`, and a bot's job from
  its `job` there, so the box writes a job's line there too, beside its record (`job.json`).
  <!-- compat: 0.7 bot-json-job -->
- **Its worktrees**: it kept a machine's worktrees itself. A Mac that has such records gives them
  to the machine with `POST kuvo/worktrees/record`, those it removed too (`removed`), so the box's
  session lists file their sessions as that Mac did.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 worktrees -->
- **Its kit and your time zone**: it gave each box a kit (`bots/kit.json`: your time zone and its
  rules, the machine's projects, the personalities you made), put your zone above a machine's
  conversations' wake-ups (`wakes/timezone`) and started its engine with `KUVO_TZ`. A box carries
  them into its own facts ("Your time zone"; `kuvo/bots`, what a box makes its bots with), and goes
  by `KUVO_TZ` while it has no zone of its own.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 bot-kit -->
- **Its agents bridge** installed the agents' programs in `~/.kuvo-code/agents/runtime` on a
  machine, carried the Mac's sign-ins over (`<file>.from-mac`), and kept its downloads in its cache
  (`cache/install`): the agents bridge takes those away as it starts.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 agents-runtime -->
- **Updates**: the newest release on GitHub (0.7.2) has no `boxes.json`, which a box takes as
  "current", not a failure, until a release that has one is the newest.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 no-boxes-json -->
- **Plan limits from before `rows`** (#210): a client from before them (a released Mac, a phone)
  reads each box's own `accounts` and merges them itself. A box that let a peer's reading stand
  for a read of an account lists it there with that reading's numbers (`accounts`, "Plan limits"),
  so such a client doesn't show it stale or empty.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 limits-own-numbers -->
- **Updating an agent's program**: such a Mac asks `POST kuvo/agents/api/integration/<provider>/update`
  and waits for its answer, which no box gives now (`404`): its Update button for an agent's
  program says it couldn't, until that Mac updates. (The other way round, a client of this version
  meets no box from before `kuvo/updates`: "The update gate". Coding agents still running a build
  from before it, as they move to the new one, answer `404`, which a client says as "haven't moved
  to this version yet", asking no program the old way.)

**This Mac's own group chats, from 0.5 to 0.8.0-beta.1.** Those Macs ran their group chats in the
app (`groups.json`, each chat's messages in `groups/<id>.json`). A Mac with this version moves
them into its coding agents' bridge at launch, before the bridge starts (`GroupMigration`), and
can be cut short and run again: each chat's messages first, its record (`groups/<id>/group.json`,
written whole and renamed) last, a chat with a record left as it is, one moving as the app last
quit `held` for the move's recovery. A seat it made on a machine for a bot there (one the machine
doesn't know as a seat, with no `kuvo.seat` metadata) is taken out of the chat, so the bot's next
turn makes one there, and listed in `groups/orphan-seats.json` (by machine), which the app keeps out
of the lists and deletes on that machine's engine once it connects. What a bot whose machine was
away was still to be told goes to `groups/pending-memory.json` (the bridge tells it once that bot
is known there); every bot here gets `bot.json` and `session` in its folder. Once every chat is
there, the old files are copied to `Backups/groups-<version>-<the list's hash>` and left where they
are, and what was taken is noted (`groups/imported.json`: the list's hash and every chat's ID); one
that couldn't move is tried again at the next launch. A `groups.json` an older version writes later
(after going back to it, where its chats are as it left them) is taken in by each chat's ID, and
a chat deleted since it was taken stays deleted. It can go three months after 0.8.0 ships.
<!-- compat: 0.7 mac-group-chats -->

**What else an earlier Kuvo Code left on this Mac.** A Mac with this version takes it in once. It
can go three months after 0.8.0 ships.
- **The retired Mac app was the only sender of these.** Each is something an earlier version kept
  on this Mac, which that app read as it opened and gave to this Mac's box, or to a machine's.
  Nothing else sends them, so the box's move carries each itself, into its own files ("Moving this
  Mac's box", What the move carries), or says that it doesn't (`kuvo/box/rehome`'s `dropped`):
  - Its own group chats (`groups.json`, `groups/<id>.json`): written into the coding agents'
    bridge's folder, with what a bot was still to be told in `groups/pending-memory.json` ("This
    Mac's own group chats", above).
  - Your personalities (`personalities.json`, `personalities-removed.json` in the app's folder):
    met with the box's library.
  - Your projects, your machines, the worktrees it kept and those it removed, Settings › Git, Ask
    First, and what it had added to the engine's settings once (all in its preferences): into the
    box's lists and settings.
  - Edits to machines' bots it kept while they were away (`botEditsWaiting` in its preferences, and
    `botEditOutbox`, which builds after 0.8.0-beta.1 kept): not carried, and said (a held edit is
    sealed with the link's secret, which no file can be written with).
  - Machines' bots' keys of their own, which it kept in your Keychain: gone as the box starts
    (bots have no keys of their own now: "Bots have no keys of their own").
  - Its letters and the messages kept for a machine that was away: into the box's outbox, for
    machines whose boxes talk to others; the rest said.
  - The sign-ins it saved (Keychain internet passwords), and the sites an agent may sign in to
    for you with their accounts (`passwords.agentSignIn`, `passwords.agentSignInAccounts`): into
    the vault once the box's server answers ("Moving this Mac's box", Saved sign-ins).
  - Keep This Mac Awake, off (its preferences): the box's own setting.
- **Not carried, by choice**: what it kept of machines' group chats as it last saw them
  (`machine-groups.json` and `machine-groups/<id>.json`, from 0.7.0; a copy of what each machine
  keeps, lost only for a machine that's gone for good); what it learned of GitHub Copilot's Claude
  models (`copilotClaudeModels`), which each box learns itself ("Settings per box"); and the moves
  it ran itself (`movesUnderWay`), whose `moving` hold in a folder a box lifts as it starts
  (`kuvo/moves`): one left at `switched` is said.
- The letters it sent its agents' way and those it had delivered (`agent-letters.json`,
  `agent-letters-seen.json`, 0.8.0-beta.1), and the messages it kept for a machine that was away
  (`agent-messages.json`), handed to the box's outbox (`kuvo/link/letters/take`).
  <!-- compat: beta.1 mac-letters -->
- On a machine: letters its tools or link left in `run/outbox` for a Mac to collect over SSH,
  sent by the link as its own. <!-- compat: beta.1 outbox -->
- On a machine: `run/mac-agents.json`, the agents a Mac wrote there over SSH, no longer read, and
  removed. <!-- compat: beta.1 mac-agents -->
- Settings › Git (`git.branchPrefix`, `git.commitInstructions`, `git.pullRequestInstructions` in its
  preferences), which each computer keeps its own now (`kuvo/config`, "Changes"): given to each box
  once (`POST kuvo/git/settings/move {branchPrefix?, commitInstructions?, pullRequestInstructions?}`
  → `{"moved"}`, `409 {"message"}` while a machine's settings aren't its own yet, `500
  {"message"}` when they couldn't be written), which keeps
  each where it has none of its own yet, the first time a Mac offers any (a branch prefix, or
  instructions that aren't empty: `box/git.json`'s `moved`), so a later one, or one after you
  cleared it there, changes nothing; `moved` says whether it took any now. The Mac offers them as
  each box starts or connects, and keeps them in its preferences for a computer you add later.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 mac-git-settings -->
- The branch prefix a box kept before in `box/git.json` (`branchPrefix`, the one a client last
  made a worktree with): taken into its settings' `branch_prefix` once, where they have none, as a
  machine's box starts or its settings become its own (`box adopt`), or after a Mac's Settings › Git
  is moved there (the Mac's own prefix first), then removed from `box/git.json`. <!-- compat: 0.7 box-branch-prefix -->
- `kuvo-keys` ("This Mac's box: its helper"): the Keychain items a released Kuvo Code made for
  this Mac's box (its link's keys, its integrations' keys, its vault) and the sign-ins it kept
  before the vault, handed to the box's helper as the box moves into its own home. Unlike the
  rest here it goes on the user's word, never on a date: a Mac updating late would otherwise lose
  its keys. <!-- compat: 0.7 kuvo-keys -->
- The move the box runs whole itself ("Moving this Mac's box", The whole move): an earlier Kuvo
  Code's sessions and settings (0.5 to 0.7.2 and 0.8.0-beta.1, which had no box, and a keeper
  build's box) moved into this Mac's box by the box, its engine's database brought up to date,
  what that app kept in its own files and preferences brought into the box's, and its saved
  sign-ins taken into the vault. Like `kuvo-keys`, it goes on the user's word, never on a date.
  <!-- compat: 0.7 move -->
- A box still in the folder of the retired Mac app (before 1.0), whose app ran the coding agents'
  bridge and wrote why it gave up (`run/agents-stopped`, `{why, retrying}`): while that bridge is
  down, the box says "This Mac's coding agents aren't running." with that why, and that Restart on
  the Mac starts them unless they're tried again by themselves; with none written, they're
  restarting, and a request doesn't wait for them ("The coding agents' state"). It goes on the
  user's word, once no Mac runs the retired app. <!-- compat: 0.7 app-agents-stopped -->

**Kuvo Code 0.8.0-beta.1.** It can go once 0.8.0 is out (a beta copy is offered the release).
- It signs no documents: its setup and mail give its peers as a list (`peers`, with `peersAt` or
  the mail's `at`), without `macSign`. A box keeps that Mac's newest by its own `at` (`legacy` in
  link.json, compared only with that Mac's earlier ones) and counts it as that Mac's peers
  document, but never passes it on, nor gives that Mac documents. Once that Mac gives a signing key
  in setup, its documents take the list's place. Lists a 0.9.23 bridge passed on (`vouched`) and
  the personalities it sent (`{"personalities"}`) count for nothing.
  <!-- compat: beta.1 peers-list -->
- It meets a machine's personalities over SSH every minute (`kuvo-link.js box personalities`,
  the library in, the met library out), which still works; the bridge tells your other computers
  what changed. It still lets the newest change win over a removal, so a personality removed
  elsewhere that it changes afterwards stays on that Mac alone, until it updates.
- It notes it's connected in `run/connected/<its id>` each minute: the bridge clears `run/connected`
  (and `run/present`, which a 0.7 Mac with the phone link on wrote) as it starts. Nothing reads
  them.
  <!-- compat: beta.1 connected -->
- It lets go of a machine's bots deleted there by `~/.kuvo-code/bots/deleted.json`, which the box
  keeps ("kuvo/bots").
  <!-- compat: beta.1 deleted-bots -->
- It reads and changes a machine's settings with `kuvo-link.js box read` and `box change` over SSH,
  and sets its keys with `box key` ("Settings per box"), which `box route` does for later Macs.
  Everything its Settings change on a machine goes this way, so they stay while it connects.
  <!-- compat: beta.1 box-read-change -->
- It runs moves itself, over SSH, and its peers document's `moved` says where each conversation it
  moves lives now. A box takes that word under its own boxes' ("Peers", `moved`).
  <!-- compat: beta.1 mac-moves -->
- It asks a machine to rename a worktree's branch (`POST kuvo/worktrees/rename`, through `box
  route`), which the box names itself now: it's refused, and that Mac reads the machine's records
  again.
- It sends its own branch prefix with each worktree (`POST kuvo/worktrees {"project",
  "branchPrefix"}`): it counts for nothing, and the computer's own names the branch (Settings ›
  Git there, `kuvo/` with none). (A box from before kept the last one given in `box/git.json` for a
  client that sent none: no longer read.)
- Its keeper's box, still running after an update until the work under way ends, and a machine's
  box from before #660, are held by the update gate ("The update gate"): no client of this version
  runs Kuvo Code's own tools, git or a file walk itself for them any more.

### Antigravity conversation history

Antigravity's machine-local history is read from each Kuvo Code agent's own profile only.
SQLite databases are opened read-only; protobuf generation metadata is bounded to 1 MiB per blob.
Oversized generation records are skipped; oversized step metadata is ignored, as in Swift.
Tokens are priced with the shared catalogs and kept in UTC quarter-hour slots, then summed
across your own computers like Claude's history. Each database's WAL and file fingerprint reuse
unchanged reads; idle databases outside the history window aren't read. Removed databases leave
the total. A database written to while it's read counts what that read saw, and is read again next
round. An unreadable database retains its previous result while other databases advance; one with
no previous result that can't be read, or a conversations folder that can't be listed, is logged
and left out, as UsageKit's scanner does, and is retried next round. It never holds up the round
for other services' logs.
A new account with no conversations is empty. Places are hashed with the machine ID.
The apps read Antigravity only from the box, with no older-box fallback (#679 updates boxes first).


**A box from before beta.31** (whose code judges no update by the one health rule, leaves nothing
for new code, and may keep the engine's data for a rollback: "Updates") takes this release once,
by its own updater or by the installer an app carries. What this release does for it, and only for
it, goes once no box is from before beta.31:
- While an update is on trial, the keeper ends a `serve`, `serve --kept` or `run` started before
  `bin/kuvo-link.js` was written, no update being under way, for what keeps it to start the new
  one. <!-- compat: beta.30 old-code -->
- `kuvo-start rollback` moves a rollback's data (`updates/rollback/data`) to `updates/backups`
  before it runs that rollback's `restore.sh`, which would put it back. <!-- compat: beta.30 rollback-data -->
- `kuvo-link.js update --installer` (with `installerSteps` and `untilFree`), which `kuvo-install
  update` runs for a box from before `computers.update.here`. <!-- compat: beta.30 installer -->
- An update stops an engine its record names that an older keeper's stop left running, by that
  record, once its command line says it's this box's engine. <!-- compat: beta.30 engine-record -->
- A Kuvo Helper from before beta.31, which doesn't leave for a new build of itself, is handed over
  once by its `serve` ("This Mac's box: its helper", A helper from before beta.31). <!-- compat: beta.30 helper-handover -->

**Layout 4 setups**: older standby proposals carry the full projection, leadership certificates
may carry devices alongside the roster, and a standby can be selected before setup checkpoints
exist. <!-- compat: layout.4 setup -->

## The browser's live view

Feature `browser.view`. The resident box's keeper owns Chrome and the page
state on macOS and Linux. GPUI uses the local or paired-relay browser socket.
Released Swift Mac clients retain their raw-CDP stream. An older box without the
view can refuse the route.

Open `GET kuvo/browser/view` as a socket: locally, a WebSocket on `serve` with its
`Authorization: Basic <base64(opencode:password)>` header; through the relay, a WebSocket
request in an authenticated, paired client's Noise session. Peers cannot open sockets.
The upgrade checks the exact canonical path, method and password itself; the ordinary HTTP
handler never sees upgrades. A GET without upgrading returns 426 with `{message}`.
Opening the view starts the browser on demand. The socket can upgrade while Chrome starts
or is being installed. Wait for the keeper's `Kuvo.hello` and page facts before sending view
commands. If startup fails, the box sends `Kuvo.error` with `{kind, message}` and ends the socket.
Opening a new view asks the box to start the browser again.

Text messages are newline-delimited JSON `{id?, method, params?}`. A request with an id
gets `{id, result}` or `{id, error: {message}}`. The socket accepts only the view commands
below, never raw CDP or keeper administration. SSH `kuvo-browser.js connect` keeps its
newline JSON stream, including raw CDP compatibility.

| Direction | Method | Parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| box → client | `Kuvo.pages` | `{active, pages: [{targetId,url,title,opener,session,loading,canGoBack,canGoForward,working,held,dialog?}]}` |
| box → client | `Kuvo.viewport` | `{targetId,width,height,scale,zoom?,by: "agent" \| "viewer"}` |
| box → client | `Kuvo.frame` | `{targetId,frameId,width,height,scrollX,scrollY}`, with JPEG bytes (below) |
| client → box | `Kuvo.pages` | `{}`: request current page facts |
| client → box | `Kuvo.view` | `{targetId: string \| null,width,height,scale?,zoom?,quality?,maxFps?}`; null stops pictures |
| client → box | `Kuvo.frameAck` | `{frameId}`, only after the client consumed the picture |
| client → box | `Kuvo.frameDropped` | `{frameId,reason}`, a skipped picture: oversize, budget, unsent or backpressure |
| client → box | `Kuvo.go` | `{targetId,input? ,back?,forward?,reload?,stop?}`; one action |
| client → box | `Kuvo.input` | `{targetId,kind,...}`; kind mouse, wheel, key, text or compose |
| client → box | `Kuvo.upload` | `{targetId,files:[{name,data}]}`; data is base64, total decoded size ≤50 MiB |
| box → client | `Kuvo.fileChooser` | `{targetId,mode}`, after Chrome opens a file chooser |
| box → client | `Kuvo.external` | `{targetId,url}`, a typed address using another app's scheme |
| client → box | `Kuvo.hold` | existing `{targetId,on,mac?}` takeover vocabulary |
| client → box | `Kuvo.claim` | existing `{targetId,session}` conversation ownership vocabulary |
| box → client | `Kuvo.dialog` | `{targetId,type,message,defaultPrompt?,url?,...}`, Chrome's dialog facts |
| client → box | `Kuvo.dialogAnswer` | `{targetId,accept,promptText?}`, boolean accept and optional text |
| box → client | `Kuvo.viewQuality` | `{targetId,quality,scale,reason:"oversize" \| "recovery"}`, reduced picture settings |
| box → client | `Kuvo.status` | `{working,tool?,pages:[targetId],workers:[{targetId,session}]}`: the pages agents are at work in, as it changes |
| box → client | `Kuvo.pointer` | `{targetId,action,rect}`: where an agent is about to act in a page, for the pointer drawn over it |
| box → client | `Kuvo.cursor` | `{targetId,...}`: kept as each page's latest, like the pointer; no keeper sends it yet |

The keeper also forwards its existing hello, ask, download, status and pointer facts. Through the
relay, `Kuvo.pages`, `Kuvo.status`, `Kuvo.viewport`, `Kuvo.pointer` and `Kuvo.cursor` are state: a newer
one for the same page replaces one not yet sent.
Pages are announced when Chrome reports creation, navigation, title, loading or destruction,
and when agent status changes, only if the facts changed. The address comes from these facts even when an agent navigates.
A tab's name is its nonempty title, else its address's host without `www.`, else “New Tab”.

Input fields follow CDP's Input parameters: mouse has type, x, y, button and clickCount;
wheel has x, y, deltaX and deltaY; key has type, key and code; text has text;
compose has text, selectionStart, selectionEnd and optional replacement offsets.
Modifiers may be CDP's bitmask or an array of `alt/control/meta/shift`.
The keeper maps Control shortcuts to Command when Chrome runs on macOS.
Clients must ask the user before opening an external app URL. Page-initiated external
URLs go only to viewers of that page; a typed URL goes only to its requesting client.
Coordinates are CSS page viewport coordinates, calculated by the client from the displayed
frame's scale and letterbox. Files are written privately under `browser/tmp/upload-*`,
given only to Chrome's current chooser and retained for a later form submission. They are
removed when that page navigates or closes, or when Chrome next starts.

While an agent's status says it works in a page, a viewer cannot change that page's size.
Otherwise the latest view or input sets it. Raw clients' device metrics, page scale and
screencast calls go through that same rule. Raw agents' requested size is retained and restored
when work resumes (the native default is 1280×800 at DPR 2). When the agent stops, the
most recently shown or used viewer regains its requested size after five seconds of agent
idle, without needing input. A new working status cancels that pending restoration; individual
tool boundaries do not repeatedly reflow the watched page. If the latest viewer leaves,
restoration selects the remaining viewer. A raw viewer that never requested metrics does
not claim a default page layout. Geometry changes to a page are ordered, including an
idle restoration already in flight when another tool starts.

A raw screencast's maxima limit its picture, without changing its CSS
viewport or DPR; raw dimensions are left to Chrome rather than the new view's desktop
limits. Non-size Emulation calls pass through. Detaching a raw session stops its captures.
New view sockets do not register as clients able to answer browser asks.
The keeper captures once per target, dimensions, scale and quality class, with one capture
in progress per class, and scales the picture without changing the working page's layout.
Capture scale compensates for the source DPR and never exceeds the source device pixels.
Identical pictures are not resent, and unchanged
classes back off to a two-second poll. Raw input, page commands, navigation and page
events wake only the affected page without bypassing the class's FPS floor. Captures wait
for pending source metrics,
and stale captures from before a source-size change are discarded. Reopening a still view
gets a first picture even if its JPEG is unchanged.

On the new sockets a binary message is: four bytes of big-endian JSON header length,
that many UTF-8 bytes of `{method:"Kuvo.frame",params:{...}}`, then the JPEG.
SSH retains base64 `params.data`. Binary avoids base64's expansion; relay frames larger
than 60,000 bytes are dropped, never split. The next picture's scale halves first, down to
1x; quality then steps down by ten, to q40 before scale falls below 1x.
If needed, scale steps down further, to 0.125. Only that viewer receives Kuvo.viewQuality.
After a displayed JPEG under 20,000 bytes and two seconds without a drop, quality/scale move
gradually back toward the viewer's requested settings; a later larger frame cancels pending
recovery. Adaptation never changes page layout.
Phone-sized views (width ≤600 CSS pixels)
start at scale 1 and quality at most 50. New Kuvo views are capped at 15 fps. Legacy raw
streams keep a 60 fps ceiling and their requested quality; narrow raw views are not phone-classed.
At most two unacknowledged frames are allowed per viewer. Obsolete pictures are dropped,
never queued for a slow viewer. The relay counts messages (500/s for its whole connection);
the live view shares a ceiling of about 100 messages/s across its relay viewers.
Other box traffic retains the rest of that connection's budget. A nonzero host.unsent()
skips pictures as a backstop. Every transport skip returns Kuvo.frameDropped, never a
display acknowledgement. Drops clear that viewer's image digest and wake capture so a
still picture can be retried when pressure clears. Non-oversize drops back off per viewer
from 100 ms, doubling to two seconds; a real display acknowledgement resets that history.
Reply bursts pause keeper reads rather than close a healthy viewer; a slow serve client skips and credits pictures but retains text. A serve connection
with more than 4 MiB queued for text is closed rather than allowing unbounded buffering.
Awaited keeper calls expire after ten seconds. Frame credits and dialog answers bypass
a client's ordered command queue, so they can release a click blocked by a dialog. Stop
also bypasses a pending navigation. Page-scoped errors retain their session id and Chrome's
refusal text; a deadline failure is reported separately as a timeout. New relay sockets
keep the one-message picture bound instead of an automatic multi-message 2x stopped-page
refinement; the legacy local client retains its own sharp-screenshot path.

Examples and box-only socket path cases live in `protocol/vectors/browser-view.json`;
released Swift socket vectors stay unchanged in `protocol/vectors/link.json`. Route answers
are generated from the browser route shapes.

### Insights

The `usage.insights` feature gates Insights. The desktop reads
`GET /kuvo/agents/api/kuvo/insights` on the link, which forwards to
`GET /api/kuvo/insights` on Kuvo's agents bridge. The response is wrapped
in `data`. This index covers Kuvo's own execution, from its engine
databases, saved sessions and isolated agent homes. It keeps up to a
year of per-call metadata, with human messages counted separately.

Query parameters are `period` (7, 30, 90 or 365 calendar days, including
today), `zone` (an IANA time zone), and optional `computer`, `bot`, and
`account` or `provider`. A limits row ID from a ring is an `account`
filter. `GET /insights/sessions` pages the same selection by last activity,
and `GET /insights/sessions/:session` (or `GET /insights?session=…`) pages
one session's calls in chronological order. Both take `offset`, default
0, and return `next` or null. Session rows include `costShare` and
`tokenShare`, each a fraction of the matching total computed in the same
SQLite snapshot, or null when the share is unavailable.
`POST /insights/refresh` starts or joins a
background scan and peer sync and answers 202.

The overview returns filter choices, totals, daily readings, provider
totals, breakdowns by model, agent, day and skill, and coverage. A skill
breakdown can attribute the same call to multiple observed skills.
`state` is `loading`, `empty`, `partial`, `stale` or `ready`. A null token
bucket or cost means it could not be determined. Cost is estimated in USD
at current catalog rates. Token totals without cache reads, processed
tokens with cache reads, and the individual buckets are separate fields.
Cursor's context-only results are partial.

The `usage.insights.summary` feature adds `GET /insights/summary`, the
whole Insights screen as a box makes it. It takes `period` (7, 30 or 90),
`zone`, and at most one of `bot`, `provider`, `account`, `model` (a model
row's `id`), `computer` or `session` to narrow it. Every grouping is made
by the box; a client draws it as it comes:

- `totals`: `cost` (USD at current API rates), `tokens` (every token,
  cache reads included) and `cacheRate` (cached input over all input,
  null where no input was counted). Every row and standout has the same
  three, and `lowCache` where its rate is well under the period's.
- `change`: against the period of the same length just before, `cost`
  and `tokens` as fractions and `cacheRate` as the difference of the two
  rates, each null where it can't be said; `change` is null where
  nothing was recorded then.
- `trend`: each day's `day`, `cost` and `tokens`, oldest first.
- `lists`: ranked by cost, each `{key, name, rows}`: `bots` (a bot's row
  is its own conversations and every session it's over, their subagents
  counted in, with `sessions` it expands to; a session no bot is over is
  a row of its own), then `providers`, `models` (one name per model,
  however its id was written) and `computers`. Narrowed to a bot or a
  session, the first list is `sessions` instead: the bot's, or the
  session and its subagents. A row has `kind` (`bot`, `session`,
  `provider`, `model`, `computer`), the `id` that narrows to it, `name`,
  and where there's more to say `note` ("4 subagents", "No bot", "Own
  chat"), `provider` (whose mark to draw) and a bot's `look`. At most 200
  rows a list.
- `standouts`: at most three sessions, each with one short `reason` and
  its `kind` (`cost`, `cache` or `subagents`).
- `state`: `loading`, `empty` or `ready`.
- `asOf`: where present, this is the box's last summary for the same
  query, read then (ms), answered at once while the box reads it afresh
  (a client asks again shortly). Its last summaries are kept on disk, so
  a box that just started answers at once too. One read in the last 30 s
  is answered as it is, without `asOf`; a `loading` one is never kept.
- `countedAt`: when the box last counted its own usage (ms), absent
  before its first count. Older boxes don't send it.

`refresh=1` on `GET /insights/summary` asks the box to count again first
(after a count already under way, and syncing its peers as
`POST /insights/refresh` does), waiting up to a minute for it, then
answers the summary read afresh, never `asOf`, and keeps it as the last.
An older box ignores it and answers as usual, so a client can send it to
any box.

Each usage record carries the bot over it: a bot's own conversation and
group-chat seat are its, a session it started (`kuvo.by`) is its, a
subagent is its parent's, as far up as is known, and a session started
before its starts were marked is its starter's. `root` names the
top-level conversation a subagent's calls count under, and `botOwn`
says that conversation is the bot's own. Records from an older box lack
them: its subagents count as sessions of their own.

Authenticated peer mail uses `kind: "insights"`. Direct peers resume a
pull from the last SQLite sequence they have applied and take at most
100 usage records in a page. Records contain origin, native identity,
model, session metadata, skill names and observed token counts. Estimates
are calculated by the receiving computer with its own current catalog.

### Marketplace

A box advertises `marketplace` and serves `kuvo/marketplace` to paired Kuvo clients. The box includes an
offline catalog snapshot. `POST kuvo/marketplace/refresh` reads the configured public index and validates
the snapshot before replacing the last good copy. It answers `{refreshed, message?}`. A catalog refresh
leaves previously installed endpoints and skill bytes at the version reviewed by the user.

- **Browse.** `GET kuvo/marketplace[?q=&category=&origin=kuvo|yours]` returns three ordered `areas`.
  Each includes `id`, `title`, `count`, `categories` (title and count), visible `items`, `actions`, empty
  text, and optional filters. It includes the computer choices with their key, name and availability.
  `GET kuvo/marketplace/{apps|agents|skills}/<id>` returns the details and action labels. An app's
  advertised logo route answers PNG. Entries needing Kuvo's hosted OAuth broker are omitted.
- **Apps.** `POST apps/<id>/add` or `POST apps/custom` with `{title,url,id?,summary?,auth?}` under
  `kuvo/marketplace/` enables a Streamable HTTP server across the setup. Custom endpoints use HTTPS
  without inline credentials or query parameters. `auth` is `open`, `token`, or `oauth`. The box
  reports connection state on the computer answering. `POST apps/<id>/connect` takes `{token}`
  for a personal-token server or returns an OAuth flow (202 with `attempt`, `opens` and display words).
  Open `opens` in the browser. A browser on the box can finish on loopback. From another computer,
  submit the complete callback address and original `attempt` to `POST apps/<id>/finish`.
  Follow completion with `GET apps/<id>/status?attempt=…` or cancel with `POST apps/<id>/cancel`
  and `{attempt}`. `POST apps/<id>/disconnect` removes this computer's credentials.
  `DELETE apps/<id>` removes the app from the setup. Each computer needing service authentication
  keeps its own credentials in its vault. Engines and agents receive connection settings and a scoped
  local relay credential, and the relay supplies the service token.
- **Agents.** `GET agents/<id>/options?computer=<key>` reads models and accounts from that computer.
  It includes missing app dependencies and each routine with `enabled: false`.
  `POST agents/<id>/add` takes `{computer,model,request,version,name?,routine?}`, using an offered
  `model` and the same stable URL-safe `request` on retries. It installs required catalog skills
  and creates a bot on the selected computer using the existing bot creation boundary. The result
  is the usual `201 {bot,firstMessage}`. The scheduled routines are created paused unless `routine: true`.
  Required apps must already be connected on that computer. Marketplace bots' workspaces carry the
  selected Marketplace apps and skills, and the box and bridge use that selection when exposing tools.
- **Skills.** `POST skills/preview` takes `{link}`, `{repository,path,ref?}`, or `{folder}` on
  the answering computer. It returns `{preview,skill,files,action}`. Each file has its relative
  `path`, base64 `data` and SHA-256 `sha256`. GitHub sources include `repository`, `path` and
  `commit`. `POST skills/install` with `{preview,was?}` installs the exact bytes reviewed on that
  box. For a catalog skill, `POST skills/<id>/add` takes the available `{version,revision,was?}`.
  `POST skills/create` takes `{name,description,instructions}`. To edit an authored or folder
  skill, use `PATCH skills/<id>` with `{description,instructions,was}`. `DELETE skills/<id>`
  takes `{was}` for a shared skill. `was` is the installed revision from details. To update an
  installed GitHub skill, explicitly ask `POST skills/<id>/update-preview` and install with its
  preview ID and the previous revision. Legacy local skills still use the existing skills routes.
- **Delivery.** Installed app definitions and the reviewed skill bytes are accepted by the setup
  primary and published in signed setup state. The Work Queue peer mail carries requests to the
  primary and bot creation to the selected owner. An offline computer projects the last accepted
  copy and catches up when it sees the newer one. An installation receipt can precede the replica
  on another computer, so the client can reread after a pending change. `problems` on an install
  response gives projection conflicts on the computer that processed it.

All writes live in the box. The bridge uses OpenCode's discovered skill and MCP settings, passes the
skills as a Claude/Grok plugin tree, Codex additional skill paths, a Cursor workspace skill tree,
or a private Antigravity skills directory, and supplies each agent's native MCP connection settings.
